{{Rotten Tomatoes prose|92|3=239|4=''Precious'' is a grim yet ultimately triumphant film about abuse and inner-city life, largely bolstered by exceptional performances from its cast.|ref=y|access-date=April 18, 2026}} [[Metacritic]], which uses a [[Weighted arithmetic mean|weighted average]], assigned the film a score of 78 out of 100, based on 36 critics, indicating "generally favorable" reviews.<ref name="Metacritic">{{cite web |title=''Precious'' |url=https://www.metacritic.com/movie/precious-based-on-the-novel-push-by-sapphire |website=[[Metacritic]] |publisher=[[Fandom (website)#Fandom, Inc.|Fandom, Inc.]] |access-date=April 18, 2026 |archive-url= |archive-date= |url-status=}}</ref>

John Anderson of ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' said "to simply call it harrowing or unsparing doesn't quite cut it," having felt that the film is "courageous and uncompromising, a shaken cocktail of debasement and elation, despair and hope."<ref name="varietyreview">{{cite news |url=https://variety.com/2009/film/reviews/precious-based-on-the-novel-push-by-sapphire-2-1200473264/ |first=John |last=Anderson |title=Push: Based on the Novel by Sapphire |work=Variety |date=January 18, 2009 |access-date=November 16, 2009 |archive-date=June 6, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130606063648/http://variety.com/2009/film/reviews/precious-based-on-the-novel-push-by-sapphire-2-1200473264/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Anderson cited Carey's performance as "pitch perfect" and Patton's role as Ms. Blu Rain as "disarming."<ref name="varietyreview"/>

[[Owen Gleiberman]] of ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]'' praised Carey's performance, describing it as having "an authentically deglammed compassion" and praised the film for capturing "how a lost girl rouses herself from the dead" and for Daniels showing "unflinching courage as a filmmaker by going this deep into the pathologies that may still linger in the closets of some impoverished inner-city lives."<ref name="ewreview" /> Gleiberman described the film as being a movie "that makes you think, 'There but for the grace of God go I.' [...] It's a potent and moving experience, because by the end you feel you've witnessed nothing less than the birth of a soul", and felt that the "final scene of revelation" between Sidibe's and Mo'Nique's characters was strong enough to be able to leave viewers "tearful, shaken, [and] dazed with pity and terror."<ref name="ewreview">{{cite magazine |url=https://ew.com/article/2009/11/19/precious-based-novel-push-sapphire-2/ |date=November 11, 2009 |title=Precious: Based on the Novel "Push" by Sapphire (2009) |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |first=Owen |last= Gleiberman |author-link=Owen Gleiberman |access-date=November 17, 2009 |archive-date=November 9, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091109025519/http://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,20317518,00.html |url-status=live }}</ref> He identified how Daniels uses one of the rich scenes created by Fletcher to position Mo'Nique in a painful confrontation with Sidibe that results in a masterful and thought-provoking performance that delivers the final "push" needed by Sidibe: "The more Precious tries to get away from her mother, the more she's pulled back".<ref name="ewreview" />

[[Roger Ebert]] of the ''[[Chicago Sun-Times]]'' praised Mo'Nique and Sidibe's performances.<ref name="ebertreview"/> Ebert described Mo'Nique's performance as being "frighteningly convincing" and felt that "the film is a tribute to Sidibe's ability to engage our empathy" because she "completely creates the Precious character." He noted that Carey and Patton "are equal with Sidibe in screen impact."<ref name="ebertreview"/> Ebert praised Daniels because, rather than [[Star vehicle|casting the actors for their names]], "he was able to see beneath the surface and trust that they had within the emotional resources to play these women, and he was right."<ref name="ebertreview">{{cite news |last=Ebert |first=Roger |author-link=Roger Ebert |date=November 4, 2009 |title=Precious: Based on the Novel Push by Sapphire |url=https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/precious-based-on-the-novel-push-by-sapphire-2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130513074218/http://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/precious-based-on-the-novel-push-by-sapphire-2009 |archive-date=May 13, 2013 |access-date=November 17, 2009 |work=[[Chicago Sun-Times]]}}</ref> 

Betsy Sharkey, of the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' described the film as being a "rough-cut diamond... [A] rare blend of pure entertainment and dark social commentary, it is a shockingly raw, surprisingly irreverent and absolutely unforgettable story."<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2009-nov-06-et-precious6-story.html |first=Betsy |last=Sharkey |work=Los Angeles Times |date=November 6, 2009 |title='Precious' cuts deep |access-date=November 17, 2009 |archive-date=February 5, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100205103824/http://articles.latimes.com/2009/nov/06/entertainment/et-precious6 |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Claudia Puig]] of ''[[USA Today]]'' said that while there are "melodramatic moments" in the film, the cast gives "remarkable performances" to show audiences the film's "inspiring message."<ref name="usatodayreview">{{cite news |last=Puig |first=Claudia |author-link=Claudia Puig |date=November 6, 2009 |title='Precious' is raw and painful but poignant |url=https://www.usatoday.com/life/movies/reviews/2009-11-06-precious06_ST_N.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091109113755/http://www.usatoday.com/life/movies/reviews/2009-11-06-precious06_ST_N.htm |archive-date=November 9, 2009 |access-date=November 17, 2009 |work=[[USA Today]]}}</ref> [[Peter Travers]], of ''[[Rolling Stone]]'' called Mo'Nique "dynamite," a performance that "tears at your heart."<ref name="r.s.review">{{cite magazine |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/movies/reviews/precious-20091105 |title=Precious Review |first=Peter |last=Travers |author-link=Peter Travers |date=November 5, 2009 |magazine=[[Rolling Stone]] |access-date=November 16, 2009 |archive-date=December 1, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201201932/http://www.rollingstone.com/movies/reviews/precious-20091105 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Mary Pols of ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' praised the film's fantasy sequences for being able to show the audience a "joyous Wizard of Oz energy" that is able to "open the door into Precious's mind in a way even [the author] Sapphire couldn't."<ref name="timereview"/> Pols felt that, while not implying that the film has "a lack of compelling emotional material" but that the film's "few weak moments" are the "ones that dovetail with typical inspirational stories."<ref name="timereview">{{cite magazine |url=http://content.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,1935116,00.html |title=Precious Review: Too Powerful for Tears |date=November 16, 2009 |magazine=Time |first=Mary |last=Pols |access-date=November 20, 2009 |archive-date=May 2, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140502092533/http://content.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,1935116,00.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Marshall Fine of ''[[The Huffington Post]]'' praised the film as being "a film that doesn't shy away from the depths to which human beings can sink, but it also shows the strength and resilience of which we are capable, even at our lowest moments."<ref name="fine review">{{cite web |url=https://www.huffingtonpost.com/marshall-fine/movie-review-iprecious-fr_b_346569.html |title=Movie review: Precious: From the Novel PUSH by Sapphire |work=[[The Huffington Post|HuffingtonPost.com]] |date=November 5, 2009 |first=Marshall |last=Fine |access-date=November 20, 2009 |archive-date=November 10, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091110151851/http://www.huffingtonpost.com/marshall-fine/movie-review-iprecious-fr_b_346569.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Scott Mendelson, also of ''The Huffington Post'', felt that when you put the "glaring issues aside," the film "still works as a potent character study and a glimpse inside a world we'd rather pretend does not exist in America." But while the film "succeeds as a powerful acting treat and a potent character study, there are some major narrative issues that prevent the film from being an accidental masterpiece."<ref name="mendelsonreview">{{cite web |url=https://www.huffingtonpost.com/scott-mendelson/huff-post-review-precious_b_352425.html |first=Scott |last=Mendelson |title=HuffPost Review: precious (2009) |work=The Huffington Post |date=November 10, 2009 |access-date=November 20, 2009 |archive-date=November 14, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091114162503/http://www.huffingtonpost.com/scott-mendelson/huff-post-review-precious_b_352425.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Mendelson described the film as being "an acting powerhouse" based on its many emotional themes.<ref name="mendelsonreview" />

Critic Jack Mathews wrote: "Without being familiar with the source material, you really have no idea how much work went into the adaptation or how well it was done.... 'Precious: Based on the Novel 'Push' by Sapphire'... First-time screenwriter Geoffrey Fletcher did yeoman's work turning Sapphire's graphic, idiomatic novel into a coherent and inspiring story about the journey of an abused Harlem teenager."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.moviefone.com/oscars-academy-awards/features/oscar-predictions |title=Oscar Predictions 2010: Who Will Be Nominated? |website=Moviefone |access-date=February 2, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160321202137/http://www.moviefone.com/oscars-academy-awards/features/oscar-predictions |archive-date=March 21, 2016 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Erin Aubry Kaplan wrote on ''[[Salon.com]]'' that the question posed by the film is how to assess the "hopeless story of a ghetto teen... in the Age of Obama." She went on to say that "'Precious' proves you don't always have to choose between artistic and commercial success; the film's first opening weekend was record-breaking. It's a sign how much we needed to tell this story. And, perhaps, how many stories there are left to tell."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.salon.com/entertainment/movies/feature/2009/11/09/precious_feature/print.html |title=Precious in the Age of Obama |first=Erin Aubry |last=Kaplan |work=[[Salon.com]] |date=November 9, 2009 |access-date=February 2, 2010 |archive-date=January 13, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100113235147/http://www.salon.com/entertainment/movies/feature/2009/11/09/precious_feature/print.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[A. O. Scott]] identified the script's precise use of force and adept use of language, including a memorable line created by Fletcher for the adaptation: a "risky, remarkable film adaptation, written by Geoffrey Fletcher, the facts of Precious's life are also laid out with unsparing force (though not in overly graphic detail). But just as ''Push'' achieves an eloquence that makes it far more than a fictional diary of extreme dysfunction, so too does ''Precious'' avoid the traps of well-meaning, preachy lower-depths realism. It howls and stammers, but it also sings...Inarticulate and emotionally shut down, her massive body at once a prison and a hiding place, Precious is also perceptive and shrewd, possessed of talents visible only to those who bother to look. At its plainest and most persuasive, her story is that of a writer discovering a voice. 'These people talked like TV stations I didn't even watch,' she remarks of Ms. Rain and her partner (Kimberly Russell), displaying her awakening literary intelligence even as she marvels at the discovery of her ignorance."<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/11/06/movies/06precious.html |title=Lee Daniels Gives Us Howls of a Life, Buried Deep Within |work=The New York Times |access-date=February 2, 2010 |first=A. O. |last=Scott |author-link=A. O. Scott |date=November 6, 2009 |archive-date=January 7, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150107223302/http://www.nytimes.com/2009/11/06/movies/06precious.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Conversely, reflecting the transformation from script to screen, [[Dana Stevens (critic)|Dana Stevens]] of ''[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]'' disagreed with Gleiberman's suggestion that the "film makes you think" and argued that the film's "eagerness" to "drag" the audience "through the lower depths of human experience" leaves little space for independent "conclusions". Stevens noted that, while the film is about improvement and self-actualization, "it wields an awfully large cudgel", in contrast to Scott's view of balance: "unsparing force (though not in overly graphic detail)". Perhaps sharing Mathews's view regarding the daunting challenge of adapting the harsh story of ''Push'', Stevens observed that "Daniels and Fletcher no doubt intended for their film to lend a voice to the kind of protagonist too often excluded from American movie screens: a poor, black, overweight single mother from the inner city."<ref>{{cite web |last=Stevens |first=Dana |author-link=Dana Stevens (critic) |date=November 5, 2009 |title=Precious |url=http://www.slate.com/id/2234728/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100203035319/http://www.slate.com/id/2234728 |archive-date=February 3, 2010 |access-date=February 2, 2010 |website=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]}}</ref>

''Precious'' also received some negative responses from critics. Writing for the ''[[New York Press]]'', [[Armond White]] compared the film to the landmark but controversial ''[[The Birth of a Nation]]'' (1915) as "demeaning the idea of black American life," calling it "an orgy of [[prurience]]" and the "con job of the year."<ref>{{Cite news |last=White |first=Armond |author-link=Armond White |date=November 19, 2009 |title=Pride & Precious |url=http://hiphopandpolitics.com/2009/11/19/armond-white-precious-is-the-most-damaging-film-to-the-black-image-since-birth-of-a-nation/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160223181508/http://hiphopandpolitics.com/2009/11/19/armond-white-precious-is-the-most-damaging-film-to-the-black-image-since-birth-of-a-nation/ |archive-date=February 23, 2016 |access-date=December 30, 2010 |work=hiphopandpolitics.com}}</ref> He further characterized the source novel as a relic of 1990s [[identity politics]] and noted that the film "casts light-skinned actors as kind [...] and dark-skinned actors as terrors." In two separate articles, writers for ''[[The New York Times]]'' cited White's article as the most powerful negative review of ''Precious'', adding that in a 2009 interview he had remarked that the film's popularity is a result of the "fact" that "black pathology sells."<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/11/21/movies/21precious.html|title=To Blacks, Precious Is 'Demeaned' or 'Angelic'|work=The New York Times|date=November 20, 2009|access-date=March 5, 2010|first=Felicia R.|last=Lee|archive-date=October 5, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121005143024/http://www.nytimes.com/2009/11/21/movies/21precious.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Courtland Milloy]] of ''[[The Washington Post]]'' said ''Precious'' was "a film of prurient interest that has about as much redeeming social value as a porn flick."<ref name="milloyreview">{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2009/11/17/AR2009111703465.html |first=Courtland |last=Milloy |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=November 18, 2009 |title=A film as lost as the girl it glorifies |access-date=November 18, 2009 |archive-date=November 10, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121110172203/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2009/11/17/AR2009111703465.html |url-status=live }}</ref> [[David Edelstein]], of ''New York Magazine'' commented that, while the film has "elements" that are "powerful and shocking," he felt the movie was "programmed", and that the film had "its own study guide."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://nymag.com/movies/reviews/61750/ |date=November 1, 2009 |title=When Push Comes to Shove |work=[[New York (magazine)|New York]] |first=David |last=Edelstein |access-date=November 18, 2009 |archive-date=November 9, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091109232940/http://nymag.com/movies/reviews/61750/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Keith Uhlich of ''Time Out New York'' felt that the film did not live up to its "long hype", and felt that it was "bewildering" to discover the film's praise at the Sundance Film Festival, because Uhlich characterized the film as having "shrug-worthiness."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://newyork.timeout.com/articles/film/80310/precious-based-on-the-novel-push-by-sapphire-film-review |date=November 4, 2009 |title=Precious: Based on the Novel "Push" by Sapphire |first=Keith |last=Uhlich |work=[[Time Out (magazine)|Time Out]]|access-date=November 18, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091110095301/http://newyork.timeout.com/articles/film/80310/precious-based-on-the-novel-push-by-sapphire-film-review <!--Added by H3llBot--> |archive-date=November 10, 2009}}</ref>

[[Peter Bradshaw]] wrote in ''[[The Guardian]]'' that the film catalogues a "horrendous, unending nightmare of abuse" and then abruptly turns into something resembling the 1980s musical ''[[Fame (1980 film)|Fame]]''. Bradshaw commended the film's acting and energy, but said it was not quite the "transcendent masterpiece" some had made it out to be.<ref>{{cite news |last=Bradshaw |first=Peter |author-link=Peter Bradshaw |date=January 28, 2010 |title=Precious: Based on the Novel "Push" by Sapphire |url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2010/jan/28/precious-review |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150926013515/http://www.theguardian.com/film/2010/jan/28/precious-review |archive-date=September 26, 2015 |access-date=May 2, 2010 |work=The Guardian}}</ref> Sukhdev Sandhu wrote in ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]'' that he found the film "a dispiriting mix of cliché and melodrama," although he acknowledged that ''Precious'' does feature some superb acting.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/film/filmreviews/7092274/Precious-review.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220112/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/film/filmreviews/7092274/Precious-review.html |archive-date=January 12, 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|date=January 28, 2010 |title=Precious, review |first=Sukhdev |last=Sandhu |work=[[The Daily Telegraph]]|access-date=May 2, 2010}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

Noting Daniels's admiration of the work of [[John Waters (director born 1946)|John Waters]] and [[Pedro Almodóvar]] and the joking attitude he and the actors sometimes took towards their material while making the movie, Jim Emerson argued that ''Precious'' is best understood as a deliberately over-the-top piece of [[Camp (style)|camp]] in the vein of Waters's ''[[Female Trouble]]''.<ref>{{cite web |last=Emerson |first=Jim |date=December 22, 2009 |title=Precious Based on the Movie Female Trouble by John Waters |url=https://www.rogerebert.com/scanners/precious-based-on-the-movie-female-trouble-by-john-waters |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140821182900/http://www.rogerebert.com/scanners/precious-based-on-the-movie-female-trouble-by-john-waters |archive-date=August 21, 2014 |access-date=August 10, 2014 |website=RogerEbert.com}}</ref>

=== Accolades ===
{{Further|List of accolades received by Precious}}
''Precious'' received dozens of nominations in award categories, including six Academy Award nominations, not only for the film itself but for the cast's performances, the direction and cinematography, and the adaptation of the novel to the screenplay. Director Lee Daniels won the [[People's Choice Award]], an award given by audience members at the [[2009 Toronto International Film Festival]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-toronto-awards-idUSTRE58I15F20090920 |title="Precious" wins top Toronto film festival prize |date=September 21, 2009 |first=Cameron |last=French |access-date=November 16, 2009 |website=Reuters |archive-date=January 26, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160126160959/http://www.reuters.com/article/us-toronto-awards-idUSTRE58I15F20090920 |url-status=live }}</ref> Daniels won both awards for which he was nominated at the San Sebastián International Film Festival—the TVE Otra Mirada Award and the Audience Award. He was also nominated in the category of Bronze Horse at the Stockholm Film Festival, and won the Best Feature Film Award at the Hawaii International Film Festival.

''Precious'' received five awards at the 2009 [[Independent Spirit Awards]] (ISA) in the categories for Best Film, Best First Screenplay, Best Direction, Best Actress and Best Supporting Actress.<ref name="isa">{{cite news |url=http://latimesblogs.latimes.com/awards/2009/12/precious-and-the-last-station-lead-independent-spirit-award-nominations.html |date=December 1, 2009 |work=Los Angeles Times |title='Precious' and 'The Last Station' lead Independent Spirit Award nominations [Updated] |first=Susan |last=King |access-date=December 1, 2009 |archive-date=December 4, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091204135322/http://latimesblogs.latimes.com/awards/2009/12/precious-and-the-last-station-lead-independent-spirit-award-nominations.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

''Precious'' received nominations from the 67th Golden Globes for the film and for Mo'Nique and Sidibe; Mo'Nique won Best Supporting Actress.<ref name="ggnoms">{{cite web |url=http://latimesblogs.latimes.com/awards/2010/01/list-of-67th-annual-golden-globe-nominations.html |title=List of 67th annual Golden Globe nominations [Corrected] |date=January 17, 2010 |work=Los Angeles Times |access-date=August 10, 2014 |archive-date=May 27, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130527191521/http://latimesblogs.latimes.com/awards/2010/01/list-of-67th-annual-golden-globe-nominations.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

The film was nominated in all three major categories at the [[16th Screen Actors Guild Awards|2009 Screen Actor Guild Awards]]: Best Cast, Best Actress, and Best Supporting Actress (in which Mo'Nique won).<ref name="sag">{{cite press release |url=http://www.sagawards.org/media-pr/press-releases/nominations-announced-16th-annual-screen-actors-guild-awards%C2%AE |title=Nominations Announced For The 16th Annual Screen Actor Guild Awards |date=December 17, 2009 |website=[[Screen Actors Guild Awards]] |access-date=December 17, 2009 |archive-date=July 16, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160716172419/http://www.sagawards.org/media-pr/press-releases/nominations-announced-16th-annual-screen-actors-guild-awards%C2%AE |url-status=dead }}</ref>

''Precious'' was considered for the [[British Academy of Film and Television Arts|BAFTA]] awards in several categories, including Best Picture, Best Director, Best Adapted Screenplay, Best Editing, Best Leading Actress (Sidibe), and Best Supporting Actress (Mo'Nique).<ref name="baftaconsideration">{{cite web |url=http://static.bafta.org/files/long-list-0910-400.pdf |title=Orange British Academy Film Awards in 2010 – Long List |work=[[British Academy of Film and Television Arts|Static.BAFTA.org]] |access-date=January 8, 2010 |archive-date=February 15, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100215053543/http://static.bafta.org/files/long-list-0910-400.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

On February 2, 2010, the film received Academy Award nominations at the [[Academy Awards]] for Best Picture, Best Actress (Sidibe), Best Supporting Actress (Mo'Nique), Best Director (Daniels), Best Adapted Screenplay (Fletcher), and Best Film Editing (Klotz). On March 7, 2010, Mo'Nique and Fletcher won Academy Awards in their respective categories. The film was also nominated for a [[GLAAD Media Awards|GLAAD Media Award]] for "Outstanding Film – Wide Release" during the [[21st GLAAD Media Awards]].<ref>{{cite web |title=21st Annual GLAAD Media Awards – English Language Nominees |website=[[Gay & Lesbian Alliance Against Defamation]] |year=2010 |url=http://www.glaad.org/mediaawards/21/nominees |access-date=February 21, 2010 |archive-date=January 30, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100130031953/http://www.glaad.org/mediaawards/21/nominees |url-status=dead}}</ref>

'''''Red Rocket''''' is a 2021 American [[black comedy|black]] [[comedy drama]] film directed by [[Sean Baker]], and written by Baker and [[Chris Bergoch]]. It stars [[Simon Rex]], [[Bree Elrod]], and [[Suzanna Son]] in her feature film debut. The film stars Rex as a middle-aged, newly retired [[Pornographic film actor|porn star]] who leaves Los Angeles for his small Texas hometown, plotting his way back to the life he once had. Along the way, he begins dating a 17-year-old girl.

The film premiered at the [[2021 Cannes Film Festival|74th Cannes Film Festival]] in competition for the [[Palme d'Or]] on July 14, 2021. It was released in [[Limited theatrical release|select theaters]] in the United States on December 10, 2021, by [[A24]]. ''Red Rocket'' received praise for its direction and Rex's performance and various awards and nominations. The [[National Board of Review]] listed it among the top 10 films of the year. Rex also won [[Best Actor]] awards from the [[Los Angeles Film Critics Association]] and the [[37th Independent Spirit Awards|Independent Spirit Awards]].

==Plot==
Washed-up and down-on-his-luck L. A. pornstar Mikey "Saber" Davies returns to his hometown of [[Texas City, Texas]], for the first time in 17 years to start over. After a two-day bus ride and only $22 on him, he arrives at the modest home of his estranged wife and fellow ex-pornstar, Lexi, and her mother, Lil, begging them to let him stay. They reluctantly agree, but insist that he get a job and do household chores. Mikey has several job interviews, but due to the long gap in his résumé and his fame as an adult film actor, nobody hires him. Desperate, he reaches out to Leondria, the mother of a schoolmate, to give him back his old job selling [[Cannabis (drug)|cannabis]]. Leondria and her daughter June suspect that Mikey will smoke it himself, but their business arrangement continues after he returns with his earnings. Since he has no car, Mikey uses Lexi's kids' old bicycle.

After sleeping on the couch for several nights, Mikey starts having sex with Lexi. Eventually, she invites him to share her bedroom. Mikey gives Lexi and Lil a month's rent in advance and takes them to a donut shop to celebrate. He becomes smitten with Raylee, a 17-year-old girl who works at the counter and goes by the name Strawberry. He returns and shares a [[Joint (cannabis)|joint]] with her, and she recommends he consider the construction workers who frequent the shop as customers. They start a sexual relationship. One night, she plays him a piano version of "[[Bye Bye Bye]]" by [[NSYNC]].

Mikey befriends Lexi's neighbor Lonnie, whom Lexi babysat when he was younger. They spend time together. During a trip to the mall, Mikey learns that Lonnie is [[Military impostor|pretending to be an Army veteran]] to sell US flags and gets humiliated and thrown into the mall fountain by two actual veterans, who see through him.

Mikey persuades Strawberry to break up with Nash, a classmate with whom she has been having casual sex. Nash and his parents confront Mikey in the donut shop parking lot and beat him up.

Mikey repeatedly tries to persuade Strawberry to travel with him to Los Angeles to pursue a career in pornography, which he plans to manage as his way back into the business. They grow closer, causing him to become distant from Lexi. When he disappears for a weekend with Strawberry, Lexi grows suspicious and they argue. Mikey berates her and brags about the $3,000 he made selling drugs.

While riding in Lonnie's car, Mikey brags about his success with Strawberry and his comeback, which distracts Lonnie and makes him almost miss their exit, causing them to swerve across traffic, creating a [[multiple-vehicle collision]] that results in many injuries. They flee the scene and Mikey begs Lonnie to hide his involvement. Mikey is anxious, but Lonnie assumes full responsibility for the crash when he is arrested.

Using the crash as an excuse, Mikey visits Strawberry at work and asks her to come to Los Angeles with him and start her porn career. She agrees and quits her job. That evening, before going to bed, Mikey tells Lexi he is leaving for California in the morning. 

Later that night, while Mikey is sleeping, Lexi and Lil call Leondria to send her adult children, June and her brothers, to seize the $3,000 Mikey earned. They wake him and take the money. Mikey flees out the bedroom window and runs naked to Leondria's house, begging her to return his money. He realizes that all this time, Leondria has been keeping an eye on him for Lexi and Lil. She gives Mikey $200 for a bus ticket and tells him to leave town forever, and that if he is still there by tomorrow or ever comes back, he will be beaten up.

Humiliated, Mikey leaves with his few possessions in a trash bag. After walking to Strawberry's house all night, he reaches it in the morning, dehydrated and exhausted. Upon arriving, he imagines Strawberry opening the door in a red bikini and dancing, and tears up.

asked Rex to trust him, and Rex did not tell his agent about the film until after shooting had ended.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|last=Feinberg|first=Scott|date=2021-10-31|title=Savannah Film Fest: 'Red [[Principal photography]] ran in [[Texas]] from October 26 to November 19, 2020, with rigorous safety protocols implemented due to the pandemic.<ref name="Deadline">{{cite web|first=Mike Jr.|last=Fleming|date=February 9, 2021|title=FilmNation Acquires WW Rights To Sean Baker-Directed 'Red Rocket;' Will Begin Selling New Film From 'Florida Project' Helmer|url=https://deadline.com/2021/02/filmnation-acquires-ww-rights-to-sean-baker-directed-red-rocket-will-begin-selling-new-film-from-florida-project-helmer-1234690569/|access-date=February 9, 2021|work=Deadline Hollywood|archive-date=October 20, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211020084036/https://deadline.com/2021/02/filmnation-acquires-ww-rights-to-sean-baker-directed-red-rocket-will-begin-selling-new-film-from-florida-project-helmer-1234690569/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="VarietyInsight">{{cite web|title=Film and TV Projects Going Into Production - Red Rocket|url=https://www.varietyinsight.com/production_restart_full_view.php?track_id=184736|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210506185239/https://www.varietyinsight.com/production_restart_full_view.php?track_id=184736|archive-date=May 6, 2021|access-date=May 6, 2021|website=[[Variety Insight]]}}</ref> ''Red Rocket'' was shot on [[16 mm film]] by an [[Arriflex 16SR|Arriflex 16SR3]] camera with [[Panavision]] 1.44x Auto Panatars, [[Carl Zeiss AG|Zeiss]] Super Speed, [[Iscorama]] 54 and [[Canon Inc.|Canon]] Lenses.<ref name="kodak-blog-red-rocket">{{cite web |title=Director Sean Baker and DP Drew Daniels on embracing the organic aesthetic of 16mm for 'Red Rocket' |url=https://www.kodak.com/en/motion/blog-post/red-rocket |website=[[Kodak]] |access-date=16 March 2022 |date=January 27, 2022 |quote=Starlet shot on the Sony CineAlta PMW-F3, Tangerine on the iPhone 5S, and Red Rocket on the Arriflex 16SR3....Arriflex 16SR3 camera which was paired with Panavision 1.44x Auto Panatars}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Desowitz|first=Bill|date=2021-07-06|title=Cannes 2021 Has 8 Palme D'Or Entries Shot on Film, Including Wes Anderson's 'The French Dispatch'|url=https://www.indiewire.com/2021/07/cannes-2021-cinematography-the-french-dispatch-1234648567/|access-date=2021-10-22|website=[[IndieWire]]|archive-date=October 26, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211026004716/https://www.indiewire.com/2021/07/cannes-2021-cinematography-the-french-dispatch-1234648567/|url-status=live}}</ref> It had a crew of 10 people, no rehearsal time, and mostly non-actors.<ref name=":3" />

Filming locations included restaurants in Texas City and Nederland, a donut shop in [[Groves, Texas|Groves]], the [[Kemah Boardwalk]], and the [[Galveston Island Historic Pleasure Pier]].<ref name=":5"/><ref>{{Cite web|last=Shey|first=Brittanie|date=2021-10-06|title=Houston-Area Restaurants Appear in Trailer for 'Red Rocket,' Lauded Indie Director Sean Baker's Newest Film|url=https://houston.eater.com/2021/10/6/22712643/sean-baker-director-red-rocket-texas-city-galveston-restaurants-wrice-bbq-pleasure-pier|access-date=2021-12-10|website=Eater Houston}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Zuckerman|first=Esther|date=8 December 2021|title=Why Director Sean Baker Keeps Returning to the Comfort of Donut Shops|url=https://www.thrillist.com/entertainment/nation/red-rocket-director-sean-baker-interview|access-date=2021-12-10|website=Thrillist|archive-date=December 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211210124311/https://www.thrillist.com/entertainment/nation/red-rocket-director-sean-baker-interview|url-status=live}}</ref> The Donut Hole was open for business in the morning while filming took place in the evening.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Batson|first=Monique|date=2021-12-25|title=WATCH THE TRAILER — Critically acclaimed "Red Rocket" filmed locally when no one noticed|url=https://www.panews.com/2021/12/25/photo-gallery-critically-acclaimed-film-shot-in-area-when-no-one-noticed/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211226053754/https://www.panews.com/2021/12/25/photo-gallery-critically-acclaimed-film-shot-in-area-when-no-one-noticed/|archive-date=2021-12-26|access-date=2021-12-26|website=Port Arthur News}}</ref>

Securing the rights to the song "[[Bye Bye Bye]]" was not part of the initial budget. All five members of NSYNC had to approve its use.<ref>{{Cite web|last=McHenry|first=Jackson|date=2021-11-13|title=Red Rocket Had to Seek the Approval of Every 'N Sync Member to Use 'Bye Bye Bye'|url=https://www.vulture.com/2021/11/red-rocket-nsync-bye-bye-bye-simon-rex-sean-baker.html|access-date=2021-11-18|website=Vulture|archive-date=November 18, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211118195442/https://www.vulture.com/2021/11/red-rocket-nsync-bye-bye-bye-simon-rex-sean-baker.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":4" /> Son recorded a [[cover version]] of the song for the soundtrack.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Kaye|first=Ben|date=2021-12-07|title=Suzanna Son covers *NSync's "Bye Bye Bye" for A24's Red Rocket: Exclusive|url=https://consequence.net/2021/12/nsync-bye-bye-bye-cover-red-rocket-suzanna-son/|access-date=2021-12-07|website=Consequence|archive-date=December 8, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211208095324/https://consequence.net/2021/12/nsync-bye-bye-bye-cover-red-rocket-suzanna-son/|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Creative influences==
Baker has said he "devoted my career to tell stories that remove stigma and normalize lifestyles" of [[sex worker]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Kaufman|first=Amy|date=2020-08-28|title=Director Sean Baker says he is not making an OnlyFans film with Bella Thorne|url=https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/story/2020-08-28/sean-baker-onlyfans-bella-thorne-film|access-date=2021-07-15|website=Los Angeles Times|archive-date=May 9, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220509191937/https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/story/2020-08-28/sean-baker-onlyfans-bella-thorne-film|url-status=live}}</ref> He said that in ''Red Rocket'' he wanted to pay homage to "Italian eroticism" and [[Sexploitation film|sexploitation]] films by directors from the 1970s like [[Fernando Di Leo]] and [[Umberto Lenzi]]. He was also inspired by [[Steven Spielberg]]'s ''[[The Sugarland Express]]'' for the outdoor scenes.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|last=Tangcay|first=Jazz|date=2021-12-07|title=How *NSYNC's 'Bye Bye Bye' Ended Up in Sean Baker's 'Red Rocket'|url=https://variety.com/2021/artisans/news/red-rocket-nsync-bye-bye-bye-1235127945/|access-date=2021-12-09|website=Variety|archive-date=April 22, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220422200926/https://variety.com/2021/artisans/news/red-rocket-nsync-bye-bye-bye-1235127945/|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Reception ==
=== Box office ===
''Red Rocket'' grossed $1 million in the United States and Canada<ref name="BOM">{{cite Box Office Mojo |id=13453006 |title=Red Rocket (2021) |access-date=February 26, 2022 |publisher_hide=yes}}{{cbignore}}</ref><ref name="NUM">{{cite The Numbers |id=Red-Rocket-(2021) |title=Red Rocket (2021) |access-date=February 26, 2022 |publisher_hide=yes}}{{cbignore}}</ref> and $1.3 million in other territories for a worldwide total of $2.3 million,<ref name="BOM"/> plus 477,304 with home video sales,<ref name="NUM"/> against a production budget of $1.1 million.<ref name="budget1"/><ref name="budget2"/> In its opening weekend, the film earned $88,195 from six theaters for a per-screen average of $14,699.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.boxofficemojo.com/weekend/2021W50/|title=Domestic 2021 Weekend 50|website=[[Box Office Mojo]]|access-date=December 17, 2021|archive-date=December 14, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211214021424/https://www.boxofficemojo.com/weekend/2021W50/|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Critical response ===
[[File:Simon Rex during an interview, March 2022 (2) (cropped).jpg|thumb|upright|Rex's performance received critical acclaim.]]

{{Rotten Tomatoes prose|90|7.9|206|Led by Simon Rex's magnetic performance, ''Red Rocket'' is another vibrant, ground-level look at modern American life from director/co-writer Sean Baker.|ref=yes|access-date=January 15, 2021}} [[Metacritic]], which uses a [[Weighted arithmetic mean|weighted average]], assigned the film a score of 76 out of 100, based on 49 critics, indicating "generally favorable" reviews.<ref name="Metacritic">{{cite web |title=''Red Rocket'' |url=https://www.metacritic.com/movie/red-rocket |website=[[Metacritic]] |publisher=[[Fandom (website)#Fandom, Inc.|Fandom, Inc.]] |access-date= |archive-url= |archive-date= |url-status=}}</ref><ref>{{cite Metacritic|id=red-rocket|type=movie|title=Red Rocket|access-date=January 15, 2022}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

In ''[[Deadline Hollywood]]'', [[Todd McCarthy]] wrote, "Even before much happens, the sense of a very specific location and cultural mindset is very intense." He praised Baker and Rex for their "tremendous energy" and said the film "feels as creatively pure as a novel by a kid just out of college."<ref>{{Cite web|last=McCarthy|first=Todd|author-link=Todd McCarthy|date=2021-07-14|title=Cannes Review: Sean Baker's 'Red Rocket'|url=https://deadline.com/2021/07/cannes-review-red-rocket-sean-baker-1234793132/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210715034042/https://deadline.com/2021/07/cannes-review-red-rocket-sean-baker-1234793132/|archive-date=2021-07-15|access-date=2021-07-15|website=Deadline Hollywood}}</ref> [[Matt Zoller Seitz]] of ''[[RogerEbert.com]]'', on the other hand, called it a "rambling 130-minute film" and the middle section "wherein Mikey ensnares [the] freckle-faced 17-year-old donut shop employee... Strawberry" and schemes their escape to Los Angeles so that he can lead her to [[adult entertainment|adult film]] stardom "one-note and repetitious".<ref name="SeitzRogerEbert">{{cite web |author=Seitz |first=Matt Zoller |author-link=Matt Zoller Seitz |date=December 10, 2021 |title=Reviews: Red Rocket |url=https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/red-rocket-movie-review-2021 |access-date=2021-12-15 |work=[[RogerEbert.com]]}}</ref> David Rooney of ''[[The Hollywood Reporter]]'' also criticized the film mildly for "prolix stretches", saying "it could have used some tightening. But it's a pleasure to put yourself in Baker's capable hands."<ref name=":0" /> [[Peter Bradshaw]] of ''[[The Guardian]]'' wrote, "With ''Red Rocket'', Sean Baker has given us an adult American pastoral, essentially a comedy, and another study of tough lives at the margin, close in spirit to his lo-fi breakthrough ''[[Tangerine (film)|Tangerine]]''."<ref>{{Cite news|last=Bradshaw|first=Peter|author-link=Peter Bradshaw|date=2021-07-14|title=Red Rocket review – Sean Baker's vivid study of a washed-up porn star|url=http://www.theguardian.com/film/2021/jul/14/red-rocket-review-sean-baker-porn-star|access-date=2021-07-17|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> [[Richard Lawson (writer)|Richard Lawson]] in ''[[Vanity Fair (magazine)|Vanity Fair]]'' wrote, "Baker's choice is a rather perfect one—in contextual terms and actual ones, too. Rex's performance is fleet and nimble, gregarious and shaded in darkness. He and Baker make staccato music together."<ref name=":1">{{Cite magazine|last=Lawson|first=Richard|author-link=Richard Lawson (writer)|date=2021-07-14|title=Simon Rex Is Sensational in 'Red Rocket'|url=https://www.vanityfair.com/hollywood/2021/07/red-rocket-movie-review-simon-rex-cannes|access-date=2021-07-17|magazine=[[Vanity Fair (magazine)|Vanity Fair]]|archive-date=July 15, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210715071832/https://www.vanityfair.com/hollywood/2021/07/red-rocket-movie-review-simon-rex-cannes|url-status=live}}</ref>

Some reactions to the film stirred a debate about [[sexual morality]] in film in the post-[[Me Too movement|MeToo]] era. Seitz concluded that ''Red Rocket'' is "the least of the list" of Baker's and Bergoch's "impressive library of realistic movies about the rainbow coalition of the American underclass" and questioned moments where "if the filmmakers aren't exactly ''endorsing'' their protagonist's middle-aged, borderline pedo-pimp obsession with Strawberry, they're not being as rigorous about mediating it as they should."<ref name= "SeitzRogerEbert" /> In ''[[Gawker]]'', Brianna Zigler defended the film's portrayal of a morally objectionable protagonist:

{{Cquote
| quote= [T]he world is not a comfortable place, and it's often rigged in favor of guys like Mikey Saber. No matter how much of a cancerous loser we know him to be, his inflated sense of self is so grand that his losses still translate into wins. Is Mikey the sort of person I would like to be? No, but he's worth thinking about, and even trying to understand because he exists in this world with the rest of us. There is no moral high ground to be gained from disavowing art which dares to contend with the fact that people are not perfect bastions of moral good; that we can align ourselves with ugliness because ugliness exists in us all. If Mikey Saber gets off too easy for you, it's because he'd probably get away with it in real life.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Zigler |first=Brianna |date=10 December 2021 |title='Red Rocket's Mikey Saber Is a Very Bad Man |url=https://www.gawker.com/culture/red-rockets-mikey-saber-is-a-very-bad-man |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211210141113/https://gawker.com/culture/red-rockets-mikey-saber-is-a-very-bad-man |archive-date=2021-12-10 |access-date=2021-12-10 |website=[[Gawker]]}}</ref>
}}

''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]''{{'s}} Clayton Davis said the film's "risqué" subject matter could be a hindrance but encouraged award voters to nominate Rex, Baker, and Bergoch for [[Academy Awards]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Davis|first=Clayton|date=2021-09-03|title=It's Okay Academy: You Can Nominate Simon Rex for Best Actor for 'Red Rocket'|url=https://variety.com/2021/awards/awards/red-rocket-simon-rex-telluride-oscars-1235051584/|access-date=2021-09-03|website=Variety}}</ref> [[John Waters]] included ''Red Rocket'' on his list of the Top Ten films of 2021.<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=December 2021 |title=JOHN WATERS'S BEST FILMS OF 2021 |url=https://www.artforum.com/print/202110/best-films-of-2021-john-waters-87205 |access-date=2023-07-04 |magazine=[[Artforum]] |archive-date=July 4, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230704234919/https://www.artforum.com/print/202110/best-films-of-2021-john-waters-87205 |url-status=live }}</ref> Filmmaker [[Bette Gordon]] praised the film, saying that it "flows organically due to Sean Baker's love of discovering place and his desire to listen to the voices of the community of people who live there."<ref>{{Cite magazine|url=https://variety.com/lists/directors-favorite-films-2021-olivia-wilde-george-miller/|title=Directors on Directors: Filmmakers Analyze 2021 Favorites From 'In the Heights' to 'The Harder They Fall'|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=December 16, 2021|access-date=March 11, 2025|archive-date=December 16, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231216134158/https://variety.com/lists/directors-favorite-films-2021-olivia-wilde-george-miller/|url-status=live}}</ref>

In June 2025, ''[[IndieWire]]'' ranked the film 68th on its list of "The 100 Best Movies of the 2020s (So Far)."<ref name="Best">{{cite web |date=June 16, 2025 |title=The 100 Best Movies of the 2020s (So Far) |url=https://www.indiewire.com/lists/best-movies-2020s/ |access-date=2025-06-23 |archive-date=July 3, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250703025153/https://www.indiewire.com/lists/best-movies-2020s/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

'''''The Artist''''' is a 2011 French-Belgian<ref name="the_artist_2011" /><!-- BEFORE EDITING THIS SUBJECT, PLEASE CONSULT THE ARCHIVES AND THE TALK PAGE. THANK YOU.-->{{#tag:ref|There has been some confusion on whether the film is French or American. However, 17 supporting roles are played by American actors.<ref name=CannesArtist>{{cite web|url=http://www.festival-cannes.com/en/archives/ficheFilm/id/11169584/year/2011.html|title=Festival de sources list the film as a "romantic comedy" or a "romantic comedy-drama". However, there is no romance plot in the film.<ref>{{cite in the style of a [[black-and-white]] [[silent film]] or [[part-talkie]].<ref name=ACEFilmEditors>{{cite web|url=http://ace-filmeditors.org/ace-eddie-awards/nominees-recipients/|title=Nominees & Recipients: ACE Film Editors|work=[[American Cinema Editors]]|access-date=26 February 2012|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110224185421/http://ace-filmeditors.org/ace-eddie-awards/nominees-recipients/|archive-date=24 February 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.goldenglobes.org/nominations/|title=Golden Globe nominations|publisher=Goldenglobes.org|access-date=17 November 2012|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100108115828/http://www.goldenglobes.org/nominations/|archive-date=8 January 2010}}</ref><ref name=RottenTomatoes>{{cite web|url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/the_artist|title=The Artist (2011)|publisher=[[Rotten Tomatoes]]|access-date=13 November 2017|archive-date=22 October 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211022011913/https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/the_artist|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>[https://www.chicagotribune.com/entertainment/movies/sc-mov-1220-the-artist-20111220,0,2703056.column {{Webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20120723052713/http://www.chicagotribune.com/entertainment/movies/sc-mov-1220-the-artist-20111220,0,2703056.column |date=23 July 2012 }} ''[[Chicago Tribune]]''</ref> It was written and directed by [[Michel Hazanavicius]], produced by [[Thomas Langmann]] and stars [[Jean Dujardin]] and [[Bérénice Bejo]].<ref>{{cite book|title=International Film Guide 2012|first=Ian Hayden|last=Smith|year=2012|isbn=978-1908215017|page=117}}</ref> The story takes place in [[Hollywood, Los Angeles|Hollywood]], between 1927 and 1932, and focuses on the relationship between a rising young actress and an older silent film star as silent cinema falls out of fashion and is replaced by the "[[Sound film|talkies]]".

''The Artist'' received widespread critical acclaim and won many accolades. Dujardin won [[Cannes Film Festival Award for Best Actor|Best Actor]] at the [[2011 Cannes Film Festival]], where the film premiered. The film was nominated for six [[Golden Globe Award|Golden Globes]], the most of any 2011 film, and won three: [[Golden Globe Award for Best Motion Picture – Musical or Comedy|Best Motion Picture&nbsp;– Musical or Comedy]], [[Golden Globe Award for Best Original Score|Best Original Score]], and [[Golden Globe Award for Best Actor – Motion Picture Musical or Comedy|Best Actor&nbsp;– Motion Picture Musical or Comedy]] for Dujardin. In January 2012, it was nominated for twelve [[BAFTA]]s, the most of any film from 2011,<ref name=BBCBAFTA>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/entertainment-arts-16590364|title=Silent movie ''The Artist'' leads Bafta nominations|publisher=BBC News|access-date=17 January 2012|date=17 January 2012|archive-date=17 January 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120117085115/http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/entertainment-arts-16590364|url-status=live}}</ref> and won seven, including [[BAFTA Award for Best Film|Best Film]], [[BAFTA Award for Best Direction|Best Director]], [[BAFTA Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role|Best Actor]] for Dujardin, and [[BAFTA Award for Best Original Screenplay|Best Original Screenplay]] for Hazanavicius.

It was nominated for ten [[Academy Awards]] and won five,<ref name=BBCOscar>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/entertainment-arts-16699960|title=Martin Scorsese's ''Hugo'' leads Oscar charge with 11 nods|publisher=BBC News|access-date=24 January 2012|date=24 January 2012|archive-date=24 January 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120124174408/http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/entertainment-arts-16699960|url-status=live}}</ref> including [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]], [[Academy Award for Best Director|Best Director]] for Hazanavicius, and [[Academy Award for Best Actor|Best Actor]] for Dujardin, making him the first French actor ever to win in this category. It was also the first non-American/non-British film to ever win Best Picture,<ref>{{cite news|title=Oscars 2012: Billy Crystal's back and 'The Artist' could make history|work=[[Chicago Tribune]]|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/entertainment/music/sns-rt-academy-awards-awardsmt1thewrap35726-20120226,0,3195826.story|access-date=27 February 2012|archive-date=1 March 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120301113248/http://www.chicagotribune.com/entertainment/music/sns-rt-academy-awards-awardsmt1thewrap35726-20120226,0,3195826.story|url-status=live}}</ref> the first mainly silent film to win since 1927's ''[[Wings (1927 film)|Wings]]'' won at the [[1st Academy Awards]] in 1929, the first film presented in the [[Aspect ratio|4:3 aspect ratio]] to win since 1953's ''[[From Here to Eternity]]'', the first [[Black-and-white movie|black-and-white film]] to win since 1993's ''[[Schindler's List]]'', though the latter contained limited colour sequences; and the first 100% black-and-white film to win since 1960's ''[[The Apartment]]''.

In France it was nominated for ten [[César Awards]],<ref name=BBCCesar>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/entertainment-arts-16759408|title=Kate Winslet to receive honorary Cesar award|publisher=BBC News|access-date=28 January 2012|date=27 January 2012|archive-date=23 October 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181023091243/https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/entertainment-arts-16759408|url-status=live}}</ref> winning six, including [[César Award for Best Film|Best Film]], [[César Award for Best Director|Best Director]] for Hazanavicius, and [[César Award for Best Actress|Best Actress]] for Bejo. ''The Artist'' has received more awards than any other French film.<ref>{{cite news|last=Leffler|first=Rebecca|title='The Artist' Wins 6 Cesar Awards, Including Best French Film of the Year|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/race/cesar-awards-the-artist-michel-hazanavicius-294893|work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|publisher=[[Prometheus Global Media|Prometheus Global Media, LLC]]|access-date=27 February 2012|date=24 February 2012|archive-date=24 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924210534/http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/race/cesar-awards-the-artist-michel-hazanavicius-294893|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Plot==
In 1927, [[silent film]] star George Valentin is posing for pictures outside the [[premiere]] of his latest hit film when a young woman, Peppy Miller, accidentally bumps into him. Valentin reacts with humor and shows off with Peppy for the cameras. The next day, Peppy is on the front page of ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' with the headline "Who's That Girl?" She capitalizes by auditioning as a dancer and is spotted by Valentin, who insists that she have a part in Kinograph Studios' next production, despite objections from studio boss Al Zimmer. While performing a scene in which they dance together, Valentin and Peppy show great chemistry. With a little guidance from Valentin, who draws a [[beauty spot]] on her cheek, Peppy rises through the industry, earning more prominent starring roles.

Two years later, Zimmer announces plans to cease production of silent films at Kinograph Studios, but Valentin is dismissive, insisting that sound is just a fad. In a dream, he begins hearing sounds from his environment (as does the audience) but cannot speak himself. He decides to leave the studio for the chance to produce, finance, and direct his own silent film, ''Tears of Love''. The film opens on the same day as Peppy's new sound film ''Beauty Spot'' and the [[Wall Street crash of 1929|1929 stock market crash]]. Valentin's only chance of avoiding bankruptcy is for his film to be a hit. Unfortunately, audiences flock to Peppy's film instead, while only a few people attend Valentin's. With Valentin ruined, his wife, Doris, kicks him out, and he moves into an apartment with his valet/chauffeur, Clifton, and his dog. Peppy quickly becomes the first of several major new Hollywood sound film stars.

Later, the bankrupt Valentin is forced to auction his personal effects, and after realizing he has not paid the loyal Clifton in over a year, gives him his car before firing him. Depressed and drunk, Valentin sets fire to a stack of his old films. As the [[Nitrocellulose#Film|nitrate film]] blazes out of control, he is overwhelmed by the smoke and passes out inside the burning house, clutching a single film canister. However, Valentin's dog attracts the help of a nearby policeman, and after being rescued, Valentin is hospitalized for injuries suffered in the fire. Peppy visits the hospital and discovers that the film he rescued is the one with them dancing together. She asks for him to be moved to her house to recuperate. Valentin awakens in a bed at her house to find that Clifton is now working for Peppy. His ego hurt, Valentin shows ingratitude for Peppy having taken him in, prompting Clifton to remind him of his changing luck.

Peppy insists to Zimmer that Valentin co-star in her next film, threatening to quit Kinograph if he does not agree. After Valentin learns that Peppy bought his possessions at auction, he returns in despair to his burnt-out apartment. Peppy arrives and finds that Valentin is about to attempt suicide. She tells him she only wanted to help him. They embrace, and Valentin tells her it is no use; no one wants to hear him speak. Remembering Valentin's superb dancing ability, Peppy persuades Zimmer to let her make a [[Musical film#The classical sound era|musical]] production so Valentin can avoid the humiliation of having to speak.

Now the audience hears sound for the second time, as the film starts rolling for a dance scene with Peppy and Valentin and their tap-dancing can be heard. Once the choreography is complete, the two dancers are heard panting. The director of the musical calls, "Cut!" to which Zimmer adds: "Perfect. Beautiful. Could you give me just one more?" Valentin, in his only audible line, replies "With pleasure," revealing a [[French accent]].<ref name="themarysue">{{Cite web|url=http://www.themarysue.com/cinema-scope-a-short-history-of-the-end-of-silent-film/|title=Cinema Scope: A Short History of the End of Silent Film|date=15 December 2011|access-date=13 March 2013|publisher=[[Dan Abrams#The Mary Sue|The Mary Sue]]|archive-date=8 June 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130608014330/http://www.themarysue.com/cinema-scope-a-short-history-of-the-end-of-silent-film/|url-status=live}}</ref> The camera then pulls back to the sounds of the film crew as they prepare to shoot another take.

==Production==
===Development===
[[File:Équipe The Artist Cannes 2011.jpg|thumb|400px|Some of the cast and crew at the [[2011 Cannes Film Festival]]: (left to right), score composer [[Ludovic Bource]], director [[Michel Hazanavicius]], stars [[Missi Pyle]], [[Bérénice Bejo]], and [[Jean Dujardin]], director of photography [[Guillaume Schiffman]] and producer [[Thomas Langmann]].]]
Director [[Michel Hazanavicius]] had been fantasizing about making a [[silent film]] for many years, both because many filmmakers he admires emerged in the silent era, and because of the image-driven nature of the form. According to Hazanavicius, his wish to make a silent film was at first not taken seriously, but after the financial success of his spy-film pastiches ''[[OSS 117: Cairo, Nest of Spies]]'' and ''[[OSS 117: Lost in Rio]]'', producers started to express interest. The forming of the film's narrative started with Hazanavicius' desire to work again with actors [[Jean Dujardin]] and [[Bérénice Bejo]], who had both starred in ''OSS 117: Cairo, Nest of Spies''. Hazanavicius chose the form of a [[Melodrama (film genre)|melodrama]], mostly because he thought many of the films from the silent era that have aged best are of that genre. He did extensive research about 1920s Hollywood, and studied silent films to find the right techniques to make the story comprehensible without having to use too many [[intertitle]]s. The screenplay took four months to write and was principally inspired by the 1928 silent comedy, ''[[Show People]]''.<ref name=presskitmh>{{cite web|url=http://www.festival-cannes.com/assets/Image/Direct/041179.PDF|title=Interview with Michel Hazanavicius|work=English press kit The Artist|publisher=[[Wild Bunch (film company)|Wild Bunch]]|access-date=10 May 2011|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110914011421/http://www.festival-cannes.com/assets/Image/Direct/041179.PDF|archive-date=14 September 2011}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nyu.edu/alumni.magazine/issue19/pdf/NYU19.pdf|title=The Clothes Make the Man|last=Alfuso|first=Renee|date=Fall 2012|work=NYU Alumni Magazine|access-date=24 November 2019|archive-date=9 December 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191209190901/https://www.nyu.edu/alumni.magazine/issue19/pdf/NYU19.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

Chief among the influences shaping the screenplay's protagonist was [[Douglas Fairbanks]]. The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences' recent book ''Douglas Fairbanks'', by [[Jeffrey Vance]], as well as the academy's Douglas Fairbanks exhibition and screening events both in Los Angeles and New York City, afforded Hollywood's first swashbuckling hero and the academy's first president some significant media attention.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://blog.sfgate.com/tgladysz/2012/07/08/film-historian-jeffrey-vance-talks-about-douglas-fairbanks/|title=Film historian Jeffrey Vance talks about Douglas Fairbanks|author=Thomas Gladysz|date=8 July 2012|work=City Brights: Thomas Gladysz|access-date=2 April 2016|archive-date=29 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160329233551/http://blog.sfgate.com/tgladysz/2012/07/08/film-historian-jeffrey-vance-talks-about-douglas-fairbanks/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://aaspeechesdb.oscars.org/link/084-1/|title=Academy Awards Acceptance Speeches – Search Results – Margaret Herrick Library – Academy of Motion Picture Arts & Sciences|access-date=2 April 2016|archive-date=14 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160414072844/http://aaspeechesdb.oscars.org/link/084-1/|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Filming===
[[Principal photography]] on ''The Artist'' began in November 2010,<ref>{{cite magazine|author=Erin Carlson|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/uggie-the-artist-retiring-287271|title='The Artist' Dog Uggie Retiring Early Due to Mystery Illness (Report)|magazine=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|date=6 February 2014|access-date=1 September 2015|archive-date=24 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924204840/http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/uggie-the-artist-retiring-287271|url-status=live}}</ref> taking place over the course of thirty-five days,<ref name=BAFTARed>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/iplayer/episode/b01c89nf/The_Orange_British_Academy_Film_Awards_2012_Red_Carpet/|title=The Orange British Academy Film Awards&nbsp;– 2012 Red Carpet|publisher=BBC News|access-date=10 February 2012|archive-date=15 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120215211348/http://www.bbc.co.uk/iplayer/episode/b01c89nf/The_Orange_British_Academy_Film_Awards_2012_Red_Carpet/|url-status=live}}</ref> made in the 1.33:1 screen ratio commonly used in the silent film era. Though presented in black-and-white, it was shot in color by [[cinematographer]] [[Guillaume Schiffman]].<ref name=time>{{cite news|first=Gilbert|last=Cruz|title=What Is This Artist Movie That's Winning All the Awards?|url=https://entertainment.time.com/2012/01/19/what-is-this-artist-movie-thats-winning-all-the-awards/|work=Time|date=19 January 2012|access-date=12 February 2012|archive-date=31 January 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120131161418/http://entertainment.time.com/2012/01/19/what-is-this-artist-movie-thats-winning-all-the-awards/|url-status=live}}</ref> All the technical details, including lenses, lighting and camera moves, were calibrated to aesthetically match silent films of the period.<ref>Steve Rose, "Now in full retrovision", ''The Guardian'' (''The Guide'' supplement), 7 January 2012</ref> To recreate the slightly sped-up look of 1920s silent films, the film was shot at a slightly lower [[frame rate]] of 22 fps as opposed to the standard 24 fps.<ref>{{Cite news|author=Rebecca Keegan|title=Buzz is growing over a silent film|date=21 November 2011|url=https://www.latimes.com/entertainment/la-xpm-2011-nov-21-la-ca-1120-artist-silent-movie-20111121-story.html|work=Los Angeles Times|access-date=28 January 2012|archive-date=23 September 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190923210220/https://www.latimes.com/entertainment/la-xpm-2011-nov-21-la-ca-1120-artist-silent-movie-20111121-story.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Most of the film is silent, except for two brief scenes with sound as well as the [[Cinematic techniques#Sound|non-diegetic]] soundtrack. Throughout the shoot, Hazanavicius played music from classic Hollywood films while the actors performed.<ref name=presskitmh />

The film was produced by La Petite Reine and ARP Sélection for 13.47 million euro, including co-production support from [[Studio 37]] and [[France 3 Cinéma]], and pre-sales investment from [[StudioCanal]] and CinéCinéma.<ref name=outofcomp>{{cite web|last=Lemercier|first=Fabien|date=18 April 2011|url=http://cineuropa.org/newsdetail.aspx?lang=en&documentID=201597|title=Media frenzy over Sarkozy's election ''Conquest''|work=Cineuropa|access-date=10 May 2011|archive-date=7 July 2012|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120707155929/http://cineuropa.org/newsdetail.aspx?lang=en&documentID=201597|url-status=live}}</ref> The cast and the crew included both French and American members.<ref name=presskitmh /> All the scenes were shot in [[Los Angeles]], primarily in [[Hollywood, Los Angeles|Hollywood]], but also in downtown theaters, restaurants and houses, including the one in which [[Mary Pickford]] lived. Soundstage work was done at [[Ren-Mar Studios|Red Studios]], and the studio lot itself doubled for part of the fictional Kinograph Studios lot, with Red's Lillian Way entrance doubling as the Kinograph entrance in several sequences. The iconic [[Bradbury Building]] in downtown L.A. provided the location for the film's distinctive staircase sequence. The dance sequence that closes the film took seventeen takes, and required Dujardin and Bejo to spend five months studying tap dancing, with Dujardin claiming that "in the first week it's fun, the fifth week it's a little boring, at the end it's thrilling".<ref>"The Artist: The Making of An American Romance" Featurette, ''The Artist'' DVD</ref>

American [[costume design]]er [[Mark Bridges (costume designer)|Mark Bridges]] created the wardrobe for the film's cast.<ref name=sfgate>{{cite news|first=Hugh|last=Hart|title='Artist' costumer had designs on career as child|url=https://www.sfgate.com/movies/industrybuzz/article/artist-costumer-had-designs-on-career-as-child-3207438.php|work=San Francisco Chronicle|date=12 February 2011|access-date=12 February 2012|archive-date=2 February 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160202030630/https://www.sfgate.com/movies/industrybuzz/article/Artist-costumer-had-designs-on-career-as-child-3207438.php|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Music===
{{Main|The Artist (soundtrack)|l1=''The Artist'' (soundtrack)}}
The [[Film score|film's music]] was largely composed by [[Ludovic Bource]], but includes works by other composers such as [[Alberto Ginastera]]'s "Estancia". The soundtrack was recorded in Belgium by the [[Brussels Philharmonic]] and was conducted by Ernst Van Tiel; the Brussels Jazz Orchestra also cooperated. The recording took place during six days in April 2011 at [[Place Flagey|Flagey]]'s Studio 4 in Brussels.<ref>{{cite web|title=Soundtrack for 'The artist' recorded at Brussels|url=http://www.brusselsphilharmonic.be/en/news/detail/article/soundtrack-voor-the-artist-komt-uit-brussel/|publisher=Brussels Philharmonic|access-date=30 January 2012|date=3 October 2011|archive-date=23 January 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120123071058/http://www.brusselsphilharmonic.be/en/news/detail/article/soundtrack-voor-the-artist-komt-uit-brussel|url-status=live}}</ref>

The film's climactic scene is set to [[Bernard Herrmann]]'s "Scène d'amour" from [[Vertigo (film score)|his score]] to [[Alfred Hitchcock]]'s film ''[[Vertigo (film)|Vertigo]]''. In ''Vertigo'', that composition similarly accompanies an extended scene without dialogue. Only one song (sung, with lyrics) is used in the soundtrack, "[[Pennies from Heaven (song)|Pennies from Heaven]]", sung by [[Rose Murphy|Rose "Chi-Chi" Murphy]] (uncredited). This song was written in 1936 although the film is set between 1927 and 1932. The soundtrack was released on 10 October in France, and 21 October in the U.K. and U.S. through [[Sony Classical Records]].<ref>{{cite web|title=The Artist|publisher=Amazon|url=https://www.amazon.com/Artist-Ludovic-Bource/dp/B005LL4U54|access-date=30 January 2012|archive-date=3 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120203045554/http://www.amazon.com/Artist-Ludovic-Bource/dp/B005LL4U54|url-status=live}}</ref>

The film premiered on 15 May 2011 in competition at the [[2011 Cannes Film Festival]].<ref name="Cannes">{{cite web|url=http://www.festival-cannes.fr/assets/File/Web/HORAIRES%202011/Horaire%20internet.pdf|title=Horaires 2011|language=fr|work=festival-cannes.com|publisher=[[Cannes Film Festival]]|access-date=10 May 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120123034309/http://www.festival-cannes.fr/assets/File/Web/HORAIRES%202011/Horaire%20internet.pdf|archive-date=23 January 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref> It was initially announced as an out of competition entry, but was moved to the competition a week before the festival opened.<ref>{{cite web|last=Mitchell|first=Wendy|date=4 May 2011|url=http://www.screendaily.com/festivals/cannes/hazanavicius-the-artist-moves-into-competition-in-cannes/5026923.article|title=Hazanavicius' The Artist moves into Competition in Cannes|work=[[Screen International|Screen Daily]]|access-date=10 May 2011|archive-date=7 April 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140407053247/http://www.screendaily.com/festivals/cannes/hazanavicius-the-artist-moves-into-competition-in-cannes/5026923.article|url-status=live}}</ref> The French regular release was on 12 October 2011 through [[Warner Bros.|Warner Bros. France]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.allocine.fr/film/fichefilm_gen_cfilm=183070.html|title=The Artist|language=fr|work=[[AlloCiné]]|publisher=[[Tiger Management|Tiger Global]]|access-date=10 May 2011|archive-date=25 January 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120125211407/http://www.allocine.fr/film/fichefilm_gen_cfilm=183070.html|url-status=live}}</ref> [[The Weinstein Company]] bought the distribution rights for the US, UK, Australia, South Africa, Latin America and Eastern Europe, with the film also selling to Comstock and GAGA in Japan and Delphi Film in Germany.<ref>{{cite web|last=Tartaglione|first=16 May 2011|url=http://www.screendaily.com/news/distribution/wild-bunch-weinsteins-confirm-multi-territory-deal-on-the-artist/5027596.article|title=Wild Bunch, Weinsteins confirm multi-territory deal on The Artist|work=[[Screen International|Screen Daily]]|access-date=22 May 2011|archive-date=21 May 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110521081916/http://www.screendaily.com/news/distribution/wild-bunch-weinsteins-confirm-multi-territory-deal-on-the-artist/5027596.article|url-status=live}}</ref> The film was initially given a [[limited release]] in the United States on 23 November 2011.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cinemablend.com/new/Artist-Star-Jean-Dujardin-How-Gene-Kelly-Inspired-His-Work-28076.html|work=CinemaBlend.com|title=The Artist Star Jean Dujardin on How Gene Kelly Inspired His Work|date=28 November 2011|access-date=12 May 2012|first1=Katey|last1=Rich|archive-date=1 March 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120301124827/http://www.cinemablend.com/new/Artist-Star-Jean-Dujardin-How-Gene-Kelly-Inspired-His-Work-28076.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

Following its wins at the [[69th Golden Globe Awards]], it was announced Warner Bros. would re-release the film in France in 362 theaters on 25 January 2012.<ref>{{cite web|title=" The Artist " ressort en salles en France|url=http://archives.lesoir.be/-the-artist-ressort-en-salles-en-france_t-20120116-01RKP5.html|work=[[Le Soir]]|access-date=27 February 2012|language=fr|date=16 January 2012|archive-date=27 May 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130527004531/http://archives.lesoir.be/-the-artist-ressort-en-salles-en-france_t-20120116-01RKP5.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Keslassy|first=Elsa|title=France's second look at 'Artist'|url=https://variety.com/2012/film/news/france-s-second-look-at-artist-1118050616/|work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|access-date=27 February 2012|date=22 February 2012|archive-date=28 December 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131228061739/http://variety.com/2012/film/news/france-s-second-look-at-artist-1118050616/|url-status=live}}</ref> It was also re-released in Belgium on 22 February 2012.<ref>{{cite web|title="The Artist" remporte 7 Bafta Awards dont meilleur film, meilleur réalisateur et meillleur acteur.|url=http://www.cineart.be/fr/news/the-artist-remporte-7-bafta-awards-dont-meilleur-film-meilleur-realisateur-et-meilleur-acteur.aspx|publisher=cinéart.be|access-date=27 February 2012|language=fr|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130910140717/http://www.cineart.be/fr/news/the-artist-remporte-7-bafta-awards-dont-meilleur-film-meilleur-realisateur-et-meilleur-acteur.aspx|archive-date=10 September 2013}}</ref>

===Home media===
''The Artist'' was released on [[DVD region code|region 1]] [[DVD]] and [[Blu-ray Disc|Blu-ray]] on 26 June 2012.<ref name=Amazon>{{cite web|title=Amazon.com|url=https://www.amazon.com/The-Artist-UltraViolet-Digital-Copy/dp/B00782O7IY/ref=sr_1_1?ie=UTF8&qid=1337129571&sr=8-1|work=Amazon|date=15 May 2012|access-date=15 September 2017|archive-date=14 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210314071038/https://www.amazon.com/The-Artist-UltraViolet-Digital-Copy/dp/B00782O7IY/ref=sr_1_1?ie=UTF8&qid=1337129571&sr=8-1|url-status=live}}</ref> It was released in the UK by [[Entertainment Film Distributors|Entertainment in Video]] on 28 May 2012.<ref>{{cite web|author1=Webmaster|title=The Artist Detailed|url=http://www.blu-ray.com/news/?id=8486|website=Blu-ray.com|access-date=12 November 2017|date=4 April 2012|archive-date=13 November 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171113060231/http://www.blu-ray.com/news/?id=8486|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Reception==
===Box office===
''The Artist'' grossed $44,671,682 in North America, along with $88,761,174 in other territories for a worldwide total of $133,432,856.<ref name="Boxofficemojo" /> After its success at the Academy Awards, the film saw a moderate boost the following week on the box office in North America. It appeared on the week's top 10 chart and got an increase of 34% while expanding its release from 966 theaters to 1,756.<ref>{{cite news|last=McClintock|first=Pamela|title='The Artist' Enjoys Box Office Bump After Oscar Wins|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/artist-box-office-oscars-michel-Hazanavicius-Jean-Dujardin-296749|work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|publisher=[[Prometheus Global Media|Prometheus Global Media, LLC]]|access-date=4 May 2012|date=4 March 2012|archive-date=30 April 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120430091746/http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/artist-box-office-oscars-michel-Hazanavicius-Jean-Dujardin-296749|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Critical response===
<!-- WHEN UPDATING REVIEW AGGREGATE SCORES, PLEASE MAKE SURE YOU UPDATE THE NUMBER OF REVIEWS AND THE ACCESS DATE IN THE CITATION! -->
On review aggregator [[Rotten Tomatoes]] the film has an approval rating of {{RT data|score}} based on {{RT data|count}} reviews, with an average rating of {{RT data|average}}. The website's critical consensus states, "A crowd-pleasing tribute to the magic of silent cinema, ''The Artist'' is a clever, joyous film with delightful performances and visual style to spare."<ref name=RottenTomatoes/> At [[Metacritic]], which assigns a [[weighted average]] rating to reviews, the film received an average score of 89 out of 100, based on 41 critics, indicating "universal acclaim".<ref name="Metacritic">{{cite web|url=https://www.metacritic.com/movie/the-artist|title=''The Artist'' Reviews|publisher=[[Metacritic]]|access-date=27 February 2018|archive-date=13 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180213034225/http://www.metacritic.com/movie/the-artist|url-status=live}}</ref> Audiences surveyed by [[CinemaScore]] gave the film an average grade of "A" on an A+ to F scale.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/blogs/company-town-blog/story/2011-11-27/the-artist-marilyn-have-old-school-charm-at-box-office|title='The Artist,' 'Marilyn' have old-school charm at box office|first=Amy|last=Kaufman|work=Los Angeles Times|date=27 November 2011|access-date=21 January 2023|archive-date=22 January 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230122011700/https://www.latimes.com/archives/blogs/company-town-blog/story/2011-11-27/the-artist-marilyn-have-old-school-charm-at-box-office|url-status=live}}</ref>

Mark Adams of ''[[Screen International|Screen Daily]]'' called the film "a real pleasure"; "propelled elegantly forward by delightful performances from Jean Dujardin and Bérénice Bejo it is the most unlikely of feel-good movies." He added however: "The film does feel a little sluggish towards the end of the first third as the music is a little repetitive and the intertitles are infrequent, but Hazanavicius manages to give the film a real sense of charm and warmth, and film fans will be competing to spot visual and musical references."<ref>{{cite web|last=Adams|first=Mark|date=15 May 2011|url=http://www.screendaily.com/reviews/latest-reviews/the-artist/5027562.article|title=The Artist|work=[[Screen International|Screen Daily]]|access-date=22 May 2011|archive-date=17 October 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111017075148/http://www.screendaily.com/reviews/latest-reviews/the-artist/5027562.article|url-status=live}}</ref> Peter Bradshaw of ''[[The Guardian]]'' described how the film "had me on my feet cheering throughout the final credits" and stated "I can't wait to see it again".<ref>{{cite news|last=Bradshaw|first=Peter|author-link=Peter Bradshaw|title=Cannes 2011: The Artist/Michael/Footnote&nbsp;– review|url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2011/may/16/cannes-2011-the-artist-michael-footnote-review|work=The Guardian|location=UK|access-date=27 October 2011|date=16 May 2011}}</ref>
