==Legacy and aftermath==
[[File:Corrs members.jpg|thumb|left|Clockwise from top left: Siblings [[Andrea Corr|Andrea]], [[Caroline Corr|Caroline]], [[Jim Corr|Jim]] and [[Sharon Corr]] achieved international stardom with their band [[The Corrs]] after the film's release.]]

''The Commitments'' has gained [[cult film|cult status]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.thejournal.ie/are-these-the-best-irish-cult-films-ever-930542-May2013/|title=Are these the best cult Irish films ever?|date=30 May 2013|work=[[TheJournal.ie]]|access-date=29 January 2017}}</ref> and is regarded as one of the best Irish films.<ref name="Best100">{{cite web|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/455170.stm|title=Best 100 British films|date=23 September 1999|work=[[BBC News]]|access-date=4 July 2016}}</ref><ref name="TopTen">{{cite web|url=http://www.irishcultureandcustoms.com/Libr/zTopTenMovies.html|title=Top Ten Irish Movies of all Time|access-date=4 July 2016}}</ref> An image of four of the actors, in character, was [[List of people on stamps of Ireland|on an Irish postage stamp]] as part of the ''Ireland 1996: Irish Cinema Centenary'' series issued by [[An Post]]; the image includes lead singer Deco Cuffe (Andrew Strong), along with the three "Commitmentettes" – Imelda Quirke (Angeline Ball), Natalie Murphy (Maria Doyle Kennedy) and Bernie McGloughlin (Bronagh Gallagher).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.emerald-isle-gifts.com/irish-stamps---philately/commemoratives-1990-99/ireland-1996-irish-cinema-centenary-set-of-4-mnh-se-ten.asp |title=Ireland 1996: Irish Cinema Centenary |publisher=Emerald Isle Gifts, original stamps from [[An Post]] |date=17 September 1996 |access-date=4 July 2016 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141129024747/http://www.emerald-isle-gifts.com/irish-stamps---philately/commemoratives-1990-99/ireland-1996-irish-cinema-centenary-set-of-4-mnh-se-ten.asp |archive-date=29 November 2014}}</ref> In 1999, the [[British Film Institute]] ranked the film at number 38 on its list of the "100 best British films of the century", based on votes from 1,000 leading figures of the [[film industry]].<ref name="Best100" /> In 2005, a poll conducted by [[Jameson Irish Whiskey|Jameson]] and [[The Dubliner (magazine)|The Dubliner]] ranked ''The Commitments'' the "Best Irish Film of All time", based on 10,000 votes.<ref name="TopTen" /> Following the film's release, the novel also gained popularity, becoming Doyle's most well-known work, which the author resented. "I dismissed ''The Commitments'' for a long, long time to the extent I forgot I had anything to do with it", he said.<ref name="ToBe">{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2013/apr/23/the-commitments-west-end-musical|title=The Commitments to be turned into West End musical|first=Mark|last=Brown|work=[[The Guardian]]|date=23 April 2013|access-date=4 July 2016}}</ref>

Many of the actors went on to pursue various acting and musical careers.<ref name="WhateverHappened" /> Robert Arkins signed a record deal with [[MCA Records]] in 1993,<ref>{{cite web|title= Artist Profile: Robert Arkins|url= http://www.mymusicsource.com/index.aspx?page=prodbandview&bid=689|work= My Music Source|access-date= 4 July 2016|archive-date= 4 March 2016|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160304123632/http://www.mymusicsource.com/index.aspx?page=prodbandview&bid=689|url-status= dead}}</ref> although he did not finish recording the consequent album.<ref>{{cite news|first=Paul|last=Martin|title=Soul searching 10 years on|newspaper=[[Daily Mirror|The Mirror]]|date=26 November 2001}}</ref> He has produced work for a number of commercial clients, television projects, and composed music for two short films.<ref name="WhateverHappened" /> Andrew Strong went on to produce several albums, which he described as having elements of R&B and rock. He has performed alongside [[The Rolling Stones]], [[Elton John]] and [[Ray Charles]], and formed his own band, The Bone Yard Boys, in 2003.<ref>{{cite web|title=Andrew Strong: Life After The Commitments|url=http://irishamerica.com/2009/10/andrew-strong-life-after-the-commitments/|work=Irish America|date=October–November 2009|first=Tara|last=Dougherty|access-date=6 July 2016}}</ref> In 1993, two of the film's cast members, Kenneth McCluskey and Dick Massey, formed their own [[tribute act]] band, [[The Stars from the Commitments]]. The 9-piece band has since played more than 1,000 shows worldwide, and has played with [[B.B. King]], [[James Brown]] and [[Wilson Pickett]].<ref name="WhateverHappened" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.starsfromthecommitments.com/band.html|title=The Stars From The Commitments featuring Kenneth McCluskey and Dick Massey|access-date=4 July 2016|archive-date=17 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160817010350/http://www.starsfromthecommitments.com/band.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Siblings Andrea, Jim, Sharon and Caroline Corr, who had minor supporting roles, had only recently formed their family quartet, performing in their aunt's pub as [[The Corrs]]; the film's music coordinator, [[John Hughes (Irish musician)|John Hughes]], noticed them when they auditioned for the film and agreed to become their manager.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.thebiographychannel.co.uk/biography_story/1531:2061/1/The_Corrs.htm |title=The Biography Channel The Corrs biography |publisher=The Biography Channel |access-date=15 September 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070529135603/http://www.thebiographychannel.co.uk/biography_story/1531%3A2061/1/The_Corrs.htm |archive-date=29 May 2007 |url-status=dead}}</ref> The band has since achieved international stardom, releasing six studio albums and selling more than 60 million records worldwide.<ref name="WhateverHappened" /> Andrea would again collaborate with Parker on his [[Evita (1996 film)|film adaptation]] of the musical ''[[Evita (musical)|Evita]]''.<ref name="ProdNotes" /><ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/entertainment/4261178.stm|title=Thriller role for Corrs vocalist|date=19 September 2005|work=[[BBC News]]|access-date=6 July 2016}}</ref> Glen Hansard continued performing with his band, [[The Frames]], and achieved greater success and critical acclaim with the 2005 film ''[[Once (film)|Once]]''.<ref name="WhateverHappened" /> Bronagh Gallagher has since enjoyed a lengthy acting career in film and television and Maria Doyle Kennedy has, to date, released eleven studio albums and has gone on to become an award-winning actress.<ref name="ProdNotes" /> Michael Aherne is the only cast member to have not pursued an acting career after the film's release.<ref name="WhateverHappened" />

On 6 October 2010, it was announced that Strong, Arkins, Ball, Gallagher, Aherne, Hansard, Félim Gormley and Dave Finnegan would join The Stars from The Commitments for a reunion tour to celebrate the film's 20th anniversary.<ref name="State">{{cite web|url=http://state.ie/news/the-commitments-announce-reunion-tour|title=The Commitments announce reunion tour|date=6 October 2010|work=[[State (magazine)|State]]|access-date=7 July 2016}}</ref> Donations from every ticket sold were given to the [[Irish Cancer Society]], with a goal of raising [[Euro|€]]30,000.<ref name="State" /> The cast performed at The Royal Theatre, in [[Castlebar]], [[County Mayo]] on 14 March 2011, Ireland's National Events Centre (INEC) in [[Killarney]], [[County Kerry]] on 15 March 2011, [[Odyssey (Belfast)|The Odyssey]], in [[Belfast]] on 17 March 2011, and [[3Arena (Dublin)|The O2]] in Dublin on 19 March 2011.<ref name="State" />

===''The Barrytown Trilogy''===
{{Main|The Barrytown Trilogy}}
[[File:Colm Meaney - Cannes.jpg|thumb|[[Colm Meaney]] has appeared in all three films based on Doyle's ''Barrytown Trilogy'' of novels.]]
''The Commitments'' is the first book in Doyle's series known as ''The Barrytown Trilogy'', followed by ''[[The Snapper (novel)|The Snapper]]'' (1990) and ''[[The Van (novel)|The Van]]'' (1991). While all three novels focus on the Rabbitte family, Doyle expressed that he was not interested in writing or producing sequels to the 1991 film adaptation, stating, "I hope it's never made. I just think that, whereas ''The Commitments'' was very much a labour of love, ''Commitments 2'' is definitely an act of cynicism."<ref name="White 2001 34" />

Doyle was given creative freedom by the [[BBC]] over the adaptation of ''The Snapper'', for which he wrote the screenplay.<ref name="White 2001 34" /> Lynda Myles returned to produce the film and hired [[Stephen Frears]] as its director.<ref name="White 2001 35">{{harvnb|White|2001|p=35}}</ref> [[Colm Meaney]] returned in a supporting role. The adaptation was originally planned as a television film before Frears suggested that it be transferred to film. Doyle disagreed with the change, stating, "I didn't like it on the big screen—I thought it was grainy."<ref name="White 2001 35" /> ''[[The Snapper (film)|The Snapper]]'' (1993) premiered at the [[1993 Cannes Film Festival]], where it received a [[standing ovation]].<ref name="White 2001 35" /> It was a critical success, receiving largely positive reviews.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/snapper/|title=The Snapper (1993)|publisher=[[Rotten Tomatoes]]|access-date=7 July 2016}}</ref>

For the film adaptation of ''The Van'', Doyle and Myles formed their own production company, Deadly Films, and the author was given creative control over the selection of its cast and director.<ref>{{harvnb|White|2001|pp=35–36}}</ref> Frears returned as director, and Meaney was cast in the lead role. Although ''[[The Van (1996 film)|The Van]]'' (1996) premiered at the [[1996 Cannes Film Festival]] to some favourable reviews, critical reaction was negative upon release; reviewers criticised the film for its thin material and lack of strong characterisation.<ref>{{harvnb|White|2001|p=36}}</ref>

===Cancelled sequel===
In January 2000, it was announced that [[Harvey Weinstein]] had acquired the film rights to the novel for [[Miramax]]<ref name=AFINotes /> and commissioned playwright [[Warren Leight]] to write a direct sequel to ''The Commitments'', with [[Cathy Konrad]] attached as a producer. The premise involved several members of The Commitments pairing with new band members before going on tour in the United States.<ref>{{cite web|title='Commitments' encore gets Leight touch|url=https://variety.com/2000/voices/columns/commitments-encore-gets-leight-touch-1117760417/|first=Michael|last=Fleming|date=3 January 2000|work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|publisher=Variety Media, LLC|access-date=4 July 2016}}</ref> The sequel was never produced.<ref>{{cite web|title=Gone Hollywood (yes, that one and the other one)|url=http://articles.sun-sentinel.com/2007-12-09/features/0712060394_1_bart-filmmaker-brian-hecker-friend/2|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160825231426/http://articles.sun-sentinel.com/2007-12-09/features/0712060394_1_bart-filmmaker-brian-hecker-friend/2|url-status=dead|archive-date=25 August 2016|first=Phoebe|last=Flowers|date=9 December 2007|work=[[SunSentinel]]|access-date=4 July 2016}}</ref>

===Stage production===
{{Main|The Commitments (musical)}}
Doyle's novel inspired a 2013 [[Musical theatre|musical]] stage production, directed by British theatre director [[Jamie Lloyd (director)|Jamie Lloyd]].<ref name="WestEnd">{{cite news|title=Commitments West End|url=https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2013/apr/23/the-commitments-west-end-musical|work=The Guardian | location=London|first=Mark|last=Brown|date=23 April 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/uk-news/commitments-turned-musical-roddy-doyle-1850124 | title=The Commitments to be turned into musical by Roddy Doyle after novel and film success|work=[[Daily Mirror]]|date=23 April 2013|access-date=4 July 2016}}</ref> Following the film's success, Doyle had previously turned down offers to adapt his novel into a stage production.<ref name="ToBe" /><ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.irishpost.co.uk/entertainment/interview-roddy-doyle-on-the-commitments-musical|title=Roddy Doyle on The Commitments musical|publisher=[[The Irish Post]]|work=irishpost.co.uk|date=24 April 2013|access-date=4 July 2016}}</ref> ''The Commitments'' began previews on 21 September 2013 in London's [[West End theatre|West End]] at the [[Palace Theatre, London|Palace Theatre]]. Its official opening night was on 8 October 2013.<ref>{{cite news|title=Commitments West End|url=https://www.theguardian.com/stage/2013/apr/23/the-commitments-west-end-musical|work=The Guardian | location=London|first=Mark|last=Brown|date=4 July 2016}}</ref> The show had more than 1,000 performances before officially closing in London on 1 November 2015. It was announced that a United Kingdom and Ireland tour would commence in 2017.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.whatsonstage.com/london-theatre/news/commitments-musical-close-london-west-end_37865.html|title=The Commitments to close in November|publisher=WhatsOnStage.com|date=21 May 2015|access-date=4 July 2016}}</ref>

'''''The Leopard''''' ({{langx|it|Il Gattopardo|lit=The [[Serval]]}} {{IPA|it|il ˌɡattoˈpardo|}})<ref>{{cite web |last=Alù |first=Giorgia |title=Guide to the Classics: The Leopard |url=https://theconversation.com/guide-to-the-classics-the-leopard-133443 |website=The Conversation |access-date=29 August 2023 |date=22 June 2020}}</ref> is a 1963 <!-- Do not add "Italian". All reliable sources, including those cited later in the article, describe the film as an Italian-French co-production. -->[[epic film|epic]] [[historical drama]] film directed by [[Luchino Visconti]]. Written by Visconti, [[Suso Cecchi d'Amico]], [[Enrico Medioli]], [[Pasquale Festa Campanile]], and [[Massimo Franciosa]], the film is an [[Film adaptation|adaptation]] of the [[The Leopard|1958 novel]] by [[Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa]].<ref>{{AFI film|23932|The Leopard}}</ref>

[[Burt Lancaster]] stars as Don Fabrizio Corbera, an aging [[Sicilians|Sicilian]] prince caught up in the sociopolitical turmoil of the ''[[Risorgimento]]'' (Italian unification) during the mid-19th century, with [[Alain Delon]] as his opportunistic nephew Tancredi, and [[Claudia Cardinale]] as his goddaughter. [[Paolo Stoppa]], [[Rina Morelli]], [[Romolo Valli]], [[Serge Reggiani]], and [[Terence Hill]] play supporting roles. The film was an [[international co-production]] between Italian studio [[Titanus]] and French studio [[Pathé]].<ref>{{cite web|title=The Leopard (1963)|url=https://www2.bfi.org.uk/films-tv-people/4ce2b6aadb03d|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160302130803/http://www.bfi.org.uk/films-tv-people/4ce2b6aadb03d|url-status=dead|archive-date=2 March 2016|access-date=2021-06-16|website=BFI|language=en}}</ref>

The film won the [[Palme d'Or]] at the [[1963 Cannes Film Festival]],<ref name="Ress 1963"/> and was released theatrically in Italy on March 28, 1963, and in France on June 14. It was a critical and commercial success in Europe, but reception was more lukewarm in the United States, where a truncated, English-dubbed cut was released. Retrospective reviews—of the film's longer original cut—have been more positive, and the film is now widely regarded as a classic and one of [[List of films considered the best|the greatest movies ever made]].<ref name=":1"/><ref name=":2"/>

In 2008, the film was included on the [[Ministry of Cultural Heritage and Activities and Tourism|Italian Ministry of Cultural Heritage]]'s [[100 film italiani da salvare|100 Italian films to be saved]], a list of 100 films that "have changed the collective memory of the country between 1942 and 1978."<ref>{{cite web |title=Ecco i cento film italiani da salvare Corriere della Sera |url=https://www.corriere.it/spettacoli/08_febbraio_28/elenco_cento_film_d83cacd8-e5ce-11dc-ab61-0003ba99c667.shtml |access-date=2021-03-11 |website=[[Corriere della Sera]]}}</ref>

== Plot ==

In [[Kingdom of the Two Sicilies|Sicily]] in the year 1860, Don Fabrizio Corbera, Prince of [[The Leopard#Locations|Salina]], enjoys the customary comforts and privileges of his ancestry. War has broken out between the armies of [[Francis II of the Two Sicilies]] and the insurgent volunteer [[Redshirts (Italy)|redshirts]] of [[Giuseppe Garibaldi]]. Among the rebels is the Prince's nephew, Tancredi Falconeri, whose romantic politics the Prince hesitantly accepts with some whimsical sympathy. Upset by the uprising, the Prince departs to [[Palermo]]. [[Expedition of the Thousand|Garibaldi's army]] subjugates the city and expropriates Sicily from the [[House of Bourbon-Two Sicilies|Bourbons]]. The Prince muses upon the inevitability of change, with the middle class displacing the ruling class while on the surface everything remains the same. Refusing to bend to the tide of changes, the Prince departs to his summer palace at [[The Leopard#Locations|Donnafugata]].

A new national assembly calls a [[Referendum|plebiscite]] and the nationalists win 512–0, thanks to the corruption and support of the town's leading citizen, Don Calogero Sedara. Don Calogero is invited to the villa of the Corberas, and he brings his daughter Angelica with him. Both the Prince and Tancredi are taken by Angelica's beauty. Soon thereafter, Tancredi makes plans to ask for her hand in marriage. The Prince sees the wisdom of the match because he knows that, due to his nephew's vaulting ambition, Tancredi will be in need of ready cash, which Angelica's father will happily provide. With the blessing of both the Prince and Don Calogero, Tancredi and Angelica get engaged. Noticing Tancredi shift his allegiance from Garibaldi to [[Victor Emmanuel II of Italy|King Victor Emmanuel]]'s newly formed army, the Prince wistfully judges that his nephew is the kind of opportunist who will flourish in the new Italy.

Cavalier Chevalley, a representative from the [[Kingdom of Sardinia (1720–1861)|Kingdom of Sardinia]], comes to the Prince's villa. He pleads with the Prince to join the senate of the nascent [[Kingdom of Italy]], hoping that the Prince's great compassion and wisdom will help alleviate the perceived poverty and alleged ignorance on the streets of Sicily. However, the Prince demurs and refuses this invitation, observing that, in his view, Sicily prefers its traditions to the delusions of modernity because its people are proud of their ancient heritage. He says he foresees his brand of aristocratic rulers, whom he refers to as leopards and lions, being replaced by more bureaucratic rulers, whom he calls jackals and hyenas, but that everyone, including the "sheep" of the general public, will continue to see themselves as the "salt of the earth". The Prince recommends Don Calogero would make a more appropriate senator.

The Corberas, including Tancredi, attend a great ball at the villa of a neighbouring prince, and the event marks the debut of Angelica in [[high society]]. Afflicted by a combination of melancholia and the ridiculousness of the [[nouveau riche]], the Prince wanders forlornly from room to room, increasingly disaffected by the entire edifice of the society he so gallantly represents—until Angelica approaches and asks him to dance. He accepts and, momentarily, recaptures and presents the elegant and dashing figure of his past self, but, after the dance, he quickly becomes disenchanted again.

Early in the morning, the guests leave the ball. The prince leaves the ball alone. Walking with a heavy heart through the empty streets, he pauses to let a hurrying priest pass and enter a home to deliver [[last rites]], and then walks into a dark alley that symbolises Italy's fading past, to which he feels he belongs.

* Brook Fuller as Fabrizietto Corbera di Salina

* [[Lola Braccini]] as Donna Margherita
* [[Marino Masé]] as the Corberas' tutor
* {{ill|Howard Nelson Rubien|de}} as Don Diego
* [[Rina De Liguoro]] as Princess of Presicce
* Franco Gulà as Mimi, the Corberas' [[majordomo]]
* [[Olimpia Cavalli]] as Mariannina
}}

== Production ==

[[File:Palazzo Gangi.jpg|right|thumb|150px|The ballroom of Palazzo Valguarnera-Gangi, where the ballroom sequence was shot.]]

=== Development ===

[[File:Palermo, Villa Montalbo Boscogrande.jpg|left|thumb|Villa Boscogrande, one of the film's primary locations.]]

[[Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa|Tomasi]]'s novel was a bestseller in Italy and won the [[Strega Prize]], Italy's most prestigious literary award. In August 1960, Italian studio [[Titanus]] announced they would make a film based on the novel in Sicily the following summer on a budget of at least $2 million. The film was to be an Italian-American co-production, shot in various languages, with a combination of Italian and American stars. [[Ettore Giannini]] was preparing a script, although it was expected he would collaborate with another writer to finish it.<ref>Italian-U.S.Film Set On Garibaldi: ' Leopard,' di Lampedusa's Novel, to Be Produced in Sicily by Titanus of Rome By Eugene Archer. ''[[The New York Times]]'' 6 August 1960: 9.</ref>

Several treatments were reportedly done before Visconti became involved.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Hawkins |first=Robert F. |date=1961-05-07 |title=Cinema Safaris On The Sicilian Landscape |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1961/05/07/archives/cinema-safaris-on-the-sicilian-landscape.html |access-date=2025-10-24 |work=The New York Times |pages=X9 |language=en}}</ref> "The book is seen through the eyes of a Sicilian prince who has no sense of the people", said Visconti. "The people were fooled by Garibaldi and then they were destroyed by the Piedmontese. The popular conscience was strangled by the way the Piedmont upper class tried to keep the social structure of the south just as it was."<ref>A conversation with Visconti
Gilliatt, Penelope. ''The Observer'' 10 Sep 1961: 17.</ref>

In July 1961, MGM announced they had signed a co-production deal with Titanus to make the movie. [[Warren Beatty]] was in discussions with Visconti to play Tancredi, while Visconti approached [[Laurence Olivier]] and [[Spencer Tracy]] to play the Prince.<ref>{{cite news |title=M-G-M To Release Film Of 'Leopard': Warren Beatty Sought for a Top Role in Italian Movie |first=Eugene |last=Archer |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=July 1, 1961 |page=9}}</ref>

Visconti was told by producers that they needed to cast a star in order to ensure they would earn enough money to justify the big budget. The producers recommended that the star should be either [[Gregory Peck]], [[Anthony Quinn]], [[Spencer Tracy]], or Burt Lancaster, and chose Lancaster without consulting Visconti. This insulted the director, which caused tension on the set initially, but Visconti and Lancaster ended up working well together, and their resulting friendship lasted the rest of Visconti's life.<ref name="Buford 2000">{{cite book |last=Buford |first=Kate |title=[[Burt Lancaster: An American Life]] |year=2000 |publisher=Aurum |location=London |isbn=1-85410-740-2|pages=222–227}}</ref>

In November 1961, Lancaster agreed to play the lead role, with filming to start in April.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Archer |first=Eugene |date=1961-11-08 |title=Next Rossen Film To Be 'Coco Beach'; Carnival Atmosphere of Cape Canaveral to Be Subject |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1961/11/08/archives/next-rossen-film-to-be-coco-beach-carnival-atmosphere-of-cape.html |access-date=2025-10-24 |work=The New York Times |language=en}}</ref> Lancaster said he had been "long fascinated" with ''The Leopard'', even before being offered the role, saying: "I think it is the best written and most perceptive study of a man and his background that has appeared for many years."<ref name="burt">Burt Lancaster Discovers a Sicilian Prince
By Derek Prouse. The Christian Science Monitor July 18, 1962: 6.</ref> He said he had doubts about accepting the part because "the novel was so perfect as a novel", but, ultimately, decided to accept.<ref name="lan">Burt Lancaster: Circus Acrobat Changes Spots For 'Leopard'
Waldo, George. ''Los Angeles Times'' October 21, 1962: p. 6-7. Clippings at [[Newspapers.com]]: [https://www.newspapers.com/clip/157136850/ First] and [https://www.newspapers.com/clip/157136918/ second].</ref> Claudia Cardinale and Delon had made ''Rocco and His Brothers'' with Visconti.<ref name="claud">{{cite magazine|magazine=Filmink|date=26 September 2025|access-date=26 September 2025|first=Stephen|last=Vagg|url=https://www.filmink.com.au/claudia-cardinales-ten-top-hollywood-films/|title=Claudia Cardinale's Ten Top Hollywood Films}}</ref>

In April 1962, 20th Century Fox announced it had bought the film's distribution rights.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Archer |first=Eugene |date=1962-04-18 |title=2 Shorts Chosen For Film Festival; Pictures on Sea and Speed Will Compete at Cannes Task for Shostakovich Two Movies Open Today Film Satire Wins Award |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1962/04/18/archives/2-shorts-chosen-for-film-festival-pictures-on-sea-and-speed-will.html |access-date=2025-10-24 |work=The New York Times |pages=30 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Shooting ===

[[File:Il Gattopardo (Visconti, 1963) set esterno Croce dei Vespri.jpg|thumb|Visconti and Lancaster behind the scenes]]

Filming started in May 1962 in [[Palermo]]. The first two weeks of the two-month location shoot in [[Sicily]] were dedicated to battle scenes. After 22 weeks of location scenes, interiors were shot in Rome.<ref>Society To Show Films In Queens: Programs of Shorts Planned for 23 May and 19 June
By Howard Thompson. New York Times 12 May 1962: 15.</ref> The film's climactic ball scene, which was shot in [[Palazzo Valguarnera-Gangi]] in Palermo, became famous for its duration (it runs for over 46 minutes in the completed film) and opulence.

Lancaster called Visconti "the finest director I've ever worked with."<ref name="burt"/> The scenes with Lancaster were shot in English and dubbed into Italian for the Italian version of the film, while most of the other scenes were filmed in Italian and dubbed into English for the English version.<ref name="burt" /> Lancaster was dubbed by [[Corrado Gaipa]], and his French co-star [[Alain Delon]] was dubbed by [[Carlo Sabatini (actor)|Carlo Sabatini]]. [[Archibald Colquhoun (translator)|Archibald Colquhoun]] worked as the film's dialogue director.<ref>'The Leopard' In Its Original Lair: Care and Authenticity Mark screen Version of Modern Classic
By Herbert Mitgang. New York Times 29 July 1962: 69</ref> The French version was written by [[René Barjavel]].<ref>{{cite web |date=31 July 2018 |title=Origine, filiation et famille dans l'oeuvre de René Barjavel (Clermont-Ferrand) |url=https://www.fabula.org/actualites/origine-filiation-et-famille-dans-l-oeuvre-de-rene-barjavel_84565.php}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Biographie &#124; René Barjavel - Écrivain, journaliste, scénariste &#124; Futura Sciences |url=https://www.futura-sciences.com/sciences/personnalites/science-fiction-rene-barjavel-1546/}}</ref>

By May 1963, it was reported the film had cost Titanus $5 million.<ref>{{cite news |last=Hawkins |first=Robert F. |date=5 May 1963 |title=Noted on the Italian Film Scene: Overextension Blamed By Industry Experts For Roman Crisis |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1963/05/05/archives/noted-on-the-italian-film-scene-overextension-blamed-by-industry.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |page=139}}</ref>

== Versions ==

''The Leopard'' has circulated in at least five different versions. Visconti's initial [[workprint]] was 205 minutes long, but both the director and producer felt it was too long, and the film was shortened to 195 minutes for its premiere at the Cannes Film Festival. Visconti then cut the film further—to 185 minutes—for its official Italian release, and considered this version to be his preferred one. In other European countries, the film was released in a 171-minute cut.

===English 1963 version===

Twentieth Century-Fox distributed the movie in both England and the United States, making several significant alterations. They replaced Visconti's vivid [[Technicolor]] images with the far inferior [[DeLuxe Color]] process and downgraded the film from 70mm to 35mm. Additionally, they cut several key scenes, further reducing the runtime from 185 to 161 minutes.<ref name="marcus">{{cite book | last=Marcus | first=M.J. | title=Filmmaking by the Book: Italian Cinema and Literary Adaptation | publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press | year=1993 | isbn=978-0-8018-4455-3 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lu11g489AegC | access-date=2025-03-08 | page=281}}</ref><ref name="nowell">{{cite book | last=Nowell-Smith | first=G. | title=Luchino Visconti | publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing | year=2019 | isbn=978-1-83871-697-4 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=N-XxDwAAQBAJ | access-date=2025-03-08 | page=}}</ref><ref name="kehr">{{cite book | last=Kehr | first=D. | title=When Movies Mattered: Reviews from a Transformative Decade | publisher=University of Chicago Press | year=2011 | isbn=978-0-226-42941-0 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZGgPCODtVZsC | access-date=2025-03-08 | page=}}</ref><ref name="nyt1983"/>

The dubbing was also poorly executed, with issues in the translation, the voices and the synchronization. In contrast, other Italian films of the time, such as those by [[Riccardo Freda]] and [[Vittorio Cottafavi]], were carefully dubbed.<ref name="marcus"/><ref name="nowell"/><ref name="kehr"/> Burt Lancaster and supporting actor [[Leslie French]] were the only ones who re-dubbed their own dialogue.<ref name="sight">{{cite magazine |title=Can the Leopard...? |last=Davies |first=Brenda|magazine=[[Sight and Sound]]|volume=33 |issue=2|date=Spring 1964|page=99}}</ref><ref name=skep/> Critics deemed the dubbing as awful.<ref name="nyt1983">{{cite web | last=Canby | first=Vincent | title=Film View; At 20, 'The Leopard' Is Fleeter Than Ever | website=The New York Times | date=1983-09-11 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/1983/09/11/movies/film-view-at-20-the-leopard-is-fleeter-than-ever.html | access-date=2025-03-09}}</ref>

The result of these changes was a significantly inferior product. As a consequence, the movie was poorly received by both critics and audiences in the US and England, unlike with the rest of Europe where it was well received.

Visconti himself had no control on any of these changes. He threatened to sue Fox, who threatened to counter-sue the director, arguing that Lancaster supervised the American cut.<ref>{{cite news |title=Backers of Film May Site to Stop Director's Attack|newspaper=[[Chicago Tribune]]|date= 20 December 1963 |page=b19}}</ref> "I don't feel it's my film at all," Visconti said of this version.<ref>{{cite news |last=Archer |first=Eugene |date=18 August 1963 |title=Artful Odyssey of an Aristocrat |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1963/08/18/archives/artful-odyssey-of-an-aristocrat.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |page=107}}</ref> It is little surprise, therefore, that he has disavowed the English version of The Leopard and refuses to take any responsibility for it at all.<ref name="nowell"/><ref name="nyt1983"/>

===English 1983 version===
The 1983 print is a product of Fox's newly established 'classics division'. It is the 185-minute intermediate version approved by Visconti for international release. The Italian soundtrack has been restored, and the color has been enhanced to resemble the original Technicolor hues, which are now technically unreproducible. This version was received much more favorably by critics.<ref name="kehr"/><ref name="nyt1983"/>

In 2004, a restored version was released by Fox.<ref name="offscreen">{{cite web | last=Garrett | first=Daniel | title=Luchino Visconti's The Leopard and Those Who Are Not Rich in A Country of Arrangements | website=Offscreen | date=2005-02-11 | url=https://offscreen.com/view/the_leopard | access-date=2025-03-09}}</ref>

== Release ==

The film debuted at the [[1963 Cannes Film Festival]], where it won the [[Palme d'Or]].<ref name="Ress 1963">{{cite news |last=Ress |first=Paul |title='The Leopard' Is Winner of Cannes Film Award |newspaper=[[Chicago Tribune]] |date=24 May 1963 |page=a4}}</ref>

The 185-minute version of the film was finally released in the U.S. in 1983.<ref>{{cite news |title=Movies: Visconti's 'Leopard' Roars Anew |last=Thomas |first=Kevin |newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=30 October 1983 |page=u27}}</ref>

=== Preservation ===
The original 8-perforation [[Technirama]] camera negative for ''The Leopard'' survives and was used by [[The Criterion Collection]] to create their video master for DVD and Blu-ray, with [[Color grading|color timing]] supervised by the film's cinematographer, [[Giuseppe Rotunno]]. New preservation film elements were created using a [[4K resolution|4K]] digital scan of the film, done with the cooperation of the [[Cineteca di Bologna]], [[L'Immagine Ritrovata]], [[The Film Foundation]], [[Gucci]], [[Pathé]], Fondation Jérôme Seydoux-Pathé, [[Twentieth Century Fox]], and Centro Sperimentale di Cinematografia-Cineteca Nazionale.<ref name="fashionandrunway.com">{{cite web |title=Gucci Extends Five-Year Partnership with Martin Scorsese's Film Foundation |url=http://www.fashionandrunway.com/fashion/article.cfm?id_articolo=21519 |access-date=2010-04-30 |work=fashionandrunway.com}}</ref> This restoration premiered at the 2010 Cannes Film Festival.<ref name="Vanity Fair">{{cite magazine |title=Scorsese Restores ''The Leopard'' and Revives Cannes's Golden Age |url=http://www.vanityfair.com/online/oscars/2010/05/scorsese-restores-the-leopard-and-revives-canness-golden-age.html |access-date=2011-03-20 |magazine=Vanity Fair}}</ref>

=== Home media ===
There are several DVD editions of the film available:
* [[DVD region code#Region codes and countries|Region 2]] ([[Italy]]) The Medusa Home Entertainment release (released in 2001) contains the 185-minute Italian version with several bonus features and interviews. (This release is not English-friendly.)
* [[DVD region code#Region codes and countries|Region 2]] ([[U.K.]]) The [[British Film Institute|BFI Video]] release offers a restored version of the Italian cut with an audio commentary by David Forgacs and Rossana Capitano.
* [[DVD region code#Region codes and countries|Region 2]] ([[Japan]]) The [[Toho]] release contains an unrestored version of the Italian cut with both the original audio (and Japanese subtitles), and a rare alternative English dubbed track that is different from that of the shortened U.S. version of the film. Special features include text-based bios and facts in Japanese. (This release is not English-friendly.)
* [[DVD region code#Region codes and countries|Region 1]] ([[U.S.]]) [[The Criterion Collection]] release is a 3-disc set containing a restored version of the 185-minute Italian version (with optional English subtitles), several bonus features, interviews, an audio commentary by [[Peter Cowie]], and the 161-minute U.S. English-dubbed version as an extra.

Blu-ray release:
* [[Blu-ray#A|Region A]] ([[U.S.]]) [[The Criterion Collection]] 2-disc Blu-ray set boasts a transfer of the 185-min Italian version in 1080P, most of the DVD bonus materials, some newly created bonus materials, and the 161-minute U.S. English-dubbed version in 1080i.

== Reception ==
=== Box office ===

The film was successful in Europe. It grossed $370,000 in its first ten days of release in eight Italian cities,<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=17 April 1963|page=4|title='Leopard' Racks Up $370,000 in 10 Days}}</ref> and was the sixth most popular film of the year at the French box office, with 3,688,024 admissions.<ref name="delon"/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.boxofficestory.com/france-1963-c22750377|website=Box Office Story|title=French Box Office in 1963}}</ref> Due to the poor quality cut for U.S. release by Fox, the film did not perform as well in the United States, with [[theatrical rental]]s of $1.8 million.<ref name=rentals/><ref name=skep>{{cite magazine|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=17 December 1969|page=7|title=Traumatic 'Leopard' Experience Made Visconti Skeptical, But Extols WB}}</ref>

=== Critical response ===

''The Leopard'' was well received in Europe, winning the 1963 Palme d'Or at Cannes and achieving both critical and commercial success.<ref>{{cite web | title=The Contiguous World of Luchino Visconti’s The Leopard (1963) – Senses of Cinema | website=Senses of Cinema | date=2006-07-31 | url=https://www.sensesofcinema.com/2016/cteq/the-leopard/ | access-date=2025-03-09}}</ref>

Due to Fox's poor English version, at the time of its release in the summer of 1963, the majority of American critics panned the film. According to ''[[Newsweek]]'', Lancaster looked "as if he's playing [[Clarence Day]]'s ''[[Life with Father]]'' in summer stock."<ref name="Buford 2000 232">{{cite book|last=Buford|first=Kate|title=Burt Lancaster: An American Life|year=2000|publisher=Aurum|location=London|isbn=1-85410-740-2|page=232}}</ref> Jonathan Miller of ''[[The New Yorker]]'' derided Lancaster as "muzzled by whiskers and clearly stunned by the importance of his role."<ref name="Buford 2000 232"/> However, ''[[Time (magazine)|Time Magazine]]'' praised Lancaster's characterization of the Leopard as solid and convincing.<ref name="Buford 2000 232"/>

The 1983 release, featuring its restored 185-minute runtime and Italian soundtrack, received a more favorable response from critics. ''[[New York (magazine)|New York]]'' magazine called the now-famous ballroom scene "almost unbearably moving."<ref name="LLC1983">{{cite journal|title=New York Magazine|website = Newyorkmetro.com|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=J9gBAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA101|date=10 October 1983|publisher=New York Media, LLC|page=101|issn=0028-7369}}</ref> The ''New York Times'' wrote: "The reappearance of this enchanting work proves that, under the right circumstances, two decades make no difference whatsoever but 25 minutes can transform a very good film into a possibly great one."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Canby |first=Vincent |author-link=Vincent Canby |date=1983-09-11 |title=Film View; At 20, 'The Leopard' Is Fleeter Than Ever (Published 1983) |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1983/09/11/movies/film-view-at-20-the-leopard-is-fleeter-than-ever.html?searchResultPosition=1 |access-date=2025-10-24 |work=The New York Times |pages=A21 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="offscreen"/>

After seeing the 1983 re-release in full, critic for ''[[The New Yorker]]'', [[Pauline Kael]] wrote: "It's deeply satisfying to see [''The Leopard]'' in its full length" and goes on to call it a "sweeping popular epic" and that it is "so beautifully felt that it calls up a whole culture. It casts an intelligent spell, intelligent and rapturous."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kael |first=Pauline |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Age_of_Movies_Selected_Writings_of_P/tkShTL84MrcC?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=the+age+of+movies+the+selected+writings+of+pauline+kael&printsec=frontcover |title=The Age of Movies: Selected Writings of Pauline Kael: A Library of America Special Publication |date=2011-10-27 |publisher=Library of America |isbn=978-1-59853-171-8 |pages=723–729 |language=en}}</ref>

After the 2004 release, the [[Washington Post]] praised the film, saying it 'was from a time “when epics looked like epics”, that “the movie all but weeps with a sense of emotional loss” and “we have the sublime satisfaction of a first-time experience with a yesteryear classic”.'<ref name="offscreen"/><ref name="garrett">{{cite web | last=Garrett | first=Daniel | title=Luchino Visconti's The Leopard, a great film focused on Sicilian aristocracy and cultural change – Compulsive Reader | website=Compulsive Reader – Reviews of books by some of the hottest writers working today, exclusive author interviews, literary news and criticism. | date=2012-08-19 | url=https://compulsivereader.com/2012/08/19/luchino-viscontis-the-leopard-a-great-film-focused-on-sicilian-aristocracy-and-cultural-change/ | access-date=2025-03-09}}</ref>

=== Retrospective reviews ===

Mark Lager, on ''[[Senses of Cinema]]'', praised [[Giuseppe Rotunno]]'s cinematography in the film as "baroque and elegiac" and "groundbreaking and reflective".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sensesofcinema.com/2021/feature-articles/dreams-of-italys-past-giuseppe-rotunnos-cinematography-in-amarcord-and-the-leopard/|last=Lager|first=Mark|title=Dreams of Italy's Past - Giuseppe Rotunno's Cinematography in Amarcord and The Leopard|website=[[Senses of Cinema]]|date=2021}}</ref>

The film's reputation continues to rise. Directors [[Martin Scorsese]] and [[Sydney Pollack]] (who had supervised the English-dubbing of the film) consider it to be one of the greatest ever made.<ref name=":2">{{cite web|url=http://www.miramax.com/subscript/scorseses-favorite-films|title=Scorsese's 12 favorite films|publisher=Miramax.com|access-date=25 December 2013|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131226091025/http://www.miramax.com/subscript/scorseses-favorite-films|archive-date=26 December 2013}}</ref><ref name=":40">{{cite web|url=http://old.bfi.org.uk/sightandsound/polls/topten/poll/voter.php?forename=Sydney&surname=Pollack|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120626191807/http://old.bfi.org.uk/sightandsound/polls/topten/poll/voter.php?forename=Sydney&surname=Pollack|url-status=dead|archive-date=26 June 2012|title=In the 2002 Sight & Sound Directors' Poll, Pollack revealed his top ten films in alphabetical order|publisher=BFI.org|access-date=15 August 2023}}</ref> In the decennial poll of critics made by the [[British Film Institute]], ''The Leopard'' was named the 57th greatest film of all time.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.bfi.org.uk/films-tv-people/sightandsoundpoll2012/critics|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160207035347/http://www.bfi.org.uk/films-tv-people/sightandsoundpoll2012/critics|url-status=dead|archive-date=7 February 2016|title = Critics' top 100 &#124; BFI}}</ref>

On [[review aggregator]] website [[Rotten Tomatoes]], the film holds an approval rating of {{RT data|score}} based on {{RT data|count}} reviews, with an average score of {{RT data|average}}; the site's "critics consensus" reads: "Lavish and wistful, ''The Leopard'' features epic battles, sumptuous costumes, and a ballroom waltz that competes for most beautiful sequence committed to film."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/the_leopard_1963|title=The Leopard (2019)|website=[[Rotten Tomatoes]]|publisher=[[Fandango Media|Fandango]]|access-date={{RT data|access date}}}}</ref> On [[Metacritic]], the 2004 re-release of the film holds a perfect 100 out of 100 score based on 12 reviews, indicating "universal acclaim".<ref>{{Citation |title=The Leopard (re-release) |url=https://www.metacritic.com/movie/the-leopard-re-release |access-date=2022-10-27}}</ref>

The film was included by the Vatican in [[Vatican's list of films|a list of important films]] compiled in 1995, under the category of "Art".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://old.usccb.org/movies/vaticanfilms.shtml |title=Vatican Best Films List |work=Official website of the [[United States Conference of Catholic Bishops|U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops]] |access-date=2012-04-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120422064928/http://old.usccb.org/movies/vaticanfilms.shtml |archive-date=2012-04-22 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Television series ==
{{main article|The Leopard (TV series)}}A 5-part streaming television [[miniseries]] based on the novel, was released on Netflix on 5 March 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Aricò |first=Giacomo |date=2023-04-27 |title=Il Gattopardo su Netflix è una serie capolavoro tra la politica dei sentimenti, un super cast e una Sicilia meravigliosa |url=https://www.vogue.it/article/il-gattopardo-netflix-serie-trama-episodi-cast-personaggi |access-date=2025-12-30 |website=Vogue Italia |language=it-IT}}</ref>

'''''The Lighthouse''''' is a 2019<!-- Please do not add a genre to the opening sentence. See the talk page of this article for more information--> film directed and produced by [[Robert Eggers]], from a screenplay he wrote with his brother Max Eggers. It stars [[Willem Dafoe]] and [[Robert Pattinson]] as turmoiled nineteenth-century [[lighthouse keeper]]s stranded at a remote [[New England]] outpost by a violent storm. The film has defied [[Film genre|genre]] categorization in media, leading to multiple interpretations from critics.

The idea of ''The Lighthouse'' originated from a script based on [[Edgar Allan Poe]]'s incomplete short story "[[The Light-House]]", which was written by Max. Eggers researched for source material and developed the plot from [[Smalls Lighthouse#Smalls Lighthouse Tragedy|a nineteenth-century legend of an accident at a Welsh lighthouse]]. ''The Lighthouse'' draws visually from photography of 1890s New England, maritime-themed French films from the 1930s, and [[Symbolism (movement)|symbolist]] art. [[Principal photography]] took place in [[Nova Scotia]], Canada, beginning in April 2018 and lasting slightly over a month. It was shot in [[black-and-white]], with a nearly-square [[Aspect ratio (image)#Previous and currently used aspect ratios|1.19:1 aspect ratio]] to express the lighthouse's vertical orientation and isolation of the characters. [[Mark Korven]] developed the film's score, evoking the sounds and [[the sea in culture|mythologies of the sea]].

The film premiered at the [[2019 Cannes Film Festival|Cannes Film Festival]] on May 19, 2019, and was theatrically released in the United States by [[A24]] on October 18, 2019. It grossed over $18 million, against an $11 million budget, and received critical acclaim, with particular praise for the direction, visuals, and performances of Dafoe and Pattinson. Among its numerous accolades, the film was nominated for Best Cinematography at the [[92nd Academy Awards]] and the [[73rd British Academy Film Awards]].

==Plot==
<!-- Per WP:FILMPLOT, plot summaries for feature films should be set between 400 to 700 words only. -->
In the 1890s, Ephraim Winslow begins a four-week stint as a "wickie" ([[lighthouse keeper]]) on an isolated island off the coast of New England, under the supervision of former sailor Thomas Wake. Winslow discovers a small [[scrimshaw]] of a [[mermaid]] and keeps it in his jacket. Wake proves to be demanding, and Winslow empties [[chamber pot]]s, maintains the machinery, carries heavy [[kerosene]] tanks up the stairs, and paints the lighthouse. Wake bars Winslow from the lantern room; Winslow discovers Wake disrobes before the light every night. During his stay on the island, Winslow begins to hallucinate [[sea monster]]s and logs floating in the sea, and [[masturbation|masturbates]] to the mermaid on the scrimshaw. Winslow is bothered by a one-eyed [[gull]], but Wake warns him against killing it under the [[Sailors' superstitions|superstitious]] belief that gulls are reincarnated sailors. Wake reveals to Winslow that his previous wickie died after losing his sanity. Winslow tells Wake he's a former [[Lumberjack|timberman]] from [[Maine]] who was stationed in Canada and is now seeking a new trade.

The day before his scheduled departure, Winslow discovers a dead gull fouling the drinking water in the [[cistern]]. The one-eyed gull attacks him and he bludgeons it to death. The wind drastically changes and Winslow and Wake spend the night getting drunk during a severe storm that prevents the [[lighthouse tender]] from collecting them. As Winslow empties the chamber pots, he discovers the beached body of a mermaid, which waves and howls at him. He flees back to the cottage, where Wake informs him the storm has spoiled their rations. Winslow assumes the tender is merely a day late, but Wake says that they have already been stranded for weeks. 

As the storm continues to rage, Winslow and Wake get drunk every night and alternate between moments of intimacy and hostility. One night, Winslow tries unsuccessfully to steal the lantern room keys from Wake and contemplates murdering him. Winslow later sees the one-eyed head of Wake's previous wickie in a [[lobster trap]]. Winslow drunkenly confesses to Wake that his real name is Thomas Howard, and he assumed the identity of Ephraim Winslow, a cruel foreman in Canada whom he deliberately allowed to drown during a [[log driving|log drive]]. Howard has a menacing vision of Wake accusing Howard of "spilling [his] beans" and runs to the [[Dory (boat)|dory]] to try to leave the island. Wake destroys the boat with an axe. Back at their lodgings, Wake claims it was Howard who hacked up the dory, driven mad by his confession.

Howard and Wake run out of alcohol and turn to drinking sweetened [[turpentine]]. That night, a giant wave crashes through the wall of their cottage and floods it. In the morning, Howard finds Wake's logbook, in which Wake has criticized him as a drunken and incompetent employee and recommended he be fired without pay. The two men argue, and Howard attacks Wake while hallucinating the mermaid, the real Winslow, and Wake as a [[Proteus]]-like figure. Howard beats Wake into submission and takes him to the hole at the base of the lighthouse to [[Premature burial|bury him alive]]. Before losing consciousness, Wake describes a "[[Prometheus|Promethean]]" punishment that awaits those who look in the lantern, and Howard takes the keys to the lantern room.

Howard goes to get a cigarette, and Wake returns and strikes him with the axe. Howard disarms and kills Wake before ascending the lighthouse. In the lantern room, the [[Fresnel lens]] opens to Howard, who reaches in and screams before falling down the lighthouse steps. Howard ends up lying nude on the rocks with a damaged eye as a flock of gulls peck at his exposed organs.

==Production==
===Development===
[[File:Robert Eggers - The Witch,Fantastic Fest 2015-1667 (28894993650) (cropped).jpg |thumb|upright|alt=|Robert Eggers in 2015]]

The original idea for ''The Lighthouse'' was first articulated at a dinner between director [[Robert Eggers]] and his younger brother, Max Eggers. Eggers was unhappy with his film industry prospects after the pitching of his first major feature, ''[[The Witch (2015 film)|The Witch]]'' (2015), failed to secure funding.<ref name=RS1025>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/movies/movie-features/robert-eggers-the-lighthouse-interview-898545/ |title=Drunken Sailors and Movie Stars: Robert Eggers on Making 'The Lighthouse' |magazine=[[Rolling Stone]] |url-access=limited |first=David |last=Fear |date=October 25, 2019 |access-date=November 17, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191028235947/https://www.rollingstone.com/movies/movie-features/robert-eggers-the-lighthouse-interview-898545/ |archive-date=October 28, 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url= https://deadline.com/2019/10/the-lighthouse-robert-eggers-willem-dafoe-robert-pattinson-contenders-london-1202753044/ |title= How Robert Eggers Built 'The Lighthouse' – The Contenders London |website=[[Deadline Hollywood]] |first=Anthony |last=D'Alessandro |date=October 5, 2019 |access-date=February 3, 2021|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210203204340/https://deadline.com/2019/10/the-lighthouse-robert-eggers-willem-dafoe-robert-pattinson-contenders-london-1202753044/ |archive-date=February 3, 2021|url-status=live}}</ref> Max shared the basic outline of his screenplay, a lighthouse-set ghost tale tentatively titled ''Burnt Island'', based on his interpretation of [[Edgar Allan Poe]]'s unfinished short story "[[The Light-House]]".<ref name=RS1025/> Max struggled with his treatment to the extent that progress stalled.<ref name=RS1025/> Eggers began brainstorming ideas and, with his brother's support, soon began investigating for source material.<ref name=RS1025/>

One story that caught the director's attention in his research was a nineteenth-century myth of an accident at [[Smalls Lighthouse]] in [[Wales]], wherein one of two wickies, both named Thomas, died while trapped at the outpost by a destructive storm. That both men were named Thomas, Eggers recalled, persuaded him to create a film with an underlying story of identity.<ref name="Vox">{{cite web |last=Wilkinson |first=Alissa |date=October 15, 2019 |title=The Witch director Robert Eggers spills his beans about The Lighthouse |url=https://www.vox.com/culture/2019/10/15/20914097/robert-eggers-lighthouse-interview-witch |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210202015136/https://www.vox.com/culture/2019/10/15/20914097/robert-eggers-lighthouse-interview-witch |archive-date=February 2, 2021 |access-date=February 1, 2021 |website=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]}}</ref> However, Eggers stopped working on ''The Lighthouse'' when he found an investor to finance ''The Witch''.<ref name=RS1025/>

The unexpected success of ''The Witch'' elevated Eggers's directing profile. To exploit his newfound credibility, he pushed ''The Lighthouse'', among several other projects, in his negotiations with studio executives.<ref name=RS1025/> He and Max then resumed their work by exchanging and revising drafts. This coincided with more rigorous research of the period to develop the onscreen world; Eggers sought out photos of 1890s New England, 1930s maritime-themed French films, and [[Symbolism (movement)|symbolist]] art for visual reference.<ref name=RS1025/><ref name=Vox/>

The Eggers' study of literature with maritime and [[Surrealism|surrealist]] themes influenced the film's dialogue.<ref name=slate/> They looked into the writings of [[Herman Melville]], [[Robert Louis Stevenson]], and [[H. P. Lovecraft]], among others, before coming across the work of [[Sarah Orne Jewett]], a novelist best known for her [[American literary regionalism|local color works]] set in coastal Maine. Her dialect-heavy writing style provided the cadences of the lead characters, rooted in the experiences of her novel characters and real-life farmers, fishermen, and captains she had interviewed.<ref name=RS1025/><ref name="slate">{{cite web |last=Bloomer |first=Jeffrey |date=October 22, 2019 |title=The Director of The Lighthouse Spills a Few Beans About His Movie's Puzzling Ending |url=https://slate.com/culture/2019/10/the-lighthouse-ending-meaning-director-robert-eggers-interview.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210206002443/https://slate.com/culture/2019/10/the-lighthouse-ending-meaning-director-robert-eggers-interview.html |archive-date=February 6, 2021 |access-date=February 4, 2021 |work=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]}}</ref> The Eggers also referred to a dissertation on Jewett's use of dialects as guidance for more dramatic conversational scenes.<ref name=RS1025/><ref name=slate/>

Another creative force shaping ''The Lighthouse'' was the Eggers' theater background. The two men drew from playwrights that influenced their work as young teens, chiefly artists such as [[Samuel Beckett]], [[Harold Pinter]], and [[Sam Shepard]], whose writings examine male-centric perspectives of existential crises and psychosis.<ref name=RS1025/>

The film stars [[Willem Dafoe]] and [[Robert Pattinson]], who approached Eggers independently.<ref name="latimes">{{Cite news |last=Whipp |first=Glenn |date=October 24, 2019 |title=Robert Pattinson, Willem Dafoe and the 'orgasm that won't stop' in 'The Lighthouse' |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |url=https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/movies/story/2019-10-24/lighthouse-explained-robert-pattinson-willem-dafoe |url-status=live |url-access=limited |access-date=March 14, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210206100256/https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/movies/story/2019-10-24/lighthouse-explained-robert-pattinson-willem-dafoe |archive-date=February 6, 2021}}</ref> Pattinson originally met Eggers to discuss a proposal to portray a [[Victorian era|Victorian]] socialite in an unrelated project. This was rejected by Pattinson as he believed the role would fail to challenge his acting ability.<ref name=RS1025/> His next meeting with Eggers took place once he finished reading ''The Lighthouse''{{'s}} completed script. According to Eggers, during their conversation, Pattinson showed him a clip of an intoxicated man screaming "I am a demon" to express his understanding of the expectations of his role.<ref name=RS1025/>

Eggers's initial film proposals with Dafoe were also not fruitful.<ref name=RS1025/><ref name=Dl2>{{cite web |url= https://deadline.com/2019/12/the-lighthouse-robert-pattinson-willem-dafoe-robert-eggers-the-partnership-interview-news-1202810915/ |title= The Partnership: Robert Pattinson & Willem Dafoe On Their Tense Two-Hander, Contrasting Styles & Appreciation For Robert Eggers |website=[[Deadline Hollywood]] |first=Joe |last=Utichi |date=December 23, 2019|access-date=February 8, 2021|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210208184655/https://deadline.com/2019/12/the-lighthouse-robert-pattinson-willem-dafoe-robert-eggers-the-partnership-interview-news-1202810915/ |archive-date=February 8, 2021|url-status=live}}</ref> The director used Pattinson's participation in ''The Lighthouse'' to convince Dafoe because they already had a rapport.<ref name=Dl2/> When they met in person to discuss the project, Dafoe recalled that Eggers was plainspoken in the conversation: "There was no discussion. 'This is the way we're going to do this. My way or the highway.' That's very unusual, especially for a [[two-hander]], for a director to say, 'This is the way I see it. Yes or no?{{Single+double}}<ref name=Dl2/> 

Details about the actors and producers involved emerged in the media by February 2018.<ref name=DL0207>{{cite web |url=https://deadline.com/2018/02/willem-dafoe-robert-eggers-the-lighthouse-the-florida-project-a24-new-regency-1202281074/ |title=Willem Dafoe Alights For Robert Eggers-Directed 'The Lighthouse' |website=[[Deadline Hollywood]] |first=Mike Jr. |last=Fleming |date=February 7, 2018 |access-date=April 9, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180415093602/https://deadline.com/2018/02/willem-dafoe-robert-eggers-the-lighthouse-the-florida-project-a24-new-regency-1202281074/|archive-date=April 15, 2018|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://deadline.com/2018/02/robert-pattinson-robert-eggers-the-lighthouse-rodrigo-teixera-a24-new-regency-1202290094/ |title=Robert Pattinson Joins Robert Eggers' Fantasy Horror Film 'The Lighthouse' |website=[[Deadline Hollywood]] |first=Mike Jr. |last=Fleming |date=February 15, 2018 |access-date=April 9, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180403173437/https://deadline.com/2018/02/robert-pattinson-robert-eggers-the-lighthouse-rodrigo-teixera-a24-new-regency-1202290094/|archive-date=April 3, 2018|url-status=live}}</ref> At one point, [[Anya Taylor-Joy]] pursued Eggers offering to play the mermaid, which Eggers opposed.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Starkey |first1=Adam |title=Anya Taylor-Joy asked to play ''The Lighthouse'' mermaid but the director said no |url=https://www.nme.com/news/film/anya-taylor-joy-mermaid-the-lighthouse-3204991 |website=[[NME]] |date=April 14, 2022|access-date=April 17, 2022}}</ref> To prepare for their scenes, each actor employed different techniques at the rehearsals. Dafoe, citing his theater background with the experimental troupe [[The Wooster Group]], drew from his spontaneous acting style in rehearsals, whereas Pattinson planned his rehearsing from the discussion of the script.<ref name=RS1025/><ref name=latimes/>
{{clear}}

===Filming===
[[File:NS-00082 - The Lighthouse film set (41472530721).jpg|thumb|upright|alt=A lighthouse|''The Lighthouse'' film set, [[Nova Scotia]], Canada (pictured in April 2018)]]

Because the filmmakers could not find a lighthouse suitable for the needs of the production, they constructed a 70-foot (20-meter) makeshift lighthouse on [[Cape Forchu, Nova Scotia|Cape Forchu]] in Leif Erikson Park in [[Yarmouth County]], [[Nova Scotia]].<ref name=RS1025/><ref name=AP0519/><ref name=varietyforchu/> The lighthouse was outfitted with a replica [[Frensel lens#Lighthouse lens sizes|3rd-order Fresnel lens]] built by Artworks Florida, a company specializing in reproduction lenses.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.awardsdaily.com/2019/10/28/interview-craig-lathrop-on-building-the-sets-for-the-lighthouse/ |title=Interview: Craig Lathrop on Building the Sets for ‘The Lighthouse’ |last=Anderson |first=Erik |publisher=[[Awards Daily]] |date=October 28, 2019 |access-date=August 3, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230129144319/https://www.awardsdaily.com/2019/10/28/interview-craig-lathrop-on-building-the-sets-for-the-lighthouse/|archive-date=January 29, 2023|url-status=live}}</ref> It was made of [[Poly(methyl methacrylate)|plexiglass]] and had an [[octopus]]-like design with eight panels.<ref name=asc/> [[A24]] later auctioned the lens alongside other props from the film for charity, though it failed to sell.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://decider.com/2020/04/22/uncut-gems-the-lighthouse-a24-auctions/ |title=A24 Auctions off Props from ‘The for a $1.673 million tax subsidy from the Nova Scotian government.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://globalnews.ca/news/6403349/nova-scotia-academy-award-nomination-the-lighthouse/ |title= ‘The Lighthouse,’ shot in Nova Scotia, nominated for Academy Award in cinematography |first=Graeme |last=Benjamin |publisher=[[Global News]]|date=January 13, 2020|access-date=August 6, 2026|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20260311195520/https://globalnews.ca/news/6403349/nova-scotia-academy-award-nomination-the-lighthouse/ |archive-date=March 11, 2026|url-status=live}}</ref>
 
''The Lighthouse'' is director of photography [[Jarin Blaschke]]'s third collaboration with Eggers.<ref name=asc/><ref name=LATimes1112>{{cite web |url=https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/movies/story/2019-11-12/crafts-lighthouse |title=Atmosphere infuses the 'particularly photographic' black-and-white 'Lighthouse' |website=[[Los Angeles Times]] |first=Daron |last=James |date=November 12, 2019 |access-date=November 18, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191117110143/https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/movies/story/2019-11-12/crafts-lighthouse |archive-date=November 17, 2019 |url-status=live |url-access=limited}}</ref> Eggers wanted to film in [[black-and-white]] with a boxy [[aspect ratio]].<ref name=RS1025/><ref name=kodak>{{cite web |url= https://www.kodak.com/en/motion/blog-post/robert-eggers-the-lighthouse |title= Kodak B&W; film delivers a unique visual signature to Robert Eggers' acclaimed fantasy horror 'The Lighthouse' |publisher=[[Kodak]]|date=May 16, 2019|access-date=May 23, 2022|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20211224041504/https://www.kodak.com/en/motion/blog-post/robert-eggers-the-lighthouse |archive-date=December 24, 2021|url-status=live}}</ref> They faced opposition from executives seeking a more widespread distribution in theaters, but felt shooting in color would undermine the film's artistic integrity.<ref name=asc/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.creativeplanetnetwork.com/news/lost-in-time-how-the-cinematography-of-the-lighthouse-evokes-the-19th-century|title=Lost in Time: How the Cinematography of "The Lighthouse" Evokes the 19th Century|date=December 3, 2019|first=Jennifer|last=Wolfe|website=Creative Planet Network|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210405180225/https://www.creativeplanetnetwork.com/news/lost-in-time-how-the-cinematography-of-the-lighthouse-evokes-the-19th-century|archive-date=April 5, 2021|url-status=live|access-date=April 5, 2021}}</ref> In pre-production, Eggers planned to shoot the film in 1.33:1 aspect ratio. He reconsidered when Blaschke suggested shooting in [[Aspect ratio (image)#Previous and currently used aspect ratios|1.19:1 aspect ratio]], which was used fleetingly during the film industry's transition to [[sound film|sound]], as a joke.<ref name=asc/><ref name=kodak/> They found that the footage better conveyed the lighthouse's vertical orientation, the isolation of the characters, and a sense of confinement when Winslow and Wake are together.<ref name=asc/> The filmmakers cited ''[[M (1931 film)|M]]'' (1931), ''[[Man of Aran]]'' (1934), ''[[Pickpocket (film)|Pickpocket]]'' (1959), ''[[In Cold Blood (film)|In Cold Blood]]'' (1967), and the works of [[Béla Tarr]] and [[Ingmar Bergman]] as significant influences on the film's visual hallmarks.<ref name=asc/><ref name=kodak/>

===Cinematography===

''The Lighthouse'' was shot on [[35 mm movie film|35&nbsp;mm film]] using [[Panavision cameras#Panaflex Millennium|Panavision Panaflex Millennium XL2]] cameras with vintage Bausch and Lomb Baltar lenses. Occasionally, to capture flashback sequences or scenes of heightened conflict, the camera crew shot with three [[Petzval lens]]es and another 50 mm lens that had been refurbished by [[Panavision]].<ref name=asc/> Filmmakers created the onscreen world with a stark visual palette reminiscent of [[Orthochromasia|orthochromatic]] film. One of Blaschke's initial responsibilities was to produce the shots with a sufficient antique quality. He developed a process of testing the utility of digital footage in color negative film stock, first with [[List of motion picture film stocks#Vision3 color negative (ECN-2 process 2007–present)|Kodak Vision3 500T 5219]] film and then [[Eastman Kodak|Eastman]] Double-X 5222 stock.<ref name=kodak/> Blaschke continued this process after acquiring the Baltar lenses for the shoot, this time with [[optical filter#Shortpass|shortpass filters]]—a class of scientific optical filters—and [[photographic filter]]s most transparent to blue-green and ultraviolet light.<ref name=kodak/> The specifications were so unusual that it required the manufacture of custom sets of filters by [[Schneider Kreuznach]], which was expensive and time-consuming. Blaschke recalled, "I sketched a desired spectrograph on graph paper, indicating a complete elimination of all light beyond 570 nanometers [mid-yellow] while allowing all shorter wavelengths to pass freely. At that point, I was unsure of the true light loss and I was pretty nervous about it."<ref name=asc/> Post-production editing of ''The Lighthouse'' occurred simultaneously at the [[FotoKem]] film laboratories in [[Burbank, California]].<ref name=kodak/>

[[File:TheLighthouseLighting.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|Screenshot of Wake and Winslow in a drunken argument at night. The filmmakers deployed artificial lighting for both day and nighttime scenes, in this case a single lantern equipped with a halogen bulb.]]

Lighting, especially for night scenes, posed a challenge for the camera crew because they were shooting at a low [[film speed]], which made film stock less sensitive to light.<ref name=kodak/><ref name=LATimes1112/> This was compounded by the fact that the Double-X 5222 stock had a substantially lower capacity for [[exposure latitude]] than either color film stock or digital film.<ref name=kodak/><ref name=varietylighting>{{cite magazine |last=Valentini |first=Valentina I. |date=October 17, 2019 |title=How Bright Bulbs Enabled ‘The Lighthouse’s’ Tough Black-and-White Shoot |url=https://variety.com/2019/artisans/spotlight/the-lighthouse-cinematography-black-and-white-1203373400/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250817121841/https://variety.com/2019/artisans/spotlight/the-lighthouse-cinematography-black-and-white-1203373400/ |archive-date=August 17, 2025 |access-date=August 7, 2026 |magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]}}</ref> The filmmakers therefore deployed artificial lights when scenes could not be sufficiently rendered with only natural lighting.<ref name=kodak/> They rigged exterior nighttime scenes with 9K and 18K [[hydrargyrum medium-arc iodide lamp|HMI]] lamps manufactured in Nova Scotia and Toronto; these lamps were also used for daytime shots, in a setup involving the reflection of light off of stretched [[muslin]] fixtures.<ref name=LATimes1112/><ref name=indielighting>{{cite web |last=O'Falt |first=Chris |date=January 31, 2020 |title=The Visual Language of ‘The Lighthouse’ Is So Much More Than Black-and-White |url=https://www.indiewire.com/awards/industry/the-lighthouse-best-cinematography-oscar-nominee-jarin-blaschke-robert-eggers-1202207495/|url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250312200506/https://www.indiewire.com/awards/industry/the-lighthouse-best-cinematography-oscar-nominee-jarin-blaschke-robert-eggers-1202207495/ |archive-date=March 12, 2025 |access-date=August 6, 2026 |website=[[IndieWire]]}}</ref> For the interior night scenes, sets were lit by a single [[lantern]] equipped with 500- and 800-[[watt]] [[halogen lamp|halogen bulbs]], occasionally supplemented by a [[paper lantern]] for close up shots.<ref name=LATimes1112/><ref name=varietylighting/> The lights, according to Blaschke, were so bright that some camera crew wore sunglasses on the set.<ref name=indielighting/>

===Costumes===

Eggers worked with costume designer [[Linda Muir]] to develop ''The Lighthouse''{{'s}} costumes.<ref name=costumes1>{{cite web |last=|first=|date=October 18, 2019 |title=So You Think You Can Dress Like a Period-Accurate 19th Century Lighthouse Keeper |url=https://a24films.com/notes/2019/10/so-you-think-you-can-dress-like-a-19th-century-lighthouse-keeper |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260625035836/https://a24films.com/notes/2019/10/so-you-think-you-can-dress-like-a-19th-century-lighthouse-keeper |archive-date=June 25, 2026 |access-date=August 6, 2026 |publisher=[[A24]]}}</ref> The setting, the film's black-and-white aesthetic, and the personalities of the characters, Muir says, compelled her clothing choices.<ref name=costume3/> Muir dressed Dafoe in ragged clothes to project a "maritime look and feel" for his character.<ref name=costume2/> For example, with Wake's jackets, she indicates his demeanor by the number, type, and placement of buttons.<ref name=costume2/> On the other hand, Pattinson's costumes reflected a style Muir said was deliberately ambiguous.<ref name=costume4>{{cite magazine |last=Wells |first=Jonathan |date=October 23, 2020 |title=How to pick your knitwear, according to The Lighthouse costume designer |url=https://www.thegentlemansjournal.com/article/jumpers-sweater-lighthouse-costumer-designer-willem-dafoe-robert-pattinson-knitwear/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201023214329/https://www.thegentlemansjournal.com/article/jumpers-sweater-lighthouse-costumer-designer-willem-dafoe-robert-pattinson-knitwear/ |archive-date=October 23, 2020 |access-date=August 6, 2026 |magazine=The Gentleman's Journal}}</ref> Eggers used photos of lighthouse workers in different [[workwear]] as reference material, but was not consciously seeking to convey ideas through the costumes beyond Winslow and Wake's occupation.<ref name=costume3>{{cite magazine |last=Renwick |first=Finlay |date=February 3, 2020 |title=Inside The Salty Seadog Style Of The Lighthouse |url=https://www.esquire.com/uk/culture/film/a30745953/the-lighthouse-movie-style-robert-pattinson-willem-dafoe/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251208020656/https://www.esquire.com/uk/culture/film/a30745953/the-lighthouse-movie-style-robert-pattinson-willem-dafoe/ |archive-date=December 8, 2025 |access-date=August 6, 2026 |magazine=[[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]]}}</ref><ref name=costume2>{{cite magazine |last=Tangcay |first=Jazz |date=December 18, 2019 |title=A Look at the Photo Research Behind Robert Eggers’ ‘The Lighthouse’ |url=https://variety.com/2019/artisans/awards/robert-eggers-willem-dafoe-robert-pattinson-the-lighthouse-1203447497/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251212191534/https://variety.com/2019/artisans/awards/robert-eggers-willem-dafoe-robert-pattinson-the-lighthouse-1203447497/ |archive-date=December 12, 2025 |access-date=August 6, 2026 |magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]}}</ref>

Winslow and Wake's wardrobe consists of four looks each; a uniform, undergarments, a thick [[cable knitting|cable knit]] sweater outfit, and an [[oilskin]] outfit waterproofed with wax or oil.<ref name=costumes1/> The designers sourced and created many pieces anew because there were not widely available for purchase.<ref name=costume2/> It was particularly expensive to produce period accurate footwear, such as [[Wellington boot]]s.<ref name=costume5>{{cite magazine |last=Antrim |first=Taylor |date=October 21, 2019 |title=Behind the Scenes of The Lighthouse, the Strangest, Spookiest Movie of the Year |url=https://www.vogue.com/article/robert-eggers-interview-the-lighthouse |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260517183845/https://www.vogue.com/article/robert-eggers-interview-the-lighthouse |archive-date=May 17, 2026 |access-date=August 6, 2026 |magazine=[[Vogue (magazine)|Vogue]]}}</ref> To rectify the issue, the filmmakers made use of shoes commonly used in professional [[theater]].<ref name=costume5/> The most difficult items for the filmmakers to obtain were the oilskin pieces, given that there were no readily available garments in circulation.<ref name=costume3/> The costume-making crew designed hats, overalls, and coats that Muir then waxed and dried in the sun to achieve the desired quality.<ref name=costume2/> They also developed the cable knit sweaters from scratch on finding that modern sweaters were lacking the appropriate detail.<ref name=costume2/><ref name=costumes6>{{cite magazine |last=Tashjian |first=Rachel |date=October 31, 2019 |title=“The Lighthouse” Is a Film About Men Arguing In Moldy, Beautiful Sweaters |url=https://www.gq.com/story/the-lighthouse-sweaters |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260103152401/https://www.gq.com/story/the-lighthouse-sweaters |archive-date=January 3, 2026 |access-date=August 6, 2026 |magazine=[[GQ]]}}</ref>

=== Music ===
{{Main|The Lighthouse (soundtrack)|l1=''The Lighthouse'' (soundtrack)}}

''The Lighthouse'' was scored by composer [[Mark Korven]], his second film collaboration with Eggers. The filmmakers distinguished the score from ''The Witch'' with music suggestive of the sounds and [[The sea in culture|mythologies of the sea]]. They also aimed to express the reactions of the characters in isolation.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Erbland |first=Kate |date=September 25, 2019 |title='The Lighthouse' Exclusive: Try Staying Sane Listening to Mark Korven's Original Score |url=https://www.indiewire.com/features/general/the-lighthouse-composer-mark-korven-soundtrack-1202176365/ |access-date=June 8, 2023 |website=IndieWire |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="fmm">{{Cite web |last=Macaulay |first=Scott |date=December 10, 2019 |title=Sonic Menace: Composer Mark Korven on Scoring Robert Eggers's The Lighthouse |url=https://filmmakermagazine.com/108698-sonic-menace/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220706233941/https://filmmakermagazine.com/108698-sonic-menace/ |archive-date=July 6, 2022 |access-date=June 8, 2023 |website=Filmmaker Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=flaunt>{{Cite web |date=January 18, 2017 |title=Robert Eggers' of The Lighthouse Q+A {{!}} Motion Picture Soundtrack Release |url=https://archive.flaunt.com/content/robert-eggers-qa-mark-korven-the-lighthouse |website=Flaunt Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref> The earliest musical approach was inspired by [[sea shanties]] and [[conch (instrument)|conch music]], and the filmmakers created a placeholder [[temp score]] from a playlist containing horror movie scores, ancient Greek conch music, and compositions of Italian composer [[Giacinto Scelsi]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 31, 2023 |title=Mark Korven on horror, Robert Eggers and the brilliance of Bach |url=https://faroutmagazine.co.uk/mark-korven-on-horror-robert-eggers/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230608145638/https://faroutmagazine.co.uk/mark-korven-on-horror-robert-eggers/ |archive-date=June 8, 2023 |access-date=June 8, 2023 |website=Far Out Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Scorer |first=The Film |date=December 5, 2021 |title=An Interview with Mark Korven |url=https://thefilmscorer.com/an-interview-with-mark-korven/ was recorded using a cello, double bass, brass, percussion, woodwinds, a [[harmonica]], and [[mallet]]s that produced friction noises when rubbed on rough surfaces.<ref name="fmm" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Burlingame |first=Jon |date=November 14, 2019 |title=Film Composers Tap Into Offbeat Inspirations for Scores request.<ref name="fmm" /> Korven found scoring the ending scene the most difficult because the music had to support the scene's emotionally intense tone.<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 22, 2020
