The [[The Lighthouse (soundtrack)|soundtrack]] was released by [[Milan Records]] digitally on October 18, 2019, followed by the rollout of an [[LP record]] by [[Sacred Bones Records]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mark Korven: The Lighthouse - Soundtrack |url=https://milanrecords.com/release/the-lighthouse-original-motion-picture-soundtrack/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211028084915/https://milanrecords.com/release/the-lighthouse-original-motion-picture-soundtrack/ |archive-date=October 28, 2021 |access-date=June 8, 2023 |website=Milan Records |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The Lighthouse: Original Soundtrack |url=https://www.sacredbonesrecords.com/products/sbr232-mark-korven-the-lighthouse |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200919023624/https://www.sacredbonesrecords.com/products/sbr232-mark-korven-the-lighthouse |archive-date=September 19, 2020 |access-date=June 8, 2023 |website=Sacred Bones Records |language=en}}</ref>

==Analysis==
===Genre===
''The Lighthouse'' has been described as a [[horror film]] by critics such as [[Manohla Dargis]] of ''[[The New York Times]]'', and as a [[psychological thriller]] by critics such as Lee Marshall of ''[[Screen Daily]]''.<ref name="NYT">{{Cite news|last=Dargis|first=Manohla|author-link=Manohla Dargis|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/10/16/movies/the-lighthouse-review.html|title='The Lighthouse' Review: Dark Nights, Troubled Souls, Hairy Men|date=October 16, 2019|work=The New York Times|access-date=March 28, 2020|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200417042921/https://www.nytimes.com/2019/10/16/movies/the-lighthouse-review.html|archive-date=April 17, 2020|url-access=limited}}</ref><ref name="ScreenDaily" /> Other critics said it was a film that could not be pigeonholed, with [[Owen Gleiberman]] of ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' declaring that "you may feel in your bones that you're watching a supernatural shocker [...] Are we seeing a slice of survival, a horror film, or a study in slow-brewing mutual insanity? How about all of the above?"<ref name="varrev" /> [[Michael Phillips (critic)|Michael Phillips]] of ''[[The Chicago Tribune]]'' echoed Gleiberman's statements, noting that the film's plot did not operate "as any sort of conventional ghost story, or thriller, or anything".<ref name="CTReview">{{cite web|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/entertainment/movies/michael-phillips/sc-mov-lighthouse-pattinson-dafoe-rev-1016-20191016-nfiv6urxtfce7br5lhg4lu73lm-story.html|title='The Lighthouse' review: Robert Pattinson and Willem Dafoe in a bamboozler of a tale from the maker of 'The Witch'|date=October 16, 2019|url-access=limited|first=Michael|last=Phillips|author-link=Michael Phillips (critic)|website=[[Chicago Tribune]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210405175632/https://www.chicagotribune.com/entertainment/movies/michael-phillips/sc-mov-lighthouse-pattinson-dafoe-rev-1016-20191016-nfiv6urxtfce7br5lhg4lu73lm-story.html|archive-date=April 5, 2021|url-status=live|access-date=April 5, 2021}}</ref>

Eggers himself describes the genre as being akin to "a [[Weird fiction|weird tale]]".<ref>{{Cite web |date=July 17, 2019 |title=Deep Cuts with Robert Eggers & Ari Aster |url=https://a24films.com/notes/2019/07/deep-cuts-with-robert-eggers-and-ari-aster |access-date=September 3, 2023 |website=a24films.com |language=en}}</ref> Pattinson stated in ''[[GQ]]'' that he thinks the film is "100% a comedy" and how when the film was up for awards season, he tried to convince the [[Hollywood Foreign Press Association]] that the film should be eligible for a nomination in  the [[Golden Globe Award for Best Motion Picture – Musical or Comedy|Golden Globe for Best Motion Picture – Musical or Comedy]] category.<ref>{{cite AV media

===Psychoanalysis===
Eggers said the film's subtext was influenced by [[Sigmund Freud]] and he hoped that "it's a movie where both [[Carl Jung|Jung]] and Freud would be furiously eating their popcorn".<ref name="Joho-2019">{{Cite web|url=https://mashable.com/article/the-lighthouse-robert-eggers-meaning-explained-ending/|title=What the hell did 'The Lighthouse' even mean?|last=Joho|first=Jess|date=October 20, 2019|website=[[Mashable]]|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200329002700/https://mashable.com/article/the-lighthouse-robert-eggers-meaning-explained-ending/|archive-date=March 29, 2020|access-date=March 28, 2020}}</ref><ref name="Jacobs-2019">{{Cite news|last=Jacobs|first=Matthew|url=https://www.huffingtonpost.ca/entry/the-lighthouse-homoeroticism-robert-pattinson-willem-dafoe_n_5da9c888e4b0e71d65b801ae?ri18n=true|title='He Sort Of Wants A Daddy': Decoding The Homoeroticism In 'The Lighthouse'|date=October 20, 2019|work=[[Huffington Post]]|access-date=March 28, 2020|archive-date=June 25, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210625173607/https://www.huffingtonpost.ca/entry/the-lighthouse-homoeroticism-robert-pattinson-willem-dafoe_n_5da9c888e4b0e71d65b801ae?ri18n=true|url-status=live}}</ref> Given his simultaneous fear and admiration of the senior lighthouse keeper, the younger keeper displays an [[Oedipus complex|Oedipal]] fixation. Pattinson commented on the father–son dynamic in the film by stating that "I was pretty conscious of how I wanted the relationship to come across. In a lot of ways, he sort of wants a daddy" and that, as the film progresses, his character is increasingly "looking for Willem [Dafoe]'s validation" as both a boss and a father-figure.<ref name="Jacobs-2019" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Dim9GE891gQ|title=Robert Pattinson & Robert Eggers Break Down a Scene from 'The Lighthouse'|last=Fandango All Access|date=October 29, 2019|via=Youtube|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200127193204/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Dim9GE891gQ|archive-date=January 27, 2020|access-date=March 28, 2020}}</ref> The film also echoes the [[Jungian archetypes|Jungian archetype]] of the [[Shadow (psychology)|shadow]], the unknown "dark side" or [[Bias blind spot|blind spot]] of one's personality. Dafoe illustrated that the two keepers are "put in this situation that's like a [[purgatory]] and then the little personality, the little sense of self that they've created for themselves starts to get stripped away. You see what their real nature is and that points them into a kind of desperation." Rosie Fletcher of ''[[Den of Geek]]'' gathered: "The way the pair embody wisdom and foolishness, hedonism and inspiration, honesty and trickery and play with masculine and feminine roles [...] seems to support the idea that one is the shadow of the other on some level and speaks further to Jung's theories."<ref name="Fletcher-2020">{{Cite web |last=Fletcher |first=Rosie |date=February 1, 2020 |title=The Lighthouse: the myths and archetypes behind the movie explained |url=https://www.denofgeek.com/movies/the-lighthouse-the-myths-and-archetypes-behind-the-movie-explained/ |access-date=June 18, 2023 |website=Den of Geek |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Mythology===
[[File:Albrecht Dürer - The Sea Monster - Google Art Project.jpg |thumb|left|upright|''[[The Sea Monster]]'' ({{circa}} 1493–1503) by [[Albrecht Dürer]]]]
In the film, the senior lighthouse keeper Thomas warns the younger keeper Ephraim of a maritime [[superstition]] that is bad luck to kill a seabird, specifically a [[seagull]]. However, after getting irritated by one, Ephraim kills it later and brings on a storm that traps the two men on the island. At the end of the film, Ephraim is seen on the ground with seagulls plucking out his organs. This plot invokes the 1798 poem "[[The Rime of the Ancient Mariner]]" by [[Samuel Taylor Coleridge]], in which a mariner kills an Albatross and brings disaster to his ship.<ref name="Fletcher-2020"/>

The fate of the younger lighthouse keeper also invokes the myth of [[Prometheus]], as, after finally reaching the light and learning what is in it, he falls down the stairs of the lighthouse and his organs are plucked out by seagulls. On the other hand, the older keeper was modeled on [[Proteus]], a "prophecy-telling ocean god who serves [[Poseidon]]", as he "makes that uncannily accurate prediction for how Ephraim will die at the end of the movie"<ref name="Joho-2019" /> and is even seen with tentacles and sea creatures stuck to his body in one of the younger man's hallucinations. [[Albrecht Dürer]]'s engraving ''[[The Sea Monster]]'' inspired Wake's appearance, with Eggers saying: "The Proteus figure that is more clearly nautical is somewhat based on a sea monster by Dürer, who carries a tortoise shell shield."<ref name="Han">{{Cite web|url=https://www.polygon.com/2019/10/23/20914085/the-lighthouse-robert-eggers-interview-ending-spoilers-mermaid-lamp-robert-pattinson|title=''The Lighthouse'' director took the movie's creepy mythology very seriously|last=Han|first=Karen|date=October 23, 2019|website=[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]]|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191129121816/https://www.polygon.com/2019/10/23/20914085/the-lighthouse-robert-eggers-interview-ending-spoilers-mermaid-lamp-robert-pattinson|archive-date=November 29, 2019|access-date=May 21, 2020}}</ref> Eggers explained the allusions to classical mythology by saying they are present "Partially because [[Herman Melville|Melville]] goes there and partially because of I'm sure our unhealthy Jungian leanings".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.thrillist.com/entertainment/nation/the-lighthouse-movie-ending-explained-twist-robert-eggers|title=Director Robert Eggers Breaks Down the Mysteries of 'The Lighthouse'|last=Zuckerman|first=Esther|date=October 18, 2019|website=Thrillist|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200329002702/https://www.thrillist.com/entertainment/nation/the-lighthouse-movie-ending-explained-twist-robert-eggers|archive-date=March 29, 2020|access-date=March 28, 2020}}</ref>

===Sexuality===
[[File:Hypnose (Schneider).jpg|thumb|upright|right|''Hypnosis'' (1904) by [[Sascha Schneider]], which provided visual reference for a scene in the film]]
The film primarily depicts two men alone in close quarters on an island and contains explicit depictions of male sexuality and [[homoeroticism]], but, when asked whether the film was "a love story", Robert Eggers replied:
{{blockquote|Am I saying these characters are gay? No. I'm not saying they're not either. Forget about complexities of human sexuality or their particular inclinations. I'm more about questions than answers in this movie.<ref name="Jacobs-2019"/>}}

The [[Phallus|phallic]] imagery of the lighthouse is explicit, as Eggers described it in the script as an erect penis, revealing that the film was meant to include "a very juvenile shot of a lighthouse moving like an erect penis and a match-cut to actual erect penis" belonging to Howard, but this sequence was removed at the request of the financiers.<ref name="Jacobs-2019" /> A [[Double (occupation)|body double]] of Pattinson was used to film the scene. Pattinson said that when he first saw the shot, he didn't even realize what he was looking at, initially mistaking it for the lighthouse. He then joked in Sky News interview that the phallus might have belonged to director Robert Eggers.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dazed |date=January 27, 2020 |title=Robert Pattinson on masturbation and the lonely eroticism of The Lighthouse |url=https://www.dazeddigital.com/film-tv/article/47574/1/robert-pattinson-willem-dafoe-robert-eggers-the-lighthouse-interview |access-date=March 29, 2023 |website=Dazed |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Stern |first=Marlow |date=October 17, 2019 |title=The Most Bonkers Movie Sex Scene of the Year Features a Very Horny Robert Pattinson and a Mermaid |work=The Daily Beast |url=https://www.thedailybeast.com/the-lighthouse-robert-pattinson-gets-weird-in-the-most-bonkers-movie-sex-scene-of-the-year |url-status=live |access-date=March 28, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200509140036/https://www.thedailybeast.com/the-lighthouse-robert-pattinson-gets-weird-in-the-most-bonkers-movie-sex-scene-of-the-year |archive-date=May 9, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=Robert Pattinson: 'I like perversity, I don't care what people think' |url=https://news.sky.com/story/robert-pattinson-i-like-perversity-i-dont-care-what-people-think-11909419 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230402131240/https://news.sky.com/story/robert-pattinson-i-like-perversity-i-dont-care-what-people-think-11909419 |archive-date=2023-04-02 |access-date=2026-08-04 |work=Sky News |language=en-GB}}</ref>

Sexual fantasy and masturbation are also recurring themes in the film. For Dafoe, the [[Androphilia and gynephilia|androphilia]] in the film is blatant, but it is also used to explore what it means to be a man: "They have a sense of guilt, of wrong [...] it's got existential roots [...] about masculinity and domination and submission."<ref name="Jacobs-2019" /> After beating the older lighthouse keeper into submission, the younger keeper assumes a dominant role, calling the older man "dog" and dragging him on a leash. Commenting on this scene, Pattinson said "there's definitely a take where we were literally trying to pull each other's pants down. It literally almost looked like [[foreplay]]."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.indiewire.com/2019/10/jojo-rabbit-the-lighthouse-gay-subtext-1202182957/|title=Why the Gay Subplots in 'The Lighthouse' and 'Jojo Rabbit' Don't Go Far Enough|last=Dry|first=Jude|date=October 21, 2019|website=IndieWire|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191205034734/https://www.indiewire.com/2019/10/jojo-rabbit-the-lighthouse-gay-subtext-1202182957/|archive-date=December 5, 2019|access-date=March 28, 2020}}</ref>

The mythological and artistic influences of the film underscore its eroticism. Eggers acknowledged the visual influence of [[Symbolism (movement)|symbolist]] artists [[Sascha Schneider]] and [[Jean Delville]], whose "mythic paintings in a homoerotic style become perfect candidates as imagery that's going to work itself into the script."<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.bafta.org/media-centre/transcripts/screenwriters-lecture-series-2019-robert-eggers|title=Screenwriters' Lecture Series 2019: Robert Eggers|last=Eggers|first=Robert|date=December 9, 2019|website=[[British Academy of Film and Television Arts|BAFTA.org]]|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191220173545/http://www.bafta.org/media-centre/transcripts/screenwriters-lecture-series-2019-robert-eggers|archive-date=December 20, 2019|access-date=May 21, 2020}}</ref> The composition of a shot in the film was consciously adapted from Schneider's ''Hypnosis''.<ref name="Han" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/the-lighthouse-director-robert-eggers-on-making-the-most-bonkers-film-of-2019-with-robert-pattinson-and-willem-dafoe/|title='The Lighthouse' Director Robert Eggers on Making the Most Bonkers Film of 2019|last=Donaghey|first=River|date=October 15, 2019|website=[[Vice (magazine)|Vice]]|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191227064722/https://www.vice.com/en_us/article/a354yz/the-lighthouse-director-robert-eggers-on-making-the-most-bonkers-film-of-2019-with-robert-pattinson-and-willem-dafoe|archive-date=December 27, 2019|access-date=May 21, 2020}}</ref>

===Home media===
''The Lighthouse'' was released on [[digital media|digital]] in the United States on December 20, 2019, and in [[Blu-ray]] and [[DVD]] formats on January 7, 2020, by [[Lionsgate Home Entertainment]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=November 25, 2019 |title='The Lighthouse' Hit Digital Dec. 20, Blu-ray January 7 |url=https://bleedingcool.com/movies/the-lighthouse-hit-digital-dec-20-blu-ray-january-7/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220720082315/https://bleedingcool.com/movies/the-lighthouse-hit-digital-dec-20-blu-ray-january-7/ |archive-date=July 20, 2022 |access-date=February 20, 2024 |work=[[Bleeding Cool]]}}</ref> Later, it was released on [[Ultra HD Blu-ray|4K Ultra HD Blu-ray]] by A24 on March 28, 2023.<ref>{{Cite news |date=March 20, 2023 |title='The Lighthouse' Collector's Edition 4K Ultra HD Release Now Available from A24 |url=https://bloody-disgusting.com/home-video/3755237/the-lighthouse-collectors-edition-4k-ultra-hd-release-now-available-from-a24/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230327145043/https://bloody-disgusting.com/home-video/3755237/the-lighthouse-collectors-edition-4k-ultra-hd-release-now-available-from-a24/ |archive-date=March 27, 2023 |access-date=February 20, 2024 |work=[[Bloody Disgusting]]}}</ref>

==Reception==
===Box office===
The film grossed $10.9 million in the United States and $7.5 million in other territories, for a worldwide box-office total of $18.3 million.<ref name="BOM">{{cite web|url=https://www.boxofficemojo.com/movies/?id=thelighthouse.htm|title=The Lighthouse (2019)|website=[[Box Office Mojo]]|publisher=[[IMDb]]|access-date=February 24, 2020|archive-date=June 25, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210625173532/https://www.boxofficemojo.com/release/rl3305670145/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="NUM"/>

Its limited opening weekend in the U.S., the film grossed $419,764 from eight theaters, for an average of $52,471 per venue.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://deadline.com/2019/10/maleficent-mistress-of-evil-zombieland-double-tap-weekend-box-office-1202763525/ |title='Maleficent: Mistress Of Evil' No Magic With $36M+, 'Joker' Still Stealing 2nd Place From 'Zombieland 2' With $28M+ |last=D'Alessandro |first=Anthony |work=[[Deadline Hollywood]] |date=October 20, 2019 |access-date=October 20, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191019220728/https://deadline.com/2019/10/maleficent-mistress-of-evil-zombieland-double-tap-weekend-box-office-1202763525/ |archive-date=October 19, 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://deadline.com/2019/10/jojo-rabbit-fox-searchlight-taika-waititi-the-lighthouse-a24-robert-eggers-robert-pattinson-willem-dafoe-parasite-neon-bon-joon-ho-specialty-box-office-1202764508/|title='Jojo Rabbit' Opens Strong; 'The Lighthouse' Shines; 'Parasite' Continues To Thrive – Specialty Box Office|date=October 20, 2019|first=Dino-Ray|last=Ramos|website=[[Deadline Hollywood]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210405181108/https://deadline.com/2019/10/jojo-rabbit-fox-searchlight-taika-waititi-the-lighthouse-a24-robert-eggers-robert-pattinson-willem-dafoe-parasite-neon-bon-joon-ho-specialty-box-office-1202764508/|archive-date=April 5, 2021|url-status=live|access-date=April 5, 2021|quote=The A24 film, which was co-financed and produced by New Regency, earned an estimated $419,764, with a per-screen average of $52,471.}}</ref> Its second weekend, the film expanded to 586 theaters and grossed $3.75 million, placing eighth at the box office.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://deadline.com/2019/10/joker-maleficent-2-black-and-blue-countdown-halloween-box-office-weekend-1202769043/ |title='Joker' Has The Edge Over 'Maleficent: Mistress Of Evil' With $18.9M In Fierce Slow Pre-Halloween B.O. Battle |last=D'Alessandro |first=Anthony |work=[[Deadline Hollywood]] |date=October 27, 2019 |access-date=October 27, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191030094937/https://deadline.com/2019/10/joker-maleficent-2-black-and-blue-countdown-halloween-box-office-weekend-1202769043/ |archive-date=October 30, 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref> The following weekend, the film expanded to 978 theaters, but its gross fell 34.7% to $2 million, and it finished in 13th place.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://deadline.com/2019/11/inside-game-idreammachine-raw-miilk-parasite-neon-jojo-rabbit-fox-searchlight-the-lighthouse-a24-the-irishman-netflix-specialty-box-office-1202776404/|title='Parasite', 'Jojo Rabbit' Continue To Hold Strong On Quiet Weekend; 'Inside Game' Shoots Air Ball – Specialty Box Office|date=November 3, 2019|first=Dino-Ray|last=Ramos|website=[[Deadline Hollywood]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210405181438/https://deadline.com/2019/11/inside-game-idreammachine-raw-miilk-parasite-neon-jojo-rabbit-fox-searchlight-the-lighthouse-a24-the-irishman-netflix-specialty-box-office-1202776404/|archive-date=April 5, 2021|url-status=live|access-date=April 5, 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=D'Alessandro |first=Anthony |title=How 'Terminator: Dark Fate' Conked Out With $27M+ & Why 'The Irishman' Is Not A Missed Strategic Opportunity – Box Office |url=https://deadline.com/2019/11/terminator-dark-fate-linda-hamilton-harriet-motherless-brooklyn-weekend-box-office-1202774477/ |website=[[Deadline Hollywood]] |access-date=November 3, 2019 |date=November 4, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191103043256/https://deadline.com/2019/11/terminator-dark-fate-linda-hamilton-harriet-motherless-brooklyn-weekend-box-office-1202774477/ |archive-date=November 3, 2019 |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Critical response===
On [[review aggregation]] website [[Rotten Tomatoes]], the film holds an approval rating of 90% based on 398 reviews, with an average score of 8/10. The site's consensus reads: "A gripping story brilliantly filmed and led by a pair of powerhouse performances, ''The Lighthouse'' further establishes Robert Eggers as a filmmaker of exceptional talent."<ref>{{Cite Rotten Tomatoes |id={{RT data|rtid|noprefix=y}} |type=m |title=The Lighthouse |access-date={{RT data|access date}} |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190919214703/https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/the_lighthouse_2019 |archive-date=September 19, 2019 |url-status=live}}</ref> On [[Metacritic]], the film has a [[Weighted arithmetic mean|weighted average]] score of 83 out of 100 based on 52 critics, indicating "universal acclaim".<ref>{{Cite Metacritic |id=the-lighthouse-2019 |type=movie |title=The Lighthouse |access-date=April 21, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210421183135/https://www.metacritic.com/movie/the-lighthouse-2019 |archive-date=April 21, 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Owen Gleiberman]] of ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' called the film "darkly exciting" and "made with extraordinary skill," commenting that "the movie, building on ''[[The Witch (2015 film)|The Witch]]'', proves that Robert Eggers possesses something more than impeccable genre skill. He has the ability to lock you into the fever of what's happening onscreen."<ref name="varrev">{{cite magazine |url=https://variety.com/2019/film/reviews/the-lighthouse-review-robert-pattinson-willem-dafoe-1203220127/ |title=Cannes Film Review: Robert Pattinson and Willem Dafoe in 'The Lighthouse' |last=Gleiberman |first=Owen |author-link=Owen Gleiberman|date=May 19, 2019 |magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|access-date=May 27, 2019|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190522232123/https://variety.com/2019/film/reviews/the-lighthouse-review-robert-pattinson-willem-dafoe-1203220127/|archive-date=May 22, 2019}}</ref> [[Robbie Collin]] of ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]'' gave the film a perfect score, calling Dafoe's performance "astounding" and comparing Pattinson's to that of [[Daniel Day-Lewis]] in ''[[There Will Be Blood]]'', saying, "that's no comparison to make lightly, but everything about ''The Lighthouse'' lands with a crash. It's cinema to make your head and soul ring."<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/films/0/lighthouse-review-film-will-make-head-soul-ring/ |title=The Lighthouse, review: 'A film that will make your head and soul ring' |last=Collin |first=Robbie |author-link=Robbie Collin |date=May 19, 2019 |website=[[The Daily Telegraph]] |access-date=September 15, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190610224450/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/films/0/lighthouse-review-film-will-make-head-soul-ring/ |archive-date=June 10, 2019 |url-status=live|url-access=registration}}</ref> [[Peter Bradshaw]] of ''[[The Guardian]]'', in addition to praising the performances of Dafoe and Pattinson, also praised the screenplay, stating that the "script is barnacled with resemblances to [[Samuel Taylor Coleridge|Coleridge]], [[William Shakespeare|Shakespeare]], [[Herman Melville|Melville]] – and there's also some staggeringly cheeky black-comic riffs and gags and the two of them resemble no-one so much as [[Wilfrid Brambell]] and [[Harry H. Corbett]]: [[Steptoe and Son]] in hell."<ref>{{cite web |last1=Bradshaw |first1=Peter |author-link=Peter Bradshaw|title=The Lighthouse review – Robert Pattinson shines in sublime maritime nightmare |url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2019/may/19/the-lighthouse-review-robert-pattinson-shines-in-sublime-maritime-nightmare |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=May 19, 2019 |access-date=September 3, 2020 |archive-date=May 19, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190519140006/https://www.theguardian.com/film/2019/may/19/the-lighthouse-review-robert-pattinson-shines-in-sublime-maritime-nightmare |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Manohla Dargis]] of ''[[The New York Times]]'' praised the character development, production design, acting, and themes,<ref name="NYT" /> and [[Michael Phillips (critic)|Michael Phillips]] of the ''[[Chicago Tribune]]'' gave the film three stars out of five, comparing it to ''[[The Odd Couple (film)|The Odd Couple]]'' (1968) and ''[[The Dumb Waiter]]'' (1957), and lauding the cinematography.<ref name="CTReview"/>

Conversely, [[Sandra Hall (writer)|Sandra Hall]] of ''[[The Sydney Morning Herald]]'' said the film's attempts at suspense were not successful,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.smh.com.au/culture/movies/the-lighthouse-a-gothic-construction-that-fails-to-illuminate-20200205-p53xw3.html|title=The Lighthouse: a Gothic construction that fails to illuminate|date=February 5, 2020|first=Sandra|last=Hall|author-link=Sandra Hall (writer)|website=[[The Sydney Morning Herald]]|access-date=June 24, 2021|archive-date=January 28, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210128101638/https://www.smh.com.au/culture/movies/the-lighthouse-a-gothic-construction-that-fails-to-illuminate-20200205-p53xw3.html|url-status=live}}</ref> and Simran Hans of ''The Guardian'' gave it two stars out of five, saying the performances felt more like an "experiment than conducive to eliciting meaning."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2020/feb/02/the-lighthouse-review-robert-pattinson-willem-dafoe-the-witch-robert-eggers|title=The Lighthouse review – inner demons get lost in the fog|date=February 2, 2020|first=Simran|last=Hanks|website=[[The Guardian]]|access-date=June 24, 2021|archive-date=April 24, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210424105435/https://www.theguardian.com/film/2020/feb/02/the-lighthouse-review-robert-pattinson-willem-dafoe-the-witch-robert-eggers|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Mick LaSalle]] of the ''[[San Francisco Chronicle]]'' said the film was well-made, but "fails to give us the one thing that might have sustained an audience's interest over the course of 109 excruciating minutes: a compelling story."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://datebook.sfchronicle.com/movies-tv/review-the-lighthouse-is-a-film-so-well-made-that-it-stinks|title=Review: 'The Lighthouse' is a film so well-made that it stinks|date=October 15, 2019|first=Mick|last=LaSalle|website=[[San Francisco Chronicle]]|access-date=June 24, 2021|archive-date=February 27, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210227224520/https://datebook.sfchronicle.com/movies-tv/review-the-lighthouse-is-a-film-so-well-made-that-it-stinks|url-status=live}}</ref> Dana Stevens of ''[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]'' concluded her review by stating that "''The Lighthouse'' is at its strongest when it resembles the dark comedy of a [[Samuel Beckett|Beckett]] play, complete with earthy scatological humor. [...] But as the mythological references pile up and the forbidden light atop the tower accrues ever more (and ever vaguer) symbolic meaning, the film sometimes seems funny [...] not because of but in spite of the filmmakers' intentions", and that, by the end, she became "impatient" with Eggers' "reliance on atmosphere [...] to take the place of story" and found herself "identifying with the stranded seafarers: I desperately wanted to get out."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://slate.com/culture/2019/10/the-lighthouse-movie-review-robert-pattinson-horror-farts.html|title=''The Lighthouse'' Is Both Artsy and Fartsy|date=October 16, 2019|first=Dana|last=Stevens|website=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]|access-date=June 24, 2021|archive-date=February 25, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210225084540/https://slate.com/culture/2019/10/the-lighthouse-movie-review-robert-pattinson-horror-farts.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2025, the film ranked number 97 on the "Readers' Choice" edition of ''[[The New York Times]]''{{'}} list of "The 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century."<ref>{{cite web |title=Readers Choose Their Top Movies of the 21st Century |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2025/movies/readers-movies-21st-century.html |website=The New York Times |date=July 2, 2025 |access-date=2 July 2025}}</ref>

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: The Player (1992 film)

{{short description|1992 film by Robert Altman}}

'''''The Player''''' is a 1992 American [[Satire (film and television)|satirical]] [[black comedy]] [[neo-noir]] [[mystery film]] directed by [[Robert Altman]] and written by [[Michael Tolkin]], based on his 1988 novel.<ref>{{cite book|last=Tolkin |first=Michael |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KSCdACRt0qkC |title=The Player |edition=1st |location=New York  |publisher=Atlantic Monthly Press |year=1988 |isbn=0-87113-228-1}}</ref> The film stars [[Tim Robbins]], [[Greta Scacchi]], [[Fred Ward]], [[Whoopi Goldberg]], [[Peter Gallagher]], [[Brion James]] and [[Cynthia Stevenson]], and is the story of a [[Cinema of the United States|Hollywood]] [[film studio]] executive who kills an aspiring screenwriter he believes is sending him death threats.

''The Player'' has many film references and Hollywood in-jokes, with 65 celebrities making [[cameo appearance]]s in the film. Altman once stated that the film "is a very mild satire," offending no one.<ref name="DVD">{{cite video|title=''The Player'' – Commentary by Robert Altman, Michael Tolkin |medium=DVD|publisher=[[New Line Home Video]]}}</ref> The film received three nominations at the [[65th Academy Awards]]: [[Academy Award for Best Director|Best Director]], [[Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay|Best Adapted Screenplay]] and [[Academy Award for Best Film Editing|Best Editing]]. The film also won two [[Golden Globe Award|Golden Globes]], [[Golden Globe Award for Best Motion Picture – Musical or Comedy|Best Motion Picture – Comedy or Musical]] and [[Golden Globe Award for Best Actor – Motion Picture Musical or Comedy|Best Actor – Comedy or Musical]] for Robbins. Although the film did not receive any acting nominations, the film is notable for having more Oscar-nominated actors than any other film, with 24.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.goldderby.com/gallery/movies-starring-most-oscar-winners/|title=Top 22 movies starring the most Oscar winners|website=Goldderby.com|first=Matthew|last=Stewart|date=November 1, 2023|access-date=July 15, 2026}}</ref>

==Plot==
Griffin Mill is a [[Cinema of the United States|Hollywood]] studio executive dating story editor Bonnie Sherow. He hears story pitches from [[screenwriter]]s and decides which have the potential to be made into films, green-lighting only twelve out of 50,000 submissions every year. His job is threatened when up-and-coming exec Larry Levy begins working at the studio. Mill has also been receiving death threat postcards, assumed to be from a screenwriter whose pitch he rejected.

Mill surmises that the disgruntled writer is David Kahane, and Kahane's girlfriend June Gudmundsdottir tells him that Kahane is at the [[Rialto Theatre (South Pasadena, California)|Rialto Theater]] in [[South Pasadena, California|South Pasadena]], at a screening of ''[[Bicycle Thieves|The Bicycle Thief]]''. Mill pretends to recognize Kahane in the lobby and offers him a scriptwriting deal, hoping this will stop the threats. The two go to a nearby bar where Kahane gets intoxicated and rebuffs Mill's offer, calling him a liar and continuing to goad him about his job security at the studio. In the bar's parking lot, the two men fight. Mill goes too far and drowns Kahane in a shallow pool of water while screaming, "Keep it to yourself!" Mill then stages the crime to make it look like a botched robbery.

The next day, after Mill is late for and distracted at a meeting, studio security chief Walter Stuckel confronts him about the murder and says that the police know that he was the last one to see Kahane alive. At the end of their conversation Mill receives a [[fax]] from his stalker. Thus, Mill has killed the wrong man, and the stalker apparently knows this. Mill attends Kahane's funeral and gets into conversation with Gudmundsdottir. Detectives Avery and DeLongpre suspect Mill is guilty of murder.

Mill receives a postcard from the stalker suggesting that they meet at a hotel bar. While Mill is waiting, he is cornered by two screenwriters, Tom Oakley and Andy Sivella, who pitch ''Habeas Corpus'', a legal drama featuring no major stars and with a depressing ending. Because Mill is not alone, his stalker does not appear. After leaving the bar, Mill receives a fax in his car, advising him to look under his raincoat. He discovers a live rattlesnake in a box and, terrified, bludgeons it with his umbrella.

Mill tells Gudmundsdottir that his near-death experience made him realize he has feelings for her. Apprehensive that Levy continues encroaching on his job, Mill invites the two writers to pitch ''Habeas Corpus'' to him, convincing Levy that the movie will be an [[Oscar bait|Oscar contender]]. Mill's plan is to let Levy shepherd the film through production and have it flop. Mill will step in at the last moment, suggesting some changes to salvage the film's box office, letting him reclaim his position at the studio. Having persuaded Sherow to leave for [[New York City|New York]] on studio business, Mill takes Gudmundsdottir to a Hollywood awards banquet and their relationship blossoms.

After Sherow confronts Mill about his relationship with Gudmundsdottir, Mill coldly severs their relationship in front of two writers. Mill takes Gudmundsdottir to an isolated [[Desert Hot Springs, California|Desert Hot Springs]] resort and spa. In the middle of Mill and Gudmundsdottir making love, Mill confesses his role in Kahane's murder, and Gudmundsdottir responds by saying she loves him. Mill's attorney informs him that studio head Joel Levison has been fired, and that the Pasadena police want Mill to participate in a [[police lineup|lineup]]. An eyewitness has come forward, but she fails to identify Mill.

One year later, studio power players are watching the end of ''Habeas Corpus'' with a new, tacked-on, upbeat ending and famous actors in the lead roles. Mill's plan to save the movie has worked and he is head of the studio. Gudmundsdottir is now Mill's wife and pregnant with his child. Sherow objects to the film's new ending and is fired by Levy. Mill rebuffs her when she appeals her termination to him. Mill receives a pitch over the phone from Levy and a man who reveals himself as the postcard writer. The man pitches an idea about a studio executive who kills a writer and gets away with murder. Recognizing the pitch as blackmail, Mill gives the writer a deal, if he can guarantee an ending in which the executive lives happily with the writer's widow. The writer's title for the film is ''The Player''.

==Production==
Writer-producer [[Michael Tolkin]] initially had no intention of allowing his 1988 novel, ''The Player'', to be adapted into a film, having written it to distance himself from his career in the movie industry. However, when producer [[David Brown (producer)|David Brown]] acquired the film rights, he urged Tolkin to adapt it himself. Throughout the late 1980s and early 1990s, as they sought financing and refined the script, Tolkin ventured into directing with ''[[The Rapture (1991 film)|The Rapture]]'' (1991) and enlisted that film's producer, [[Nick Wechsler (film producer)|Nick Wechsler]], to join ''The Player''{{'}}s production team. The producers encountered difficulties in selling the film, as studio executives doubted the appeal of a narrative centered on the inner workings of Hollywood filmmaking. Cary Brokaw, the CEO of Avenue Pictures, rejected the script twice, in 1989 and 1990. However, in 1991, after witnessing Altman's work on the British film ''[[Vincent & Theo]]'' (1990), Brokaw approached Altman, who eagerly embraced the project.<ref name="AFI">{{cite web|url=https://catalog.afi.com/Film/67076-THE-PLAYER|title=''The Player''|website=[[American Film Institute]]|access-date=March 4, 2024}}</ref>

Principal photography for the film commenced in mid-June 1991 in Los Angeles, California, with an eight-week schedule. Before production, meticulous planning went into crafting the film's opening scene, an eight-minute unbroken tracking shot. Models were utilized to map out the shot, and the studio lot location was resurfaced to ensure smooth movement for the dolly and crane. The day before filming, the actors and crew rehearsed the scene. Altman filmed ten takes. Notably, Altman instructed actor [[Fred Ward]], portraying a studio security chief, to incorporate references to other films renowned for their tracking shots into his dialogue to add irony to the scene.<ref name="AFI" />

Altman also successfully persuaded a plethora of [[A-list]] actors to make cameo appearances in the film based on his esteemed reputation in the industry. These stars agreed to participate without reviewing the script and contributed their union-scale salaries for one day of filming to the [[Motion Picture & Television Fund|Motion Picture & Television Country House and Hospital]], a retirement community for industry professionals. Despite the large ensemble, the film was completed within a budget ranging from approximately $8 to $10 million. Funding for the project came from Avenue Pictures' "internal funds" and the pre-sale of foreign rights to Spelling International. Furthermore, principal actors agreed to defer their wages.<ref name="AFI" /> [[Chevy Chase]] was interested in playing the role of Griffin Mill, but Warner Bros. didn't want Chase to star in the film.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.vulture.com/2011/09/the-lost-roles-of-chevy-chase.html|title=The Lost Roles of Chevy Chase|date=September 22, 2011|website=[[Vulture (website)|Vulture]]}}</ref>

Despite the difficulties of funding, the film's distribution rights were highly sought after by nearly every major Hollywood studio. Eventually, [[Fine Line Features]], a division of [[New Line Cinema]], secured the rights with a guarantee of $5.1 million. President of Fine Line Features, Ira Deutchman, stated that the film would be promoted as a comedy to attract audiences who might not typically be interested in a movie about Hollywood. Release dates were strategically planned to coincide with the [[64th Academy Awards]] in March 1992, aiming to capitalize on the ceremony's publicity and generate [[word-of-mouth]] buzz. Preview screenings were positive. The filmmakers hoped audiences would be drawn to the film's story rather than its celebrity cameos; therefore, Altman insisted on not featuring the actors' names in advertisements.<ref name="AFI" />

==Reception==
On [[Rotten Tomatoes]], the film has an approval rating of 97% based on 66 reviews, with an average rating of 8.90/10. The site's critical consensus reads: "Bitingly cynical without succumbing to bitterness, ''The Player'' is one of the all-time great Hollywood satires — and an ensemble-driven highlight of the Altman oeuvre."<ref>{{rotten tomatoes|player}}</ref> On [[Metacritic]], the film has a score of 86 out of 100, based on 20 critics, indicating "universal acclaim".<ref>{{Metacritic film}}</ref>

[[Roger Ebert]] gave the film four stars out of four and called it: {{cquote|a smart movie, and a funny one. It is also absolutely of its time. After the savings and loan scandals, after [[Michael Milken]], after junk bonds and stolen pension funds, here is a movie that uses Hollywood as a metaphor for the avarice of the 1980s. It is the movie ''[[The Bonfire of the Vanities (film)|The Bonfire of the Vanities]]'' wanted to be.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/the-player-1992 |title=The Player |last=Ebert |first=Roger |author-link=Roger Ebert |date=April 24, 1992 |website=[[RogerEbert.com]] |access-date=December 12, 2018 }}</ref>}} [[Gene Siskel]] also gave the film a perfect four-star grade and wrote, "If you knew nothing and cared nothing about the movie business, you can still appreciate ''The Player'' as a ripping good thriller, too."<ref>[[Gene Siskel|Siskel, Gene]] (April 24, 1992). "Altman targets Hollywood in masterful ''Player''". ''[[Chicago Tribune]]''. Section 7, p. C.</ref> [[Vincent Canby]] of ''[[The New York Times]]'' wrote, "Robert Altman has not really been away. Yet his new Hollywood satire titled ''The Player'' is so entertaining, so flip and so genially irreverent that it seems to announce the return of the great gregarious film maker whose ''[[Nashville (film)|Nashville]]'' remains one of the classics of the 1970's".<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/1992/04/10/movies/review-film-inside-hollywood-an-impious-tale.html | title=Inside Hollywood: An Impious Tale | first=Vincent | last=Canby | author-link=Vincent Canby | work=[[The New York Times]] | date=April 10, 1992 | page=C-16 | access-date=October 13, 2019}}</ref>

[[Todd McCarthy]] of ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' wrote: "Mercilessly satiric yet good-natured, this enormously entertaining slam dunk represents a remarkable American come-back for eternal maverick Robert Altman."<ref>[[Todd McCarthy|McCarthy, Todd]] (March 16, 1992). "Reviews: The Player". ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]''. 58.</ref> [[Terrence Rafferty]] of ''[[The New Yorker]]'' called it "a brilliant dark comedy about the death of American filmmaking," adding: "In this picture Altman is doing one of his specialties: exploring an odd American subculture—revealing its distinctive textures and explicating the peculiar principles of social intercourse which keep it functioning. But when his idiosyncratic style of anthropological realism is applied to the tight community of Hollywood 'players' it has an almost hallucinatory effect."<ref>[[Terrence Rafferty|Rafferty, Terrence]] (April 20, 1992). "The Current Cinema". ''[[The New Yorker]]''. 81.</ref> Peter Rainer of the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' wrote that "Altman has made a movie that's supremely deft and pleasurable. As if to taunt his detractors, he even 'tells a story' this time, and he does a better job of it than the hacks who have been getting work when he couldn't."<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1992-04-19-ca-735-story.html | title=Here's the Deal: 'The Player' Takes Hollywood Genre One Step Beyond | first=Peter | last=Rainer | work=[[Los Angeles Times]] | date=April 19, 1992 | page=46 | access-date=October 13, 2019}}</ref>

''The Player'' was Altman's comeback to making films in Hollywood.<ref name="Murray">{{cite web |last=Murray |first=Noel |title=Vincent & Theo |date=March 30, 2015 |work=[[The Dissolve]] |url=http://thedissolve.com/reviews/1475-vincent-theo/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160407084439/http://thedissolve.com/reviews/1475-vincent-theo/ |archive-date=2016-04-07 |url-status=live |quote=When ''The Player'' came out in 1992, it was greeted as a welcome comeback for director Robert Altman, who spent much of the previous decade working small—making filmed plays instead of the ambitious, character-heavy genre reinventions he'd been known for in the 1970s. But Altman actually reclaimed his critics' darling status two years earlier with ''Vincent & Theo'', a luminous biopic about painter Vincent Van Gogh (played by Tim Roth) and his art-dealer brother (Paul Rhys).}}</ref> Altman was praised for the sex scene in which Robbins and Scacchi were filmed from the neck up. Scacchi later claimed that Altman had wanted a [[nude scene]], but that it was her refusal which led to the final form.<ref>{{cite news|title=Greta Scacchi: 'I'm done with taking off my clothes on screen'|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/film/starsandstories/3557111/Greta-Scacchi-Im-done-with-taking-off-my-clothes-on-screen.html|access-date=14 October 2012|newspaper=Daily Telegraph|date=25 July 2008}}</ref> The editing of ''The Player'' by Geraldine Peroni was honored by a nomination for the [[Academy Award for Best Film Editing]]. In 2004, [[Anthony Sloman|Tony Sloman]] wrote an appreciation of the film's editing:<ref name="independent">{{Cite news |last=Sloman |first=Tony |title=Geraldine Peroni Obituary: Oscar-nominated film editor on 'The Player' |work=[[The Independent]] |date=August 31, 2004 |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/geraldine-peroni-550379.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160108105910/http://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/geraldine-peroni-550379.html |archive-date=January 8, 2016 |access-date=September 16, 2017 |url-status=live |df=mdy-all }}</ref>{{blockquote|''The Player'' is a marvellous example of collaborative editing, Peroni matching Altman's tone with exactitude. Early on, a cut from a zoom-in to the gun in Humphrey Bogart's hand on a postcard sent to Tim Robbins is perfectly successively matched with what appears to be a black frame, in which a reveal shows that it's an open drawer in which the postcard has been placed. Another felicitous sequence is the one in the Pasadena police station, where the Robbins character is arraigned as Lyle Lovett swats a fly and Whoopi Goldberg and her associates ridicule Robbins with laughter. This is beautifully edited; well-shot, too, but the rhythm is built in the cutting.}}

''The Player'' was placed on 80 critics' year-end best lists, second only to ''[[Howards End (film)|Howards End]]'' in 1992.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1993-01-24-ca-2356-story.html | title=106 Doesn't Add Up | first=David | last=Rothman | author-link=David Rothman (statistician) | date=January 24, 1993 | work=Los Angeles Times}}</ref>

==Legacy==

In 1997, the film was adapted into a [[television pilot]] that wasn't picked up. It starred [[Patrick Dempsey]], [[Michael Parks]], [[Arye Gross]], [[Shelley Duvall]], [[Natasha Gregson Wagner]], [[Jennifer Grey]], and [[Seymour Cassel]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Player (1997) |url=https://www.avclub.com/film/reviews/the-player-1997 |access-date=2023-05-23 |website=The A.V. Club |language=en}}</ref>

In 2015, ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]''{{'}}s 25th anniversary year, it named ''The Player'' in its list of the 25 best movies since the magazine's beginnings.<ref>{{cite magazine|title=EW's 25 Best Movies in 25 Years|date= October 16, 2015|url=https://ew.com/gallery/25-best-movies-25-years|magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]]|access-date=14 November 2022}}</ref> ''[[Rolling Stone]]'' listed ''The Player'' as one of the best movies of the 90's.<ref>{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.rollingstone.com/movies/movie-lists/the-100-greatest-movies-of-the-nineties-195513/the-matrix-1999-197758/|title = The 100 Greatest Movies of the Nineties|magazine = [[Rolling Stone]]|date = July 12, 2017}}</ref>

A character named Griffin Mill appears in the 2025 TV series ''[[The Studio (TV series)|The Studio]]'', played by [[Bryan Cranston]].<ref name="indiewire">{{cite web|url=https://www.indiewire.com/criticism/shows/the-studio-review-seth-rogen-series-1235100634/|title='The Studio' Review: Seth Rogen's Lavish Hollywood Satire Offers Big Laughs but a Light Bite

'''''The Secret Agent''''' ({{langx|pt|'''O Agente Secreto'''}}) is a 2025 [[Historical drama|historical]] [[political thriller film]] written and directed by [[Kleber Mendonça Filho]]. It follows Armando ([[Wagner Moura]]), a former professor caught in the political turmoil in the midst of the [[Military dictatorship in Brazil|Brazilian military dictatorship]], attempting to flee persecution. The supporting cast includes Carlos Francisco, [[Tânia Maria]], Robério Diógenes, [[Gabriel Leone]], [[Maria Fernanda Cândido]], [[Alice Carvalho]], and [[Udo Kier]] in his final film role.

The film had its world premiere at the [[2025 Cannes Film Festival]] on 18 May, where it received widespread acclaim and became the festival's most awarded film, winning the [[Cannes Film Festival Award for Best Actor|Best Actor]] award for Moura, the [[Cannes Film Festival Award for Best Director|Best Director]] award for Mendonça Filho,<ref name=":2" /> the [[International Confederation of Art Cinemas|Art House Cinema Award]] and the [[International Federation of Film Critics|FIPRESCI Prize]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=FIPRESCI Concludes a Special Participation at 78th Cannes Film Festival |url=https://fipresci.org/news/fipresci-concludes-a-special-participation-at-78th-cannes-film-festival/ |access-date=2025-12-08 |language=en-GB |archive-date=14 November 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251114062514/https://fipresci.org/news/fipresci-concludes-a-special-participation-at-78th-cannes-film-festival/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":3" /> At the [[83rd Golden Globe Awards]], it became the first Brazilian film nominated for [[Golden Globe Award for Best Motion Picture – Drama|Best Motion Picture – Drama]], winning [[Golden Globe Award for Best Actor in a Motion Picture – Drama|Best Actor in a Motion Picture – Drama]] (Wagner Moura) and [[Golden Globe Award for Best Foreign Language Film|Best Foreign Language Film]]. At the [[98th Academy Awards]], it was nominated for [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]], [[Academy Award for Best Actor|Best Actor]] for Moura, [[Academy Award for Achievement in Casting|Best Casting]] and [[Academy Award for Best International Feature Film|Best International Feature Film]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Canfield |first=David |date=2026-01-22 |title='The Secret Agent' Lands Brazil's Second Best Picture Oscar Nomination |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/the-secret-agent-wagner-moura-brazil-oscar-nominations-2026-1236480978/ |access-date=2026-01-22 |website=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] |language=en-US}}</ref> It won four [[Grande Prêmio do Cinema Brasileiro|Grande Otelo Awards]] ([[Grande Prêmio do Cinema Brasileiro for Best Film|Best Film]], Cinematography, Art Direction, and Visual Effects).

It was theatrically released in Brazil and Germany on 6 November 2025 by Vitrine Filmes and Port-au-Prince Films, respectively, and was released in France on 17 December by [[Ad Vitam (company)|Ad Vitam]].

==Plot==
In 1977, during the political turmoil of the [[Military dictatorship in Brazil|Brazilian military dictatorship]], former researcher Armando travels during the [[Brazilian Carnival|carnival]] holiday to [[Recife]], where his young son Fernando has been living with his in-laws since the death of Armando's wife, Fátima. He arrives at a refuge operated by former [[Anarchist communism|anarcho-communist]] Dona Sebastiana, where he adopts the name Marcelo and befriends other political dissidents including Claudia, Haroldo and [[Angolan Civil War]] [[Angolans in Brazil|refugees]] Thereza Vitória and Antonio. Meanwhile, corrupt [[Civil Police (Brazil)|Civil Police]] chief Euclides and his sons Sergio and Arlindo are called in during the holiday to investigate a severed human leg that has been found inside a captured shark.

Armando is placed by his dissident network in a job at the city's [[Identity document|identity card]] office under the alias "Marcelo", where he has a chance encounter with Euclides, who offers him his friendship and protection. Armando is visibly annoyed by Euclides's arrogant behaviour, which includes harassing Hans, a Jewish [[Holocaust survivors|Holocaust survivor]] who is mistakenly assumed to be a [[Ratlines (World War II)|Nazi fugitive]]. Armando's job also affords him the opportunity to search for files on his late mother, of whom he has few memories. Meanwhile, in [[São Paulo]], hitmen Bobbi and Augusto are hired by former [[Eletrobras]] executive director Henrique Ghirotti to kill Armando, against whom he has a political and personal vendetta.

Armando meets Elza, the leader of a political resistance movement in the [[Northeast Region, Brazil|Brazilian northeast]], at the {{interlanguage link|Cinema São Luiz|pt}}, where his father-in-law Sr. Alexandre works as a [[projectionist]]. Recording a testimony about Ghirotti's corrupt activities, Armando recounts a dinner he attended with Fátima that ended in a physical altercation with Ghirotti and his son, following remarks on the couple's lower socioeconomic class and supposed [[Red Scare|communist sympathies]]. Elza informs Armando that a [[contract killing]] has been ordered and instructs him to flee the country. Sergio and Arlindo dispose of the human leg in the [[Capibaribe River]], where it suddenly revives and attacks gay men [[Cruising for sex|cruising]] in a public park at night; the story, presumably a newspaper cover-up for the political corruption and violence during the carnival week, creates a [[The Hairy Leg|public frenzy]]. Augusto and Bobbi hire a local gunman, Vilmar, to find Armando. Anticipating a departure, Armando bids farewell to Dona Sebastiana and the other refugees.

The following day, Armando's cover is blown after Bobbi surveils Sr. Alexandre. Vilmar identifies Armando but fails to kill him, shooting Arlindo and another police officer. Bobbi, watching from afar, chases a bleeding Vilmar through Recife's city centre and is killed by Vilmar in a barbershop.

In the present day, history student Flavia researches Elza's resistance network through audio recordings and newspaper archives, learning that Armando was murdered and framed as a corrupt professor. Travelling to Recife, Flavia meets with Fernando, now a middle-aged doctor, who agrees to be interviewed after Flavia donates blood. The pair discuss Armando's political past and subsequent assassination, and the identity of Armando's mother "''[[Indigenous peoples in Brazil|India]]''". Fernando states he does not have a single memory of his father, but fondly recalls watching ''[[Jaws (film)|Jaws]]'' with his grandfather at a cinema which has since become the blood bank where he works.

The film is a neo-noir historical political thriller,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Mullen |first=Pat |date=2025-09-04 |title=The Secret Agent Review: TIFF 2025 |url=https://thatshelf.com/the-secret-agent-review-tiff-2025/ |access-date=2025-10-09 |website=That Shelf |language=en-US |archive-date=11 October 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251011065832/https://thatshelf.com/the-secret-agent-review-tiff-2025/ |url-status=live }}</ref> heavily inspired by [[Robert Altman]], [[Brian De Palma]], [[Sam Peckinpah]], [[Martin Scorsese]] and [[Steven Spielberg]] productions of the 1970s.<ref name="FidalgoVogueGlobo20251106">{{Cite web |author=Fidalgo, Sabrina & Mendonça Filho, Kleber |date=2025-11-06 |title=Entre voos, lentes e memórias: Kleber Mendonça Filho fala sobre o desejo de filmar o Brasil em 'O Agente Secreto' |url=https://vogue.globo.com/cultura/noticia/2025/11/entre-voos-lentes-e-memorias-kleber-mendonca-filho-fala-sobre-o-desejo-de-filmar-o-brasil-em-o-agente-secreto.ghtml |access-date=2025-12-11 |website=[[Vogue Brasil]] (Vogue.Globo.com) |language=pt-br |format=interview with reporter's introduction |quote=<small>...a gente é o fruto da dieta que consome. ''The Secret Agent's'' main motifs also echo Spielberg's ''[[Jaws (film)|Jaws]]'' (1975), particularly in that [[Recife]] is a coastal city plagued by [[tiger shark]] attacks.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2012-09-27 |title=The beautiful Brazilian beaches plagued by shark attacks |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-radio-and-tv-19720455 |access-date=2025-12-11 |work=BBC News |language=en-GB |archive-date=1 August 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180801231739/https://www.bbc.com/news/world-radio-and-tv-19720455 |url-status=live }}</ref> Some scenes take place during a screening of [[Richard Donner]]'s ''[[The Omen]]'' (1976) at the {{ill|Cinema São Luiz|pt|Cinema São Luiz}}.

Aspects of the "[[The Hairy Leg|Hairy Leg]]" story are based on real newspaper reports from the late 1970s that created a public frenzy in Recife, particularly on the coverage by [[Diário de Pernambuco]] (''Pernambuco Daily''). The story allowed the press to disguise censored news about [[Police violence in Brazil|police violence]], [[Corruption in Brazil|corruption]] and [[homophobia]] during the late years of the [[Military dictatorship in Brazil|Brazilian Military Dictatorship]].<ref>[[Kleber Mendonça Filho]]: ''"The hairy leg was actually created by a local journalist who was so fed up with not being able to write about what happened last night in terms of violence — because, of course, the police or the military inflicted the terror on the gay population, people having sex in parks, smoking pot. And so he developed a ‘hairy leg’ as a code. So, [he would write], ‘The hairy leg struck again last night,’ and everybody knew that something bad related to the police force was involved."'' {{cite web |last=Carey |first=Matthew |date=2025-05-20 |title='The Secret Agent's Kleber Mendonça Filho And Wagner Moura On Brazil's Urban Legend Of The Hairy Leg: “It Hops And Kicks” – Cannes Studio |url=https://deadline.com/video/the-secret-agent-interview-kleber-mendonca-filho-wagner-moura/ |access-date=2026-01-17 |publisher=Deadline Hollywood |archive-date=2 March 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260302200541/https://deadline.com/video/the-secret-agent-interview-kleber-mendonca-filho-wagner-moura/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The typical Brazilian public phones known as "[[orelhão]]" are extensively used throughout the story by Armando, and also became a promotional symbol of the film.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://g1.globo.com/pop-arte/noticia/2025/12/07/a-inusitada-origem-do-orelhao-que-virou-estrela-em-o-agente-secreto.ghtml |title=A inusitada origem do orelhão, que virou 'estrela' em 'O Agente Secreto' |date=7 December 2025 |website=[[Globo.com]] |access-date=2026-02-16 |language=pt-BR |archive-date=20 January 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260120034008/https://g1.globo.com/pop-arte/noticia/2025/12/07/a-inusitada-origem-do-orelhao-que-virou-estrela-em-o-agente-secreto.ghtml |url-status=live }}</ref> 

The production marked Wagner Moura's first [[Portuguese language|Portuguese]] language production in eight years.<ref>{{cite web |date=2 May 2024 |title=Wagner Moura set to lead political thriller 'The Secret Agent' |url=https://www.thehindu.com/entertainment/movies/wagner-moura-set-to-lead-political-thriller-the-secret-agent/article68131716.ece |access-date=18 February 2025 |website=Thehindu.com |archive-date=20 February 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250220170146/https://www.thehindu.com/entertainment/movies/wagner-moura-set-to-lead-political-thriller-the-secret-agent/article68131716.ece |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=5 December 2024 |title=Honored at CCXP, Wagner Moura says he thinks less about his career and more about life: 'I want to feel comfortable in my own skin' |url=https://oglobo.globo.com/english/noticia/2024/12/05/honored-at-ccxp-wagner-moura-says-he-thinks-less-about-his-career-and-more-about-life-i-want-to-feel-comfortable-in-my-own-skin.ghtml |access-date=18 February 2025 |website=[[O Globo]] |archive-date=20 February 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250220170146/https://oglobo.globo.com/english/noticia/2024/12/05/honored-at-ccxp-wagner-moura-says-he-thinks-less-about-his-career-and-more-about-life-i-want-to-feel-comfortable-in-my-own-skin.ghtml |url-status=live }}</ref> It was [[Udo Kier]]'s final feature film role before his death in November 2025,<ref>{{cite web |last=Debruge |first=Peter |date=9 November 2024 |title=At 80, Udo Kier — Who's Starred in Everything From Andy Warhol's Films to 'Ace Ventura' — Looks Back on a Lifetime of Cult Encounters |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250220170143/https://variety.com/2024/film/features/udo-kier-80th-birthday-lifetime-achievement-1236202718/ |url-status=live }}</ref> in his second collaboration with Mendonça Filho following ''[[Bacurau]]'' (2019).

===Filming===
[[File:Galo da Madrugada, Carnival 2014 - Recife, Pernambuco, Brazil.jpg|thumb|[[Brazilian Carnival|Carnival]] parade in Recife near Cinema São Luiz.]][[Principal photography]] took place over ten weeks in 2024, shooting on location in [[Recife]], [[Pernambuco]]. Many scenes were filmed in historical buildings throughout the city, such as the {{ill|Cinema São Luiz|pt|Cinema São Luiz}} (one of the last art house cinemas in Brazil) and on several of Recife's colonial bridges.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Bento |first=Emannuel |date=2024-07-24 |title='O Agente Secreto': Gravações do filme de Kleber Mendonça despertam nostalgia e curiosidade no Recife |url=http://jc.uol.com.br/cultura/2024/07/24/o-agente-secreto-gravacoes-do-filme-de-kleber-mendonca-no-recife.html |access-date=2025-09-12 |website=JC |language=pt-br}}</ref> For the "hairy leg attack" scenes, shooting took place on location at the [[Capibaribe River]], featuring its usual [[capybara]] inhabitants, and at "[[Lei Áurea|May 13th]] Park" (''{{ill|Parque 13 de Maio|pt|Parque 13 de Maio}}''). [[Brazilian Carnival|Carnival]] scenes were reenacted near Aurora Street (''Rua da Aurora''), where Recife's main carnival parade take place. Scenes featuring the captured [[tiger shark]] and Armando's teaching past were shot at the [[Federal University of Pernambuco]] campus, a [[Public university#Brazil|state owned university]].<ref name=":0" />
Additional scenes featuring Diógenes and Leone's characters were filmed in [[São Paulo]]. Principal photography wrapped by late August 2024.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.troiscouleurs.fr/cinema/cinema-news/le-tournage-de-the-secret-agent-avec-wagner-moura-vient-de-se-terminer/|website=Trois Couleurs|access-date=18 February 2025|title=Le tournage de "The Secret Agent" avec Wagner Moura vient de se terminer|trans-title=Filming of "The Secret Agent" with Wagner Moura has just finished |first=Romaine|last=Nesme|date=26 August 2024|language=fr}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Toledo |first=Marina |title="O Agente Secreto": filme de Kleber Mendonça com Wagner Moura encerra filmagens |url=https://www.cnnbrasil.com.br/entretenimento/o-agente-secreto-filme-de-kleber-mendonca-com-wagner-moura-encerra-filmagens/ |access-date=2025-02-18 |website=[[CNN Brasil]] |date=20 August 2024 |language=pt-BR |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260124235223/https://www.cnnbrasil.com.br/entretenimento/o-agente-secreto-filme-de-kleber-mendonca-com-wagner-moura-encerra-filmagens/ |archive-date=24 January 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref> [[Pick-up (filmmaking)|Pick-up]] scenes were shot in [[Brasília|Brasilia]] in December 2024.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-01-13 |title='O Agente Secreto' usou prédios de Brasília para ambientação; confira |url=https://g1.globo.com/df/distrito-federal/noticia/2026/01/13/o-agente-secreto-usou-predios-modernistas-no-centro-de-brasilia-para-ambientar-cenas-veja.ghtml |access-date=2026-02-07 |website=G1 |language=pt-BR |archive-date=12 February 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260212135325/https://g1.globo.com/df/distrito-federal/noticia/2026/01/13/o-agente-secreto-usou-predios-modernistas-no-centro-de-brasilia-para-ambientar-cenas-veja.ghtml |url-status=live }}</ref>

Mendonça Filho and his long-time partner [[Emilie Lesclaux]] produced the film through their film company CinemaScópio. The film also marks Russian-French cinematographer Evgenia Alexandrova's first collaboration with the filmmaker,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-05-29 |title=Conheça a diretora de fotografia russa do premiado filme brasileiro "O Agente Secreto" |url=https://www.rfi.fr/br/cultura/20250529-conhe%C3%A7a-a-diretora-de-fotografia-russa-do-premiado-filme-brasileiro-o-agente-secreto |access-date=2025-09-12 |website=RFI |language=pt-BR |archive-date=2 October 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251002104301/https://www.rfi.fr/br/cultura/20250529-conhe%C3%A7a-a-diretora-de-fotografia-russa-do-premiado-filme-brasileiro-o-agente-secreto |url-status=live }}</ref> who shot the film with [[Panavision]] anamorphic lenses and vintage camera equipment, aiming to replicate the visual style of the 1970s movies.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2025-09-10 |title=The Secret Agent |url=https://tiff.net/films/the-secret-agent |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=TIFF |language=en |archive-date=16 September 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250916211316/https://www.tiff.net/films/the-secret-agent |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Post-production ===
The film entered post-production in September 2024, shortly after the [[81st Venice International Film Festival]] where Mendonça Filho was a jury member for the main competition. As usual for the director's films, it features many [[Música popular brasileira|MPB]] songs ([[Lula Côrtes|Lula Cortês]], [[Zé Ramalho]], [[Angela Maria|Ângela Maria]], [[Waldick Soriano]], Orquestra Nelson Ferreira, Banda de Pífanos de Caruaru) alongside its original score by Mateus Alves and Tomaz Alves Souza.<ref name="FilmmakerMagReview">{{cite web |access-date=2025-05-29 |date=2025-05-19 |language=en |title=Cannes Film Festival 2025: The Secret Agent (Kleber Mendonça Filho) |url=https://filmmakermagazine.com/125990-cannes-film-festival-2025-the-secret-agent-kleber-mendonca-filho/ |website=Filmmaker Magazine}} {{Dead link|date=October 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}<!-- auto-translated from Portuguese by Module:CS1 translator --></ref> It also features international pop songs from [[Chicago (band)|Chicago]] and [[Donna Summer]], alongside [[Ennio Morricone]]'s ''Guerra e Pace, Pollo e Brace'' from the Italian drama film [[Come Play with Me (1968 film)|''Come Play with Me'']] (1968).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Abecassis |first=Sandro |date=2025-10-30 |title=Trilha sonora de o Agente Secreto: a história por trás da música de Ennio Morricone • Nave Criativa |url=https://www.navecriativa.com/trilha-sonora-de-o-agente-secreto-a-historia-por-tras-da-musica-de-ennio-morricone/ |access-date=2026-02-07 |website=Nave Criativa |language=pt-BR}}</ref>

==Reception==
===Box office===

million) and ''[[Black Phone 2]]'' fourth weekend (R$1.8 million).<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-11-10 |title='O Agente Secreto' estreia na liderança da bilheteria nacional
