But, if anything, that self-imposed discipline – and utter lack of sentimentality – speaks to the profound respect he has for the subject."<ref>{{cite news|last=Clarke|first=Donald|date=22 May 2023|title=One film has shaken Cannes festival like few others in recent memory|url=https://www.irishtimes.com/culture/film/2023/05/22/one-film-shakes-cannes-festival-like-few-others-in-recent-memory/|url-status=live|newspaper=[[The Irish Times]]|archive-url=https://archive.today/20230522100353/https://www.irishtimes.com/culture/film/2023/05/22/one-film-shakes-cannes-festival-like-few-others-in-recent-memory/|archive-date=22 May 2023|access-date=22 May 2023|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Raphael Abraham of the ''[[Financial Times]]'' wrote, "Glazer has achieved something much greater than just making the monstrous mundane&nbsp;– by rendering such extreme inhumanity ordinary he reawakens us to its true horror."<ref>{{cite news|last=Abraham|first=Raphael|date=22 May 2023|title=The Zone of Interest review — devastating portrait of the commandant of Auschwitz|url=https://www.ft.com/content/2934bd7d-8dcc-41ca-8b77-878e68942cfa|url-status=live|newspaper=[[Financial Times]]|archive-url=https://archive.today/20230522171430/https://www.ft.com/content/2934bd7d-8dcc-41ca-8b77-878e68942cfa|archive-date=22 May 2023|access-date=22 May 2023|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Jonathan Romney of ''[[Screen International]]'' wrote that the film "eschews false rhetoric, leaving maximum space for the audience's imaginative and emotional response".<ref>{{cite magazine|last=Romney|first=Jonathan|date=19 May 2023|title='The Zone Of Interest': Cannes Review|url=https://www.screendaily.com/reviews/the-zone-of-interest-cannes-review/5182303.article|url-access=limited|url-status=live|magazine=[[Screen International]]|archive-url=https://archive.today/20230523034907/https://www.screendaily.com/reviews/the-zone-of-interest-cannes-review/5182303.article|archive-date=23 May 2023|access-date=23 May 2023}}</ref>

David Ehrlich of ''[[IndieWire]]'' praised Glazer's camera process for instilling "a flattening evenness into a film where the lack of drama becomes deeply sickening unto itself".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.indiewire.com/criticism/movies/the-zone-of-interest-review-jonathan-glazer-1234865296/|title='The Zone of Interest' Review: Jonathan Glazer's Holocaust Anti-Drama Is a Chilling Look at the Banality of Evil|last=Ehrlich|first=David|date=19 May 2023|website=[[IndieWire]]|access-date=22 May 2023|archive-date=26 May 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230526190317/https://www.indiewire.com/criticism/movies/the-zone-of-interest-review-jonathan-glazer-1234865296/|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Robbie Collin]] of ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]'' wrote, "Through painstaking framing and sound design, its horrors gnaw at the edge of every shot."<ref>{{cite news|last=Collin|first=Robbie|author-link=Robbie Collin|date=19 May 2023|title=The Zone of Interest, Cannes review: Jonathan Glazer's Auschwitz film is horrifying in its banality|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/films/0/zone-of-interest-review-jonathan-glazer-cannes-2023/|url-status=live|newspaper=[[The Daily Telegraph]]|archive-url=https://archive.today/20230519183952/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/films/0/zone-of-interest-review-jonathan-glazer-cannes-2023/|archive-date=19 May 2023|access-date=22 May 2023}}</ref> In a four-star review, [[Peter Bradshaw]] of ''[[The Guardian]]'' called it "a film which for all its artistry is perhaps not entirely in control of its (intentional) bad taste", while also praising the "superb score by Mica Levi and sound design by [[Johnnie Burn]]".<ref>{{cite news|last=Bradshaw|first=Peter|author-link=Peter Bradshaw|date=19 May 2023|title=The Zone of Interest review – Jonathan Glazer adapts Martin Amis's chilling Holocaust drama|url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2023/may/19/the-zone-of-interest-review-jonathan-glazer-adapts-martin-amiss-chilling-holocaust-drama|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|access-date=22 May 2023|archive-date=29 May 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230529051743/https://www.theguardian.com/film/2023/may/19/the-zone-of-interest-review-jonathan-glazer-adapts-martin-amiss-chilling-holocaust-drama|url-status=live}}</ref>

Writing for [[Worldcrunch]], the German critic Hanns-Georg Rodek wrote that the film "concentrates in one garden the attitude of an entire nation that wanted to know nothing."<ref>{{cite web |last=Rodek |first=Hanns-Georg |title=Where 'The Zone Of Interest' Won't Go On Auschwitz — A German Critique Of New Nazi Film |url=https://worldcrunch.com/culture-society/zone-of-interest-german-criticism |website=WorldCrunch |access-date=25 May 2023 |archive-date=25 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230525203603/https://worldcrunch.com/culture-society/zone-of-interest-german-criticism |url-status=live}}</ref> Conversely, the Italian film critic Davide Abbatescianni's review published by [[Cineuropa]] was less positive. He criticised the film for its disturbing atmosphere, which he found to be well-crafted but monotonous, and for the performances, which he felt could not bring any change to the concept presented in a film that he thought lacked variety and remained stagnant for two hours.<ref>{{cite web |last=Abbatescianni |first=Davide |title=Review: The Zone of Interest |url=https://cineuropa.org/en/newsdetail/442800/ |website=Cineuropa |date=21 May 2023 |access-date=26 May 2023 |archive-date=27 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230527223443/https://cineuropa.org/en/newsdetail/442800/ |url-status=live}}</ref> Among the other rare negative reviews, ''[[Cahiers du Cinéma]]'' found, "The problem is not only the weakness of (the film's) formal lurches, which are much more derisory than those of ''Under The Skin'', and remain here at the stage of mannerisms (why dispense them in such a furtive manner, if not to frustrate needlessly?). It's also that this fantastic idea of off-camera poisoning the frame without ever showing the forbidden image ends up running empty and looking at itself."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sadat |first=Yal |date=22 May 2023 |title=The Zone of Interest de Jonathan Glazer l l'actualité du cinéma |url=https://www.cahiersducinema.com/actualites/the-zone-of-interest-de-jonathan-glazer/ |access-date=18 March 2024 |website=Cahiers du Cinéma |language=fr-FR}}</ref>

''The Irish Times'' commented that German reviews were generally less favorable than English language reviews.<ref>{{Cite news |title='It is dishonest': Germany divided over Oscar-nominated Auschwitz film The Zone of Interest |url=https://www.irishtimes.com/culture/film/2024/03/10/it-is-dishonest-germany-divided-over-oscar-nominated-auschwitz-film-the-zone-of-interest/ |access-date=19 March 2024 |newspaper=The Irish Times |language=en}}</ref> Writing for the ''[[Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung]]'', however, Andreas Klib stated that "Here the camera repeatedly jumps over the axis between the characters – a deadly sin in illusion cinema – to show the back of the event. Because we are not supposed to take part in it, but rather pay attention to details: the clouds of steam from a locomotive on the horizon. The smoke rising from the crematorium into the evening air. The reddish glow of the night sky. The ash that fertilizes the rose beds. At Cannes, where ''The Zone of Interest'' won the Grand Jury Prize, some critics criticized the film for its lack of storytelling. But that's exactly the point of Glazer's film: it doesn't paint a story, but a world."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Kilb |first=Andreas |date=28 February 2024 |title="The Zone of Interest" mit Sandra Hüller und Christian Friedel neu im Kino |url=https://www.faz.net/aktuell/feuilleton/kino/the-zone-of-interest-mit-sandra-hueller-und-christian-friedel-neu-im-kino-19549669.html |access-date=19 March 2024 |work=FAZ.NET |language=de |issn=0174-4909}}</ref>

''[[Sight and Sound]]'' put the film at 2 and 14 on their lists of the best 50 movies of 2023 and 2024, respectively.<ref name="films">{{Cite web |date=8 December 2023 |title=The 50 best films of 2023 |url=https://www.bfi.org.uk/sight-and-sound/polls/50-best-films-2023 |access-date=2 March 2025 |website=BFI |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=6 December 2024 |title=The 50 best films of 2024 |url=https://www.bfi.org.uk/sight-and-sound/polls/50-best-films-2024 |access-date=2 March 2025 |website=BFI |language=en}}</ref> In June 2025, ''[[IndieWire]]'' ranked the film at number 2 on its list of "The 100 Best Movies of the 2020s (So Far)."<ref name="Best">{{cite web |date=16 June 2025 |title=The 100 Best Movies of the 2020s (So Far)|url=https://www.indiewire.com/lists/best-movies-2020s/ |access-date=23 June 2025}}</ref> It also ranked number 12 on ''[[The New York Times]]''{{'}} list of "The 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century" and number 56 on the "Readers' Choice" edition of the list.<ref name="Times">{{cite web | url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2025/movies/best-movies-21st-century.html | title=The 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century | date=23 June 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Readers Choose Their Top Movies of the 21st Century |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2025/movies/readers-movies-21st-century.html |website=The New York Times |access-date=2 July 2025}}</ref> In July 2025, it ranked number 77 on ''[[Rolling Stone]]''{{'}}s list of "The 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century."<ref name="Rolling"/>

===Additional reactions===
The film was publicly praised by many filmmakers, including [[Steven Spielberg]] who said ''The Zone of Interest'' was the best film about the [[Holocaust in film|Holocaust]] since his film ''[[Schindler's List]]'' (1993), "It's doing a lot of good work in raising awareness, especially about the [[banality of evil]]."<ref>{{cite web | url=https://screenrant.com/zone-of-interest-steven-spielberg-review/ | title="Best...I've Witnessed": Steven Spielberg Reviews A24s the Zone of Interest | website=[[Screen Rant]] | date=21 February 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-features/schindlers-list-oral-history-steven-spielberg-liam-neeson-1235830436/ | title='Schindler's List': An Oral History of a Masterpiece | website=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] | date=21 February 2024|author=Feinberg, Scott}}</ref> [[Alfonso Cuarón]] described ''The Zone of Interest'' as "probably the most important film in this century."<ref>{{cite web | url=https://faroutmagazine.co.uk/alfonso-cuaron-hails-the-zone-of-interest-as-the-most-important-film-of-the-century/ | title=Alfonso Cuaron: 'The Zone of Interest' is 'film of the century' | date=6 February 2024}}</ref> Other filmmakers who praised the film include [[Allison Anders]], [[Robert Eggers]], [[Reinaldo Marcus Green]], [[Bill Hader]], [[Andrew Haigh]], [[Chad Hartigan]], [[Don Hertzfeldt]], [[Zoe Lister-Jones]], [[Karyn Kusama]], [[Rachel Morrison]], [[James Ponsoldt]], [[Jonathan Vinel]] and [[Adam Wingard]].<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.indiewire.com/gallery/directors-best-movies-tv-2023-bill-hader-lulu-wang-robert-eggers/mcdhold-uc030/ |title=38 Directors Pick Their Favorite Films of 2023 |magazine=[[IndieWire]] |date=31 December 2023 |access-date=6 March 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=20 December 2024 |title=The Best Films of 2024 As Chosen by Some of Its Key Filmmakers |url=https://filmmakermagazine.com/128311-the-best-films-of-2024-as-chosen-by-some-of-its-key-filmmakers/ |access-date=22 March 2025 |work=[[Filmmaker (magazine)|Filmmaker]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=O'Flat |first=Chris |title=65 Directors Pick Their Favorite Films of 2024 |url=https://www.indiewire.com/gallery/directors-pick-best-films-2024/ |access-date=30 December 2024 |work=IndieWire |date=30 December 2024}}</ref>

In a [[Variety (magazine)|''Variety'']] essay expressing his admiration for the film [[Todd Field]] wrote: {{blockquote|"For those familiar with Glazer's films it's no surprise his approach here is unencumbered by tropes, genre conceits, or the cinematic shorthand we often take for granted. Over his twenty-four-year career as one of our finest filmmakers, Glazer has consistently executed high-wire interpretations of genre, and in the process completely reinvented them: crime (''[[Sexy Beast]]''), the paranormal (''[[Birth (2004 film)|Birth]]''), science fiction (''Under the Skin''). His pictures within these frames are mind-blowingly unique, as if he'd never seen anything that had been done before. ''The Zone of Interest'' is just as enigmatic and urgent. For we live in a time fraught with all kinds of walls used to [[ghetto]]ize the ''[[Other (philosophy)|other]]''. A paradise from which it feels harder and harder to escape. Glazer's art drives us to a place where we have no choice but to try."<ref>{{cite web |last=Field |first=Todd |display-authors=etal |date=13 December 2023 |title=16 Directors Praise 2023's Best Films: Alfonso Cuarón on 'Killers of the Flower Moon,' Jane Campion on 'Priscilla' and More |url=https://variety.com/lists/directors-best-films-2023/the-zone-of-interest-2/ |access-date=23 January 2024 |website=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |archive-date=1 January 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240101174308/https://variety.com/lists/directors-best-films-2023/the-zone-of-interest-2/ |url-status=live}}</ref>}}Upon its release in Japan on 24 May 2024, video game designer [[Hideo Kojima]] hailed the work, "The sounds that plead to the audience through the wall and the torture of deliberately not showing anything at all are used to draw images from the audience's minds. The film tests your 'zone of interest' and paradoxically questions the present's fading memory of the Holocaust."<ref>{{Cite web |title=宇垣美里、小島秀夫、森達也らが映画「関心領域」語る こがけん「ひたすらに怖い」（映画ナタリー） |trans-title=Misato Ugaki, Hideo Kojima, Tatsuya Mori and others talk about the film "Zone of Interest" Koga Ken "It's just so scary" (Movie Natalie) |url=https://news.yahoo.co.jp/articles/79410b33777643e82466143d9a9dd74a9f99fe02 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240713230918/https://news.yahoo.co.jp/articles/79410b33777643e82466143d9a9dd74a9f99fe02 |archive-date=13 July 2024 |access-date=13 May 2024 |website=Yahoo!ニュース |language=ja}}</ref>

=== Oscars acceptance speech ===
The film's theatrical release in December 2023 came during the escalating destruction caused by the Israeli invasion of the [[Gaza Strip]]. In his Oscar acceptance speech at the [[96th Academy Awards]] in March 2024, Glazer said that ''The Zone of Interest'' shows where [[dehumanisation]] leads at its worst. He expressed criticism, as a Jewish person, both of the dehumanisation of "the victims of October the 7th in Israel" and of "the [[Gaza genocide|ongoing attack on Gaza]]", and told the audience: "Right now, we stand here as men who refute [''sic''] their [[Jewish identity|Jewishness]] and the Holocaust being hijacked by [[Israeli-occupied territories|an occupation]] which has led to conflict for so many innocent people."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Stevens |first=Matt |date=10 March 2024 |title=Jonathan Glazer Condemns 'Occupation' and Violence in Israel and Gaza. Glazer, the director of 'The Zone of Interest,' spoke about the war while accepting the Oscar for best international feature. |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/03/10/movies/jonathan-glazer-the-zone-of-interest-oscars-speech-israel-gaza.html |access-date=11 March 2024 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Li |first=Shirley |date=11 March 2024 |title=Jonathan Glazer's Warning at the Oscars. The director of ''The Zone of Interest'' accepted his award with an anti-war speech that drew praise and confusion.|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/culture/archive/2024/03/jonathan-glazer-israel-gaza-speech/677714/ |access-date=11 March 2024 |work=[[The Atlantic]] |language=en}}</ref>

Glazer's speech led to a significant reaction in the news media, especially after a widely circulated quotation truncated his remarks, suggesting that Glazer had simply refuted his Jewish identity, rather than refuting said identity "being hijacked by an occupation".<ref name="Rahman 2024 h824">{{cite web | last=Rahman | first=Abid | title=Jonathan Glazer's Oscar Speech Becomes Latest Battleground in Israel-Gaza Conflict | website=The Hollywood Reporter | date=11 March 2024 | url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/zone-of-interest-jonathan-glazer-2024-oscar-speech-israel-gaza-conflict-1235848917/ | access-date=13 March 2024}}</ref> Producer James Wilson said at the [[British Academy Film Awards]]: "I had a friend that texted me the other day. He said he couldn't stop thinking about the walls we build in our daily lives that we don't choose... There's obviously things going on in the world, in Gaza, that remind us starkly of the sort of selective empathy, that there seems to be groups of innocent people being killed that we care about less than other innocent people."<ref name="The Irish News 2024 u092">{{cite web | title=The Zone Of Interest producer: Gaza conflict reminds us of 'selective empathy' |first=Hannah |last=Roberts |author2=Charlotte McLaughlin| website=The Irish News | date=18 February 2024 | url=https://www.irishnews.com/entertainment/the-zone-of-interest-producer-gaza-conflict-reminds-us-of-selective-empathy-5OJWPYRALNJMDB7PESNFOJWVIY/ | access-date=13 March 2024}}</ref>

On 15 March, [[Cinema of Hungary|Hungarian filmmaker]] [[László Nemes]], who previously made the Oscar winning ''[[Son of Saul]]'', made a public statement with ''[[The Guardian]]'' denouncing the speech, claiming the filmmaker "should have stayed silent instead of revealing he has no understanding of history and the forces undoing civilization, before or after the Holocaust..." and accused him of resorting to "talking points disseminated by propaganda meant to eradicate, at the end, all Jewish presence from the Earth."<ref>{{cite  news |last1=Shoard |first1=Catherine |title=Jonathan Glazer's Oscars speech condemned by Son of Saul director: 'He should have stayed silent' |url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2024/mar/15/jonathan-glazer-oscars-speech-condemned-by-son-of-saul-director-laszlo-nemes |work=[[The Guardian]] |access-date=4 June 2026}}</ref>  On 18 March, an [[open letter]] denouncing the speech as [[blood libel]] was signed by more than 1,000 "Jewish creatives, executives, and [[Cinema of the United States|Hollywood]] professionals", including [[Amy Pascal]], [[Jennifer Jason Leigh]], [[Julianna Margulies]], [[Debra Messing]], [[Eli Roth]], and [[Michael Rapaport]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Siegel |first=Tatiana |date=18 March 2024 |title=Over 450 Jewish Creatives and Professionals Denounce Jonathan Glazer's 'Zone of Interest' Oscars Speech in Open Letter (EXCLUSIVE) |url=https://variety.com/2024/film/news/jonathan-glazer-oscar-speech-zone-of-interest-open-letter-1235944880/ |access-date=19 March 2024 |website=Variety |language=en-US}}</ref> On 5 April, a second open letter defending Glazer was signed by over 150 Jewish creatives in the film industry. Eventually, over 450 Jewish creatives signed the letter, including [[Joel Coen]], [[Todd Haynes]], [[Joaquin Phoenix]], [[Elliott Gould]], and [[Wallace Shawn]]; the film's composer, Mica Levi, was also a signatory.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Shafer |first=Ellise |date=5 April 2024 |title=Joaquin Phoenix, Elliott Gould, Chloe Fineman and More Jewish Creatives Support Jonathan Glazer's Oscars Speech in Open Letter (EXCLUSIVE) |url=https://variety.com/2024/film/global/jonathan-glazer-oscars-speech-support-jewish-creatives-open-letter-1235960158/ |access-date=5 April 2024 |website=Variety |language=en-US}}</ref> The playwrights [[Tony Kushner]] and [[Zoe Kazan]] were among the speech's earlier supporters.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Shoard | first=Catherine | title='Unimpeachable, irrefutable': US playwright Tony Kushner praises Jonathan Glazer's Oscars speech | website=The Guardian | date=21 March 2024 | url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2024/mar/21/unimpeachable-irrefutable-us-playwright-tony-kushner-praises-jonathan-glazers-oscars-speech | access-date=24 March 2024}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | last=Kazan | first=Zoe | title=............kind of shocked that anyone who saw zone of interest could be shocked by what glazer said at the oscars | website=X | date=19 March 2023 | url=https://twitter.com/zoeinthecities/status/1769860643413168334&ved=2ahUKEwiZ5O-s0oyFAxUxWkEAHfIFBgoQgtAMegQIFxAB&usg=AOvVaw1_KzvNkvXoRqhLnLXsZpEQ | access-date=24 March 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=In Oscars Speech, Director Jonathan Glazer Denounces 'Occupation' and 'Dehumanization' in Israel and Gaza |url=https://www.jewishexponent.com/in-oscars-speech-director-jonathan-glazer-denounces-occupation-and-dehumanization-in-israel-and-gaza/ |website=Jewish Exponent |access-date=13 March 2024 |date=11 March 2024}}</ref> That month, Glazer donated seven signed ''Zone of Interest'' posters to a [[Medical Aid for Palestinians]] fundraiser.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Vlessing |first=Etan |date=3 April 2024 |title=Jonathan Glazer Donates Signed 'Zone of Interest' Posters to Gaza Humanitarian Relief Auction |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/jonathan-glazer-zone-interest-posters-gaza-relief-1235865523/ |access-date=26 September 2024 |website=The Hollywood Reporter |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Ntim |first=Zac |date=8 April 2024 |title=Jonathan Glazer Adds Further Gifts To Cinema For Gaza Fundraising Campaign Alongside Spike Lee, Olivia Colman, Susan Sarandon & Paul Mescal |url=https://deadline.com/2024/04/cinema-for-gaza-jonathan-glazer-spike-lee-tessa-thompson-paul-mescal-1235878202/ |access-date=26 September 2024 |website=Deadline |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Shafer |first=Ellise |date=3 April 2024 |title=Jonathan Glazer Donates Signed 'Zone of Interest' Posters to Cinema for Gaza Auction; Fundraiser Reaches Over $50,000 in First Day |url=https://variety.com/2024/film/global/jonathan-glazer-gaza-auction-zone-of-interest-posters-1235958798/ |access-date=26 September 2024 |website=Variety The '''Toronto International Film Festival''' ('''TIFF''') is one of the most prestigious and largest publicly attended [[film festival]]s in the world.

Founded in 1976, the festival takes place every year in early September, in [[downtown Toronto]]. The organization behind the film festival is also a permanent destination for film culture at the [[TIFF Lightbox]], which serves as a venue for some film screenings during the festival as well as cinematheque film series, commercial art house and independent film screenings, and other specialty film festivals, throughout the year.

The [[Toronto International Film Festival People's Choice Award|TIFF People's Choice Award]] – which is based on audience balloting – has emerged as an indicator of success during [[Film awards seasons|awards season]], especially at the [[Academy Awards]]. Past recipients of this award include Oscar-winning films, such as ''[[Chariots of Fire]]'' (1981), ''[[Life Is Beautiful]]'' (1998), ''[[American Beauty (1999 film)|American Beauty]]'' (1999), ''[[Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon]]'' (2000), ''[[Slumdog Millionaire]]'' (2008), ''[[The King's Speech]]'' (2010), ''[[Silver Linings Playbook]]'' (2012), ''[[12 Years a Slave (film)|12 Years a Slave]]'' (2013), ''[[The Imitation Game]]'' (2014), ''[[La La Land]]'' (2016), ''[[Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri]]'' (2017), ''[[Green Book (film)|Green Book]]'' (2018), ''[[Jojo Rabbit]]'' (2019), ''[[Nomadland (film)|Nomadland]]'' (2020), ''[[Belfast (film)|Belfast]]'' (2021) and ''[[American Fiction (film)|American Fiction]]'' (2023).

TIFF starts the Thursday night after Labour Day (the first Monday in September in Canada) and lasts for eleven days. The [[2024 Toronto International Film Festival]] took place from September 5 through 15, 2024.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2024-06-18 |title=TIFF 2024: Amy Adams, Elton John and Lupita Nyong’o films lead lineup as Toronto festival aims for post-strike comeback |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/arts/film/article-amy-adams-elton-john-and-lupita-nyongo-films-lead-lineup-as-tiff-aims/ |access-date=2024-11-04 |work=The Globe and Mail |language=en-CA}}</ref> The [[2025 Toronto International Film Festival]] took place from September 4 through 14, 2025.

Along with [[Berlin International Film Festival|Berlin]], [[Cannes Film Festival|Cannes]], [[Venice Film Festival|Venice]], and [[Sundance Film Festival|Sundance]], TIFF is one of the Big Five international film festivals.<ref>{{Cite web |last=ROXBOROUGH |first=SCOTT |date=February 16, 2020 |title=Berlin Rebooted: Festival Shuffles Lineup, Aims for Recharged Market |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/berlin-rebooted-festival-shuffles-lineup-aims-recharged-market-1278615/ |access-date=October 21, 2026 |website=[[THE Hollywood REPORTER]]}}</ref>

==Background==
The Toronto International Film Festival was first launched as the '''Toronto Festival of Festivals''', collecting the best films from other film festivals around the world and showing them to eager audiences in Toronto. Founded by [[Bill Marshall (producer)|Bill Marshall]], [[Dusty Cohl]], and [[Henk Van der Kolk]],<ref name=tstar>{{cite news |first=Peter |last=Goffin |title=TIFF co-founder Bill Marshall, 77, remembered as pioneer of Canadian film |url=https://www.thestar.com/entertainment/2017/01/01/tiff-co-founder-bill-marshall-77-remembered-as-pioneer-of-canadian-film.html |work=[[Toronto Star]] |date=January 1, 2017 |access-date=January 3, 2017 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170102173841/https://www.thestar.com/entertainment/2017/01/01/tiff-co-founder-bill-marshall-77-remembered-as-pioneer-of-canadian-film.html |archive-date=January 2, 2017 }}</ref> the inaugural event took place from October 18 through 24, 1976. That first year, 31,500 filmgoers watched 155 feature films from 30 countries presented in ten programmes.<ref>{{Cite magazine |date=April 13, 1977 |title=Will U.S. Again Snub Canada? |magazine=Variety |page=3}}</ref> [[File:TIFFBellLightbox2.JPG|thumb|Lightbox is the cultural centrepiece and home to TIFF programming outside festival dates|left]]TIFF was once centred on the [[Yorkville, Toronto|Yorkville]] neighbourhood, but, following the closure of the [[University Theatre (Toronto)|University Theatre]] in 1986, which had been used for the nightly gala presentations, the festival moved downtown to the [[Toronto Entertainment District]], with most galas initially being held at the [[Ryerson Theatre]] and the closing night gala at [[Roy Thomson Hall]].<ref>{{cite news |url = https://www.thestar.com/article/851243 |work = [[Toronto Star]] |first = Raju |last = Mudhar |date = August 25, 2010 |access-date = September 7, 2010 |title = From mega clubs to mega culture in Entertainment District |url-status = live |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100831074356/http://www.thestar.com/article/851243 |archive-date = August 31, 2010 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url = http://www.toronto.com/article/696280?bn=1 |work = [[Toronto Star]] |first = Kate |last = Allen |date = August 24, 2011 |access-date = August 25, 2011 |title = TIFF's great migration |url-status = dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120323021413/http://www.toronto.com/article/696280?bn=1 |archive-date = March 23, 2012 }}</ref><ref name=selections>{{cite magazine|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|page=55|date=September 7, 1988|title=Mainstream To Esoteric In Toronto|last=Adilman|first=Sid}}</ref><!-- As of 2013, TIFF maintains extensive connections with the Yorkville area.<ref>{{cite web
|last        = Moran
|first       = Andrew
|title       = Yorkville the hot spot in Toronto during film festival
|publisher   = [[DigitalJournal.com|Digital Journal]]
|date        = September 2009
|url         = http://www.digitaljournal.com/article/279106
|access-date  = May 29, 2010
}}</ref> --> TIFF is known for the celebrity buzz it brings to the area with international media setting up near its restaurants and stores for photos and interviews with the stars. In 2010, TIFF opened its permanent headquarters, TIFF Lightbox, a year-round home for the appreciation of film in the heart of downtown Toronto, although TIFF films are still screened at a wider variety of venues, including the [[Scotiabank Theatre Toronto]], rather than exclusively at the Lightbox.

TIFF has grown, steadily adding initiatives throughout the years. [[TIFF Cinematheque]] (formerly Cinematheque Ontario) and the Film Reference Library (FRL) opened in 1990. The TIFF Kids International Film Festival (formerly Sprockets) launched in 1998.<ref>Brad Wheeler, [https://www.theglobeandmail.com/arts/film/tiff-kids-film-festival-salutes-pioneer-in-stop-motion-animation/article29556132/ "TIFF kids' film festival salutes pioneer in stop-motion animation"]. ''[[The Globe and Mail]]'', April 7, 2016.</ref> Film Circuit began exhibiting independent and Canadian films in under-serviced cities across Canada in 1994.

The festival also organizes the TIFF Film Circuit, a program which partners with local organizations in other Canadian towns and cities to present screenings of films that have previously been shown at TIFF.

In May 2024, TIFF announced that it will launch a full film market in 2026.<ref>Jeremy Kay, [https://www.screendaily.com/news/tiff-to-launch-official-market-in-2026/5193553.article "Toronto film festival to launch official market in 2026"]. ''[[Screen Daily]]'', May 16, 2024.</ref>

== Leadership ==
Throughout its history, TIFF has had numerous periods when the same individual served as both a head of the festival and the parent organization. Other times, the positions have diverged. It also has had co-directors at some times.

=== Festival Director ===
After the founding, [[Wayne Clarkson]] became festival director in 1978, when it was still known as the Toronto Festival of Festivals.<ref name="scott">[[Jay Scott]], "Festival of Festivals gets a new look". ''[[The Globe and Mail]]'', April 7, 1978.</ref>  In 1986, the founder of the  Vancouver International Film Festival, Leonard Schein, became festival director, but resigned after just one festival cycle.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kelly |first=Brendan |date=2000-08-25 |title=Toronto Time Capsule |url=https://variety.com/2000/film/news/toronto-time-capsule-1117785590/ |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=Variety |language=en-US}}</ref> Deputy director [[Helga Stephenson]] was elevated as interim head of the organization before taking over the position permanently in 1987.<ref name="elevates">"Toronto film festival elevates interim director to top position". ''[[Toronto Star]]'', December 20, 1986.</ref> 

In 1994, [[Piers Handling]] became the festival's director, as well as CEO, which was an unusually powerful combination.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2018-08-27 |title=TIFF 2018: Piers Handling on 24 years at the top of the biggest film festival in the world, and what’s next |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/arts/film/article-tiff-2018-piers-handling-on-24-years-at-the-top-of-the-biggest-film/ |access-date=2026-09-21 |work=The Globe and Mail |language=en-CA}}</ref> In 2004, [[Noah Cowan]] became co-director of TIFF. Longtime programmer [[Cameron Bailey]] succeeded Cowan as co-director in 2007 when Cowan became the artistic director of the newly opened [[TIFF Lightbox]], 

In 2018, upon her ascent as executive director, Joana Vicente also became co-director of the festival.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Vlessing |first=Etan |date=2018-08-28 |title=Toronto: IFP’s Joana Vicente Hired as Festival Co-Head |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/general-news/toronto-ifp-head-joana-vicente-hired-as-festival-head-1137788/ |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=The Hollywood Reporter |language=en-US}}</ref> 

=== CEO and Executive Director ===
[[Piers Handling]] was the first official CEO starting in 1994, a position he held until 2018, when he was succeeded by Joana Vicente as the top business executive. Vicente served as executive director and co-head of the organization.  Vicente left in 2021 to run the Sundance Institute and Cameron Bailey was elevated to be singular CEO of TIFF in 2021.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Press |first=The Canadian |title=Cameron Bailey appointed CEO of Toronto International Film Festival |url=https://www.thestar.com/entertainment/cameron-bailey-appointed-ceo-of-toronto-international-film-festival/article_b67d185b-6478-5a59-b762-a6420cb4249c.html |access-date=2026-09-21 |work=Toronto Star |language=en}}</ref> 

Bailey became the artistic director of the Toronto International Film Festival, as well as TIFF Lightbox's year round programming.<ref>[https://nationalpost.com/entertainment/cameron-bailey-named-artistic-director-of-toronto-international-film-festival "Cameron Bailey named artistic director of Toronto International Film Festival"] . ''[[National Post]]'', March 14, 2012.</ref>

===Current Leadership===
As of 2026, in addition to Bailey, the leadership of the organization includes [[Anita Lee (film programmer)|Anita Lee]] as chief of programming,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-09-09 |title=5 things TIFF heads Cameron Bailey and Anita Lee want you to know about 51st festival |url=https://www.yahoo.com/entertainment/movies/articles/5-things-tiff-heads-cameron-180000867.html |access-date=2026-10-04 |website=Yahoo Entertainment |language=en-US}}</ref> Jennifer Frees as chief business officer,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Vlessing |first=Etan |date=2024-01-11 |title=Toronto Film Fest Names Jennifer Frees to Chief Business and Marketing Officer Post |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/business/business-news/toronto-film-fest-chief-business-marketing-officer-post-1235786064/ |access-date=2026-10-04 |website=The Hollywood Reporter |language=en-US}}</ref> Charles Tremblay as head of market,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kay |first=Jeremy |title=Canadian distribution veteran Charles Tremblay named head of TIFF: The Market |url=https://www.screendaily.com/news/canadian-distribution-veteran-charles-tremblay-named-head-of-tiff-the-market/5208317.article |access-date=2026-10-04 |website=Screen |language=en}}</ref> [[Judy Lung]] as head of communications and strategy.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Davoli |first=Stephanie |date=2026-09-08 |title=What It Really Takes to Make TIFF Happen |url=https://fashionmagazine.com/style/what-it-really-takes-to-make-tiff-happen/ |access-date=2026-10-04 |website=FASHION Magazine |language=en-CA}}</ref>

==History==
The festival was founded in 1976 at the [[Windsor Arms Hotel]] by [[Bill Marshall (producer)|Bill Marshall]], Henk Van der Kolk and [[Dusty Cohl]].<ref>{{cite web
 |last        = Stavrou
 |first       = Philip
 |title       = Film Festival events return to their roots
 |publisher   = [[CTVglobemedia]]
 |date        = September 2005
 |url         = http://www.ctv.ca/servlet/ArticleNews/story/CTVNews/20050912/WindsorArms_20050912/20050912/
 |access-date  = September 19, 2014
|url-status     = dead
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20080210010908/http://www.ctv.ca/servlet/ArticleNews/story/CTVNews/20050912/WindsorArms_20050912/20050912/
 |archive-date = February 10, 2008
}}</ref> Beginning as a collection of the best-regarded films from film festivals around the world, it had an inaugural attendance of 35,000.<ref>{{cite press release |url = http://tiff.net/press/pressreleases/2010/35th-anniversary-fact-sheet |publisher = Toronto International Film Festival |date = September 27, 2010 |title = 35th Anniversary Fact Sheet: TIFF Facts and Figures |access-date = September 21, 2010 |url-status = dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100804042620/http://tiff.net/press/pressreleases/2010/35th-anniversary-fact-sheet |archive-date = August 4, 2010 }}</ref> Ironically, however, Hollywood studios withdrew their submissions from TIFF due to concerns that Toronto audiences would be too parochial for their feature releases.<ref>{{cite web
 |last        = Sterritt
 |first       = David
 |title       = Film Festivals - Then and Now
 |publisher   = [[FIPRESCI]]
 |date        = April 2010
 |url         = http://www.fipresci.org/undercurrent/issue_0609/sterritt_festivals.htm
 |access-date  = June 8, 2010
|url-status     = dead
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20130906171153/http://fipresci.org/undercurrent/issue_0609/sterritt_festivals.htm
 |archive-date = September 6, 2013
}}</ref>

In 1978, the festival first began billing itself as "the Toronto International Film Festival" as a supplementary name, although it retained Festival of Festivals as its primary branding.<ref>[[Jay Scott]], "Festival of Festivals gets a new look". ''[[The Globe and Mail]]'', April 7, 1978.</ref> At the same time it moved from the [[Westin Harbour Castle Hotel|Harbour Castle Hotel]] to the Plaza II, and [[Wayne Clarkson]] replaced Marshall as the festival director. The number of galas increased from one to two per night and the [[Canadian Film Awards]] were incorporated into the festival.<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=April 12, 1978|page=48|title=Toronto Re-Names, Relocates Its Festival; Wayne Clark In}}</ref>

The Festival of Festivals name was dropped in 1994, with the event becoming known exclusively as the Toronto International Film Festival at that time.<ref>"Toronto film festival changes name". ''[[The Globe and Mail]]'', February 10, 1994.</ref> From 1994 to 2009, the umbrella organization running TIFF was named "Toronto International Film Festival Group" (TIFFG). In 2009, the umbrella organization TIFFG was renamed to TIFF.<ref>{{cite web |url = http://www.torontointernationalfilmfestival.ca/abouttiff/organization/tiffhistory |title = TIFF History |access-date = September 21, 2010 |publisher = Toronto International Film Festival |url-status = dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100825030348/http://www.torontointernationalfilmfestival.ca/abouttiff/organization/tiffhistory |archive-date = August 25, 2010 }}</ref>

In 2001, Perspective Canada, the programme that had focused on Canadian films since 1984, was replaced by two programmes:
* Canada First!, a forum for Canadian filmmakers presenting their first feature-length work, featuring eight to 15 films, and
* Short Cuts Canada, which includes 30-40 Canadian [[short film]]s.
As of 2015, Canadian films are now simply included alongside international films in the other film programs rather than being grouped as a dedicated Canadian film stream.[[File:Day12filmfestboxoffice2.jpg|thumb|right|TIFF box office at the [[Manulife Centre]] in 2006]]In 2004, TIFF was featured as the site of murder mystery in the film ''[[Jiminy Glick in Lalawood]]'', a comedy film starring [[Martin Short]].

In 2007, it was announced that the organization generates an estimated annual impact of $67 million CAD.<ref>{{cite press release|work = [[Ontario Ministry of Tourism, Culture and Sport]]|date = September 7, 2007|title = McGuinty government helps promote Toronto International Film Festival|url = http://www.newswire.ca/en/story/47437/mcguinty-government-helps-promote-toronto-international-film-festival|access-date = September 10, 2012|url-status = dead|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130117004200/http://www.newswire.ca/en/story/47437/mcguinty-government-helps-promote-toronto-international-film-festival|archive-date = January 17, 2013|df = mdy-all}}</ref> By 2011, that benefit had grown to $170 million CAD.<ref>{{cite press release |url = http://tiff.net/press/pressreleases/2011/festival-announces |publisher = Toronto International Film Festival |date = August 16, 2011 |title = Festival Announces Boundary-Pushing Visions Titles |access-date = August 25, 2011 |url-status = dead |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110912052928/http://tiff.net/press/pressreleases/2011/festival-announces |archive-date = September 12, 2011 }}</ref>

In 2016, 397 films from 83 countries were screened at 28 screens in downtown Toronto venues, welcoming an estimated 480,000 attendees, over 5,000 of whom were industry professionals.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://assets.contentful.com/22n7d68fswlw/3vWZvCErh6wWsq2kAkgySS/bcccc1803d208be54a3379c6c1cd38ac/Festival_Fact_Sheet_2016_.pdf|title=2016 TORONTO INTERNATIONAL FILM FESTIVAL FACT SHEET|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161024161741/http://assets.contentful.com/22n7d68fswlw/3vWZvCErh6wWsq2kAkgySS/bcccc1803d208be54a3379c6c1cd38ac/Festival_Fact_Sheet_2016_.pdf|archive-date=October 24, 2016|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2017, TIFF reduced the number of films screened compared to [[2016 Toronto International Film Festival|the 2016 festival]]<ref name=TIFF2017sections>{{cite press release |url=http://assets.contentful.com/22n7d68fswlw/1cDGIEz3bwW2UgaasQWkMU/43df2afdeac9cd3a6adce6ae8be201ff/Festival_Programmes_and_Programmers_.pdf |title=TIFF Unveils 2017 Programmes & Programmers |publisher=Toronto International Film Festival |date=February 23, 2017 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170224033910/http://assets.contentful.com/22n7d68fswlw/1cDGIEz3bwW2UgaasQWkMU/43df2afdeac9cd3a6adce6ae8be201ff/Festival_Programmes_and_Programmers_.pdf |archive-date=February 24, 2017 }}</ref> with 255 feature-length films in [[2017 Toronto International Film Festival|2017]], and also eliminated two venues that had been used in prior years.<ref name="TIFF-downscales">{{cite news |url=https://www.thestar.com/entertainment/movies/2017/02/23/tiff-downscales-for-2017.html |author=Victoria Ahearn |agency=The Canadian Press |newspaper=Toronto Star |date=February 23, 2017 |access-date=February 23, 2017 |title=TIFF downscales for 2017 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170224022846/https://www.thestar.com/entertainment/movies/2017/02/23/tiff-downscales-for-2017.html |archive-date=February 24, 2017 }}</ref>

In 2019, it was reported that due to a request from its owner, [[Cineplex Entertainment]], no TIFF films distributed by subscription video-on-demand services (specifically [[Amazon Video]] and [[Netflix]]) are being screened at Scotiabank Theatre—which has been considered the "primary" venue of the festival.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.indiewire.com/2019/09/netflix-amazon-streaming-theater-operators-tiff-1202171757/|title=TIFF Confirms Cineplex Policy Banning Netflix and Amazon From Primary Screening Venue|last=Lindahl|first=Chris|date=September 7, 2019|website=IndieWire|language=en|access-date=September 10, 2019|archive-date=September 21, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190921021325/https://www.indiewire.com/2019/09/netflix-amazon-streaming-theater-operators-tiff-1202171757/|url-status=live}}</ref>

The 2020 edition was both in-person and virtual due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], with the virtual platform provided by [[Shift72]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Toronto International Film Festival Case StudyShift72 vs Vimeo: Comprehensive Video Platform Comparison |url=https://www.shift72.com/resource/toronto-international-film-festival |access-date=July 31, 2023 |website=www.shift72.com |language=en}}</ref> The film screenings were initially declared as "masks optional", a decision that drew criticism for creating a potential [[superspreader]] event as the social nature of the festival could increase the risk for [[COVID-19]] transmission.<ref>{{Cite web|title=As Toronto Film Fest Screenings Go Mask-Optional, Attendees Fear Event Will Be a Coronavirus "Superspreader"|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/as-toronto-film-fest-screenings-go-mask-optional-attendees-fear-event-will-be-a-coronavirus-super-spreader|date=September 8, 2020|access-date=September 9, 2020|website=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|author=Etan Vlessing|archive-date=September 9, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200909005553/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/as-toronto-film-fest-screenings-go-mask-optional-attendees-fear-event-will-be-a-coronavirus-super-spreader|url-status=live}}</ref> The festival reversed the decision within 24 hours, citing a surge of new cases in Ontario, and made masks mandatory at the physical screenings.

The 2020 festival also saw the introduction of Industry Selects, an ''ad hoc'' film market for films seeking commercial distribution. Due to the pandemic, which prevented members of the North American film industry from travelling to international film festivals where many of the Industry Selects films were screened, they were available on the festival's industry platform, but not on the commercial platform for the general public.<ref>Jeremy Kay, [https://www.screendaily.com/news/after-love-saint-narcisse-among-30-sales-titles-to-join-tiff-industry-roster/5152748.article "‘After Love’, ‘Saint-Narcisse’, among 30 sales titles to join TIFF industry roster"]. ''[[Screen Daily]]'', September 1, 2020.</ref> Introduced at the time as a temporary measure due to the pandemic,<ref>Kelly Townsend, [https://playbackonline.ca/2020/09/02/tiff-reveals-titles-for-industry-selects-distinction/ "TIFF reveals titles for Industry Selects distinction"]. ''[[Playback (magazine)|Playback]]'', September 2, 2020.</ref> it was converted into a permanent part of the TIFF program in 2022, and became the nucleus of the festival's plans to launch a full film market in 2026.<ref>Scott Roxborough and Etan Vlessing, [https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/toronto-festival-tiff-film-market-1235900913/ "Toronto Festival to Launch Film Market"]. ''[[The Hollywood Reporter]]'', May 16, 2024.</ref>

===Notable film premieres===
Films such as ''[[American Beauty (1999 film)|American Beauty]]'', ''[[Ray (film)|Ray]]'', ''[[Mr. Nobody (film)|Mr. Nobody]]'', ''[[127 Hours]]'', ''[[Black Swan (film)|Black Swan]]'', ''[[Disobedience (2017 film)|Disobedience]]'', ''[[The Five Obstructions]]'', ''[[Singapore Sling (1990 film)|Singapore Sling]]'', ''[[I Am Love (film)|I Am Love]]'' and ''[[The Fabelmans]]'' have premiered at TIFF. [[Jamie Foxx]]'s portrayal of [[Ray Charles]] ultimately won him the [[Academy Award for Best Actor]] while ''[[Slumdog Millionaire]]'' went on to win eight Oscars at the 2009 Academy Awards. ''[[Precious (film)|Precious]]'', which won the 2009 TIFF People's Choice Award, went on to win two Oscars at the 82nd Academy Awards. ''[[The King's Speech]]'', the winner of the 2010 TIFF People's Choice Award, won four Oscars at the 83rd Academy Awards, while ''[[Silver Linings Playbook]]'', the winner of the 2012 TIFF People's Choice Award, went on to win the [[Academy Award for Best Actress]] for [[Jennifer Lawrence]]. In 2019, the festival opened with ''[[Once Were Brothers: Robbie Robertson and The Band]]'', the first time the festival ever opened with a Canadian documentary film.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/toronto/tiff-2019-opening-night-gala-robbie-robert-once-were-brothers-1.5216122|title=New documentary Once Were Brothers: Robbie Robertson and The Band to open TIFF 2019|date=July 19, 2019|website=CBC News|access-date=August 7, 2019|archive-date=August 8, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190808020716/https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/toronto/tiff-2019-opening-night-gala-robbie-robert-once-were-brothers-1.5216122|url-status=live}}</ref>

Many Hollywood studios premiere their films in Toronto due to TIFF's easy-going non-competitive nature, relatively inexpensive costs (when compared to European festivals), eager film-fluent audiences and convenient timing.<ref>{{cite news

===TIFF Lightbox===
[[File:Lightbox 2010-09-11 II.JPG|thumb|[[TIFF Lightbox]]|left]]
In 2007, the Festival Group began construction on [[TIFF Lightbox]], a new facility at the corner of King and John Streets in downtown Toronto, on land donated by [[Ivan Reitman]] and family. The {{Canadian dollar|181}}{{Nbsp to space}} million facility was sponsored by [[Bell Canada]], with additional support from the [[Government of Ontario]] and [[Government of Canada]].

In 2010, the organization opened its new headquarters at TIFF Lightbox. The facility, designed by local firm [[KPMB Architects]], provides extensive year-round galleries, cinemas, archives and activities for cinephiles.<ref>{{cite news | url = https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/arts/tiff/interviews-and-features/article1702853.ece | location = Toronto | work = [[The Globe and Mail]] | first = Guy | last = Dixon | title = Lightbox aims to draw filmmakers to its facilities - The Globe and Mail | date = September 9, 2010 }}{{Dead link|date=July 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> The five-storey facility contains five cinemas, two gallery spaces, film archives and an extensive reference library, study spaces, film lab facility, and a research centre. There is also a gift shop, two restaurants, a lounge, a cafe, and a three-storey atrium.<ref>{{cite news|title = Let there be lightbox|url = http://www.nowtoronto.com/movies/story.cfm?content=176653|access-date = August 17, 2012|work = NOW|date = September 9–16, 2010|author = Norman Wilner|url-status = live|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130117004724/http://www.nowtoronto.com/movies/story.cfm?content=176653|archive-date = January 17, 2013}}</ref> Cooperatively with Daniels Corporation, there is a 46-storey condominium atop, called the Festival Tower.

The first film screening was [[Bruce McDonald (director)|Bruce McDonald]]'s ''[[Trigger (2010 film)|Trigger]]''. The first exhibition was a retrospective on [[Tim Burton]], organized by the [[Museum of Modern Art]] (New York City). Subsequent exhibitions include Fellini: Spectacular Obsessions, Grace Kelly: From Movie Star to Princess, Designing 007: 50 Years of Bond Style, and [[Stanley Kubrick]]: The Exhibition, all of which were organized by TIFF, as well as one called ''Essential Cinema'', featuring posters, images and props from TIFF's ''The Essential 100'' list of films.<ref>{{cite news|title = No place like home: Toronto film fest opens new HQ|url = http://www.utsandiego.com/news/2010/sep/09/no-place-like-home-toronto-film-fest-opens-new-hq/|access-date = September 16, 2012|work = U-T San Diego News|date = September 9, 2010|first = David|last = Germain|agency = The San Diego Union-Tribune, LLC|url-status = live|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130117004159/http://www.utsandiego.com/news/2010/sep/09/no-place-like-home-toronto-film-fest-opens-new-hq/|archive-date = January 17, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title = A look at the Stanley Kubrick Exhibition TIFF 2014|url = http://blogs.vancouversun.com/2014/11/27/stanley-kubrick-tiff-2014/|access-date = August 3, 2015|work = [[The Vancouver Sun]]|date = November 27, 2014|agency = Canoe Sun Media|archive-date = February 19, 2016|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160219015634/http://blogs.vancouversun.com/2014/11/27/stanley-kubrick-tiff-2014/|url-status = dead}}</ref>

The [[Film Reference Library]] (FRL) is a large Canadian film research collection. The library is a free resource for film lovers, filmmakers, students, scholars, and journalists, and is located on the fourth floor of the TIFF Lightbox. An affiliate member of the [[International Federation of Film Archives|International Federation of Film Archives (FIAF)]], the FRL promotes Canadian and global film scholarship by collecting, preserving, and providing access to a comprehensive collection of film prints, and film-related reference resources (including books, periodicals, scripts, research files, movies, press kits, and about 80 special collections.

In 2016, the festival received a donation of 1,400 film prints, and launched a campaign to raise money for the preservation and storage of the films.<ref>[https://www.pressreader.com/canada/toronto-star/20161116/282033326780443 "TIFF gains cache of 1,400 film prints"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161117065918/https://www.pressreader.com/canada/toronto-star/20161116/282033326780443 |date=November 17, 2016 }}. ''Toronto Star'', November 16, 2016.  Page E2.</ref>

===Canada's Top Ten===
Annually, TIFF releases a [[Canada's Top Ten]] list of the films selected by a poll of festival programmers across Canada as the ten best Canadian feature and short films of the year, regardless of whether or not they were screened at TIFF.<ref name=topten>{{cite web |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/arts/film/tiff-reveals-canadas-top-ten-film-festival-line-up/article27649543/ |title=TIFF reveals Canada's Top Ten Film Festival line-up |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151222182936/http://www.theglobeandmail.com/arts/film/tiff-reveals-canadas-top-ten-film-festival-line-up/article27649543/ |archive-date=December 22, 2015 |website=[[The Globe and Mail]] |date=December 8, 2015 |first=Barry |last=Hertz}}</ref> Formerly announced in December each year, TIFF has shifted in the 2020s to announcing each year's list in early January of the following year.

Previously, the winning films were screened at a smaller follow-up "Canada's Top Ten" festival at the Lightbox the following January, with a People's Choice Award then presented for that mini-festival.<ref name = topten /> In 2018, TIFF announced a change, under which instead of a dedicated festival, each Top Ten film would receive its own standalone theatrical run at the Lightbox throughout the year.<ref>{{cite web |url-status=live |url=https://nowtoronto.com/movies/features/tiff-scraps-canadas-top-ten-film-festival/ |title=TIFF scraps popular Canada's Top Ten Film Festival |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181205003532/https://nowtoronto.com/movies/features/tiff-scraps-canadas-top-ten-film-festival/ |archive-date=December 5, 2018 |website=[[Now (newspaper)|Now]] |date=November 7, 2018 |first=Radheyan |last=Simonpillai}}</ref> The festival has since shifted back to screening the Canada's Top Ten selections as a dedicated screening series in February each year, although it has not reintroduced a People's Choice award for the series. The Canada's Top Ten program does, however, now include a Charles Officer Award, presented in memory of film director [[Charles Officer]] to an emerging Canadian filmmaker; despite being presented at the opening of the Canada's Top Ten screening series, this award does not require the recipient to have had a film included in that program.

Since 1984, every decade TIFF has also produced a [[Top 10 Canadian Films of All Time]] list. This list is produced from a wider poll of film industry professionals and academics throughout Canada, separately from the annual top-ten list.

==Awards==
The festival's major prize, the [[Toronto International Film Festival People's Choice Award|TIFF People's Choice Award]], is given to a feature-length film. It is not a juried prize, but is given to the film with the highest ratings as voted by the TIFF-going populace.<ref>{{cite news

 |archive-date = May 26, 2012
}}</ref> Past sponsors of the award have included [[Cadillac]] and [[Grolsch]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://nationalpost.com/entertainment/lebanese-film-wins-tiff-peoples-choice-award |newspaper=National Post |author=Chris Knight |title=Lebanese film wins TIFF People's Choice Award |date=September 18, 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.tiff.net/the-review/you-pick-the-winner-how-to-vote-for-the-grolsch-peoples-choice-award/ |title=You Pick the Winner: How to Vote for the Grolsch People's Choice Award |year=2016 |publisher=TIFF |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170825042925/https://www.tiff.net/the-review/you-pick-the-winner-how-to-vote-for-the-grolsch-peoples-choice-award/ |archive-date=August 25, 2017 |access-date=August 25, 2017 }}</ref> The winners of this award have often later earned [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nominations.<ref>{{cite web |url-status=live |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/arts/awards-and-festivals/tiff/the-imitation-game-wins-peoples-choice-award-at-tiff/article20593656/ |title='The Imitation Game' wins top prize at TIFF |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161117063326/http://www.theglobeandmail.com/arts/awards-and-festivals/tiff/the-imitation-game-wins-peoples-choice-award-at-tiff/article20593656/ |archive-date=November 17, 2016 |website=[[The Globe and Mail]] |date=September 14, 2014 |first=Nick |last=Patch}}</ref> People's Choice Awards are also presented for [[Toronto International Film Festival People's Choice Award: Documentaries|Documentary]] and [[Toronto International Film Festival People's Choice Award: Midnight Madness|Midnight Madness]] films. Each of the People's Choice Awards names first and second runners-up in addition to the winners.

However, TIFF does present juried awards in some other categories. The festival presents three major awards for Canadian films: [[Toronto International Film Festival Award for Best Canadian Film|Best Canadian Film]], [[Toronto International Film Festival Award for Best Canadian First Feature Film|Best Canadian First Feature Film]], and [[Toronto International Film Festival Award for Best Canadian Short Film|Best Canadian Short Film]], as well as awards for [[Toronto International Film Festival Award for Best International Short Film|Best International Short Film]], two [[FIPRESCI]]-sponsored [[Toronto International Film Festival International Critics' Prizes|International Critics' Prizes]] for the Special Presentation and Discovery programs, and a [[Toronto International Film Festival NETPAC Prize|NETPAC Prize]] for the best film from [[Asia]] having its world premiere at the festival.<ref>{{cite web

In 2015, the festival introduced Platform, a juried programme that champions director's cinema from around the world; one film from the stream is selected as the winner of the [[Platform Prize]].

For all of the juried awards, [[honorable mention]]s may also be given, although the juries are expected to select one overall winner.

In 2019, the festival introduced the [[TIFF Tribute Awards]], a gala ceremony at which distinguished actors and filmmakers are honoured for their lifetime career achievements; unlike most award categories, the Tribute Award honorees are named in advance of the festival.<ref>Michael Rosser, [https://www.screendaily.com/news/anthony-hopkins-chloe-zhao-mira-nair-to-receive-tiff-tribute-awards/5152266.article "Anthony Hopkins, Chloe Zhao, Mira Nair to receive TIFF Tribute awards"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200815144254/https://www.screendaily.com/news/anthony-hopkins-chloe-zhao-mira-nair-to-receive-tiff-tribute-awards/5152266.article |date=August 15, 2020 }}. ==Sections==
The hundreds of films screened at the annual festival are divided into sections (referred to by TIFF as "Programmes") based on genre (e.g. [[documentary]], [[children's film]]s), format (e.g. [[short films]], [[television episode]]s), the status of filmmaker (e.g. "masters", first-time directors), and so forth. Up until the early 2010s there were sections reserved for Canadian films, but beginning in 2015 all Canadian films are integrated in sections with films from outside Canada.

Currently the festival's 14 sections are as follows:<ref name=TIFF2017sections/>
* '''Centrepiece''' (formerly Contemporary World Cinema): [[narrative film|narrative]] feature films by established directors
* '''Discovery''': films that are typically the director's first or second [[feature film]]
* '''Gala Presentations''': high-profile feature films, often featuring international movie stars, presented with a [[red carpet]]
* '''In Conversation With...''': interviews of a director or other figure from the film industry, generally accompanied by brief excerpts from films (up until the [[2014 Toronto International Film Festival|2014 festival]], this section was called "Mavericks")
* '''Masters''': feature films by "the world's most influential [[art-house]] filmmakers"
* '''Midnight Madness''': [[Film genre|genre film]]s (traditionally at TIFF each film in this section has one screening scheduled for 11:59pm and another the following afternoon); the section was launched at TIFF in 1988 and was programmed by Colin Geddes from 1998 to 2016,<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.indiewire.com/2017/02/tiff-programmer-colin-geddes-steps-down-toronto-international-film-festival-1201778911/ |work=IndieWire |title=TIFF Programmer Colin Geddes Departing After 20 Years |author=Graham Winfrey |date=February 7, 2017 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170225210306/http://www.indiewire.com/2017/02/tiff-programmer-colin-geddes-steps-down-toronto-international-film-festival-1201778911/ |archive-date=February 25, 2017 }}</ref> now programmed by [[Peter Kuplowsky]]
* '''Platform''': a competitive section launched in 2015, named for [[Jia Zhangke]]'s film ''[[Platform (2000 film)|Platform]]'', of films from around the world that do not have distribution in North America.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.indiewire.com/2015/07/why-the-toronto-film-festival-is-adding-platform-competition-sidebar-186045/ |title=Why the Toronto Film Festival is Adding 'Platform' Competition Sidebar |date=July 15, 2015 |author=Anne Thompson |website=IndieWire |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170224132235/http://www.indiewire.com/2015/07/why-the-toronto-film-festival-is-adding-platform-competition-sidebar-186045/ |archive-date=February 24, 2017 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |work=The Hollywood Reporter |author=Etan Vlessing |title=Toronto: Natalie Portman's 'Jackie' Biopic, 'Moonlight' From Brad Pitt's Plan B Join Lineup |url=http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/tiff-2016-platform-lineup-natalie-918884 |date=August 11, 2016 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160811230426/http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/tiff-2016-platform-lineup-natalie-918884 |archive-date=August 11, 2016 }}</ref> Every year the Platform section has a high-profile international jury which confers the C$25,000 [[Platform Prize]]; both documentaries and narrative films are eligible for inclusion in the section.
* '''Primetime''': television episodes making either their world premiere or North American premiere projected cinematically; this section was launched in 2015
* '''Short Cuts''': a section of [[short films]] (usually six to ten short films included at each screening) both Canadian and international; up until [[2013 Toronto International Film Festival|the 2013 festival]] only Canadian short films were screened and the section was called Short Cuts Canada, in [[2014 Toronto International Film Festival|2014]] a new section called Short Cuts International was added, and then in 2015 they were merged into a section called Short Cuts
* '''Special Presentations''': high-profile feature films, usually Canadian premieres if not [[premiere|world premieres]]
* '''TIFF Cinematheque''': unlike the other sections which present new films, the TIFF Cinematheque section has films from all eras of cinema, often classic films that have been newly [[film preservation|restored]]
* '''TIFF Docs''' (formerly called '''Reel to Reel'''): [[documentary]] films
* '''TIFF Kids''' and '''TIFF Next Wave''' (formerly called '''Sprockets'''): films for children and teenagers; however, these are not dedicated programs in their own right, but designations added to films of youth interest that are already in one of the other programs. TIFF also organizes smaller, separate TIFF Kids and [[TIFF Next Wave]] festivals in the spring of the year.<ref>Emma Badame, [https://thatshelf.com/the-2023-tiff-next-wave-film-festival-lineup-is-here/ "The 2023 TIFF Next Wave Film Festival lineup is here!"]. ''That Shelf'', March 15, 2023.</ref>
* '''Wavelengths''': [[experimental film]]s and [[art film]]s, both feature-length and shorts (this section was named for [[Michael Snow]]'s film ''[[Wavelength (1967 film)|Wavelength]]'')

In previous years, sections at TIFF have included '''Perspectives Canada''', '''Canada First!''', '''City to City''' ([[2009 Toronto International Film Festival#Controversy over Tel Aviv spotlight|2009]] to 2016), '''Future Projections''', '''Vanguard''' (up to 2016), and '''Visions''' (up to 2011).

==Recognition and media coverage==
According to the [[BBC]], TIFF is one of the largest and most prestigious events of its kind in the world.<ref name="BBCFound">{{cite news |url = https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/entertainment-arts-23681679 |title = Toronto 2013: Why the festival matters |access-date = September 5, 2013 |publisher = [[BBC News]] |date = September 4, 2013 |url-status = live |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130905180541/http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/entertainment-arts-23681679 |archive-date = September 5, 2013 }}</ref> In 1998, ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' acknowledged that TIFF "is second only to [[Cannes Film Festival|Cannes]] in terms of high-profile pics, stars, and market activity". In 2007, ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' noted that TIFF had "grown from its place as the most influential fall film festival to the most influential film festival, period".<ref>{{cite magazine |last        = Keegan
 |first       = Rebecca Winters |title       = Big-Screen Romance |magazine        = [[Time (magazine)|Time]]
 |date        = August 2007 |url         = http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,1657363,00.html/ |access-date  = May 28, 2010 |url-status     = dead |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20101009100129/http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,1657363,00.html |archive-date = October 9, 2010}}</ref>

In 2016, TIFF hosted 1,800 members of the press and print media outlets such as the ''[[Toronto Star]]'', ''[[The Globe and Mail]]'', ''[[The New York Times]]'', ''[[The Times of India]]'', ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'', ''[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]]'', ''[[Miami Herald]]'', and the ''[[Toronto Sun]]'' have published a significant amount of festival coverage.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Dargis|first1=Manohla|title=Toronto Film Festival: Separating Contenders From Pretenders|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/09/19/movies/toronto-film-festivalseparating-contenders-from-pretenders.html?_r=0|access-date=May 15, 2017|work=The New York Times|date=September 18, 2015|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171213143733/https://www.nytimes.com/2015/09/19/movies/toronto-film-festivalseparating-contenders-from-pretenders.html?_r=0|archive-date=December 13, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Kirkland|first1=Bruce|title=TIFF 2015: The most fascinating films that closed the festival|url=http://www.torontosun.com/2015/09/18/tiff-2015-the-most-fascinating-films-that-closed-the-festival|access-date=May 15, 2017|publisher=Toronto Sun|date=September 18, 2015|archive-date=November 27, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201127181951/https://torontosun.com/2015/09/18/tiff-2015-the-most-fascinating-films-that-closed-the-festival|url-status=live}}</ref> Also, the major industry trade magazines ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'', ''[[The Hollywood Reporter]]'' and ''[[Screen International]]'' all produce daily editions during TIFF. TIFF reports also appear in weekly news magazines; American, Canadian and international entertainment shows; news services; and a wide range of film and celebrity blogs.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://cinema-scope.com/tiff-reviews-home-page/ |title=Cinema Scope &#124; TIFF Reviews Index |access-date=December 13, 2017 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171025063250/http://cinema-scope.com/tiff-reviews-home-page/ |archive-date=October 25, 2017 }}</ref>

== Controversies ==
In 2008, [[Rose McGowan]] caused controversy at a TIFF press conference for her film ''[[Fifty Dead Men Walking]]'', when she noted that "I imagine, had I grown up in Belfast, I would 100% have been in the IRA".<ref>{{cite web |author=The Globe and Mail |date=19 September 2008 |title=Director apologises for Rose McGowan's IRA comments |url=https://www.belfasttelegraph.co.uk/entertainment/film-tv/news/director-apologises-for-rose-mcgowans-ira-comments/28449249.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927122848/http://www.belfasttelegraph.co.uk/entertainment/film-tv/news/director-apologises-for-rose-mcgowans-ira-comments-13978481.html |archive-date=September 27, 2011 |access-date=August 25, 2011 |work=[[Belfast Telegraph]] |agency=Phillip Crawley, Publisher}}</ref>

In 2009, TIFF's decision to spotlight films from [[Tel Aviv]] created a controversy with protesters, saying it was part of an attempt to [[Brand Israel|re-brand]] Israel<ref>{{Cite web |last=Levy-Ajzenkopf |first=Andy |date=2008-08-21 |title=Brand Israel set to launch in GTA |url=https://thecjn.ca/news/brand-israel-set-launch-gta/ |access-date=2025-11-09 |website=The Canadian Jewish News |language=en-US}}</ref> in a positive light after the January 2009 [[Gaza War (2008–09)|Gaza War]].<ref name="GlobeAndMailSept82009">{{cite news |last=Posner |first=Michael |date=February 11, 2010 |title=TIFF focus on Tel Aviv draws protests |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/arts/tiff-2009/tiff-focus-on-tel-aviv-draws-protests/article1273755/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100104210148/http://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/arts/tiff-2009/tiff-focus-on-tel-aviv-draws-protests/article1273755/ |archive-date=January 4, 2010 |access-date=August 17, 2012 |work=[[The Globe and Mail]] |location=Toronto}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Klein |first=Naomi |date=October 31, 2009 |title=We don't feel like celebrating with Israel this year |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/opinions/we-dont-feel-like-celebrating-with-israel-this-year/article1278582/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110501184304/http://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/opinions/we-dont-feel-like-celebrating-with-israel-this-year/article1278582/ |archive-date=May 1, 2011 |access-date=August 17, 2012 |work=[[The Globe and Mail]] |location=Toronto}}</ref><ref name="CBCNewsAug282009">{{cite news |date=August 29, 2009 |title=Canadian director protests TIFF Tel Aviv |archive-date=March 13, 2013 |access-date=April 16, 2013 |work=[[World Socialist Web Site]] |publisher=[[International Committee of the Fourth International]]}}</ref>

In August 2025 (a month before the festival), TIFF withdrew the invitation to screen the Israeli documentary ''[[The Road Between Us: The Ultimate Rescue]]'', which depicts rescue efforts by retired Major General [[Noam Tibon]] during the [[October 7 attacks]] in southern Israel. TIFF cited a copyright claim, stating that the filmmakers did not obtain permission to use video footage recorded by Hamas during the attacks and concerns over possible disruptions as the reason for the decision.<ref>[https://ca.news.yahoo.com/tiff-pulls-invite-documentary-oct-013343952.html "TIFF pulls invite for documentary on Oct. 7 rescue"] – Yahoo News, August 13, 2025</ref><ref>[https://www.imdb.com/fr/news/ni65425094/ "TIFF pulls invitation for 'The Road Between Us: The Ultimate Rescue'"] – IMDb News, August 13, 2025</ref> Critics noted that Hamas is designated as a terrorist organization by the Government of Canada,<ref>[https://www.publicsafety.gc.ca/cnt/ntnl-scrt/cntr-trrrsm/lstd-ntts/crrnt-lstd-ntts-en.aspx "Currently listed entities"] – Public Safety Canada. Retrieved August 13, 2025.</ref> and argued that the decision effectively required Israeli filmmakers to seek approval from a group officially recognized as such in order to depict these events,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Welk |first=Brian |date=2025-08-15 |title=TIFF Accepts Oct. 7 Doc ‘The Road Between Us’ After Public ‘Pain and Frustration,’ Cameron Bailey Says |url=https://www.indiewire.com/news/breaking-news/tiff-pulls-invite-documentary-oct-7-the-road-between-us-1235144825/ |access-date=2025-11-09 |website=IndieWire |language=en-US}}</ref> while TIFF noted that it needs to protect itself from any potential copyright issues, and requires all films exhibited at the festival to either show copyright clearances or provide an indemnity to protect the festival from legal liability in the event that a copyright lawsuit is launched over the film's screening.<ref>{{Cite web |last=D'Alessandro |first=Anthony |date=2025-08-13 |title=TIFF Pulls Invite For October 7th Documentary ‘The Road Between Us’; Filmmakers Say Fest Has “Censored Its Own Programming” |url=https://deadline.com/2025/08/tiff-pulls-october-7-documentary-from-lineup-1236484968/ |access-date=2025-11-09 |website=Deadline |language=en-US}}</ref> On August 14, 2025, following public criticism and discussions with the filmmakers, TIFF reversed its decision and reinstated the documentary in the festival's lineup.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ng |first=Curtis |date=2025-08-14 |title=TIFF and filmmaker Barry Avrich reach resolution to screen Oct. 7 doc amid outcry |url=https://www.thestar.com/entertainment/movies/tiff-and-filmmaker-barry-avrich-reach-resolution-to-screen-oct-7-doc-amid-outcry/article_3f3fe018-05dc-54f2-9516-c39680a46f13.html |access-date=2025-08-15 |website=[[Toronto Star]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Loving |first=Casey |date=2025-08-15 |title=TIFF Re-Invites 'The Road Between Us' to Festival After Pulling Oct. 7 Documentary From Lineup |url=https://www.thewrap.com/tiff-reinvites-the-road-between-us/ |access-date=2025-11-09 |website=TheWrap |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=2025-08-14 |title=In Reversal, Toronto Film Festival Will Screen Documentary About Oct. 7 Attack |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/08/14/world/canada/tiff-israel-oct-7-documentary-canceled.html |access-date=2025-11-09 |work=The New York Times |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=D'Alessandro |first=Anthony |date=2025-08-15 |title=TIFF Officially Selects October 7th Documentary ‘The Road Between Us’ Amid Outcry |url=https://deadline.com/2025/08/tiff-the-road-between-us-in-lineup-1236489170/ |access-date=2025-11-09 |website=Deadline |language=en-US}}</ref>
