==Background==
The 1963 murder of Greek politician and physician [[Grigoris Lambrakis]] and subsequent [[Greek junta|military junta]] in power from 1967–1973 served as the basis for the story.<ref>{{cite book |last=Shaw |first=Tony |date=2014 |title=Cinematic Terror: A Global History of Terrorism on Film |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing USA |page=105 |isbn=978-1441158093}}</ref> Among Costa-Gavras' references to the actual events was the frequency with which the military compared ideologies to diseases, seen when the General compares [[-isms]] to mildew.<ref name="Costa">{{cite AV media |last=Costa-Gavras |author-link=Costa-Gavras |date=2002 |title=Z Commentary Track |medium=DVD |publisher=Wellspring Media}}</ref> The opening scene with the speech of the Deputy Minister of Agriculture is based on the real speech of {{ill|Panagiotis Stavropoulos|el|Παναγιώτης Σταυρόπουλος}} held in the {{ill|Ministry of Northern Greece|el|Υπουργείο Βορείου Ελλάδος}} hours before the assassination. The Magistrate was based on real-life Greek [[jurist]] [[Christos Sartzetakis]].<ref>{{cite book |author1=Oliver Boyd Barrett |author2=David Herrera |author3=James A. Baumann |date=2011 |title=Hollywood and the CIA: Cinema, Defense and Subversion |publisher=Taylor & Francis |page=43 |isbn=978-1136806766}}</ref> Costa-Gavras opted to show the Deputy had adulteries and conflicts with his wife to demonstrate he was simply a man.<ref name="Costa"/>

Costa-Gavras was also motivated by the suspicious disappearance of [[Mehdi Ben Barka]] in 1965. Some American viewers infer parallels between the film and the [[assassination of John F. Kennedy]], particularly given how some stylistic elements seem to mimic the [[Zapruder film]]. That said, Costa-Gavras has stated that the Zapruder film had not been widely circulated in Europe at the time and that Kennedy's assassination did not influence the production.<ref name="cine">{{cite journal |title=Costa-Gavras Talks About Z |journal=Cinéasta |volume=3 |issue=3 |pages=12–16 |jstor=43551774 |year=1969 }}</ref>

==Production==
[[File:Theatre Champs Elysees 35.jpg|thumb|267px|Ballet scenes were shot at the [[Théâtre des Champs-Élysées]] in Paris]]

Principal photography took place in [[Algiers]] at actor [[Jacques Perrin]]'s suggestion, which the filmmakers approved for its Mediterranean environment and because the Ministry of Culture was accommodating.<ref name="Costa"/> In Algiers, the [[Hotel St. Georges]] and the central square were filming locations, while [[Paris]]' [[Théâtre des Champs-Élysées]] was used for the ballet scenes.<ref name="Costa"/> [[Marcel Bozzuffi]] performed his own [[stunt]]s wrestling on the "Kamikaze" vehicle due to the production's lack of budget for professional stunt performers.<ref name="Costa"/>

Costa-Gavras chose ''Z'' as the title of the film based on its common occurrence in Greek graffiti for "He lives" (or even "Lambrakis you live; it’s you who guides us!" [Λαμπράκη ζεις, εσύ μας οδηγείς!; ''Lambráki zis, esý mas odigís!'']); Costa-Gavras acknowledged a one-letter film title was unconventional and said [[Yves Montand]] expressed concern it would be confused with ''[[Zorro]]'', but Costa-Gavras said the novelty of the idea won him over.<ref name="Costa"/>

==Soundtrack==
The soundtrack by [[Mikis Theodorakis]] was a hit record. The Greek junta had placed the composer under [[house arrest]] but he was able to give his approval to Costa-Gavras for the use of existing musical pieces.

The film features, but does not credit, [[Pierre Henry]]'s contemporary hit song "[[Psyché Rock]]". The soundtrack as released on [[LP record|LP]] and [[CD]] replaces Henry's song with a similar track written by Theodorakis titled "Café Rock."

# Main Title (Antonis) from the "[[Mauthausen Trilogy]]" of Mikis Theodorakis
# The Smiling Youth 
# The Chase-The Smiling Youth
# Murmur of the Heart
# Cafe Rock
# Arrival of Helen-The Smiling Youth
# Batucada
# The Smiling Youth (Bouzouki Version)
# The Smiling Youth
# Who's Not Talking About Easter
# Finale-The Smiling Youth
# Murmur of the Heart
# In This Town

"The Smiling Youth" and "Who's Not Talking About Easter" were among the poems adapted from [[Brendan Behan]]'s play ''[[The Hostage (play)|The Hostage]]'' by Theodorakis in 1962. By referring to the [[Irish War of Independence|Irish struggle against British rule]] rather than Greek realities, the poems offered a way to circumvent [[censorship]] in Greece and condemn Greece's post-war right-wing establishment. "The Smiling Youth" (το γελαστό παιδί) was also one of the nicknames of Lambrakis.

==Release==
''Z'' was picked up for U.S. distribution by the specialty company/New York City theatre chain [[Cinema 5]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wyatt |first1=Justin |title=Donald Rugoff, Cinema V, and Commercial Strategies of 1960s–1970s Art Cinema |journal=Media Industries |date=2017 |volume=4 |issue=1 |doi=10.3998/mij.15031809.0004.104 |url=https://quod.lib.umich.edu/m/mij/15031809.0004.104/--donald-rugoff-cinema-v-and-commercial-strategies?rgn=main;view=fulltext |access-date=2023-05-10 |publisher=[[Michigan Publishing]] ([[University of Michigan Library]]) |issn=2373-9037|doi-access=free |hdl=2027/spo.15031809.0004.104 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

==Reception==
Prints of the film were acquired by the [[Black Panther Party]] and shown at underground screenings.<ref name="cine" /> An advance copy of the film was shown at the [[United Front Against Fascism]] conference in 1969.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sharpe |first1=Kenan Bezhat |title=Directing the Revolution |url=https://www.jacobinmag.com/2018/11/costa-gavras-z-1968-radical-cinema |website=Jacobin |publisher=Jacobin Magazine |access-date=22 June 2019 |date=8 November 2018}}</ref>

It first aired on American television on [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]] on 18 March 1974.<ref>{{cite news|url = https://www.nytimes.com/1974/03/17/archives/television-this-week-cable-tv-morning-details-received-too-late-for.html|title = Television This Week|date = 17 March 1974|newspaper = [[The New York Times]]|page = 135|accessdate = 29 January 2025|url-access = limited}}</ref>

===Critical response===
At the time of release, ''[[Chicago Sun-Times]]'' film critic [[Roger Ebert]], who named ''Z'' the best film of 1969, liked the screenplay and its message, and wrote: "[''Z''] is a film of our time. It is about how even moral victories are corrupted. It will make you weep and will make you angry. It will tear your guts out...When the Army junta staged its coup in 1967, the right-wing generals and the police chief were cleared of all charges and 'rehabilitated.' Those responsible for unmasking the assassination now became political criminals. These would seem to be completely political events, but the young director Costa-Gavras has told them in a style that is almost unbearably exciting. ''Z'' is at the same time a political cry of rage and a brilliant suspense thriller. It even ends in a chase: Not through the streets but through a maze of facts, alibis and official corruption."<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/z-1969 |last=Ebert |first=Roger |newspaper=The Chicago Sun-Times |title=Z |date=December 30, 1969 |access-date=2011-02-02}}</ref>

In 2006, critic [[James Berardinelli]] wrote: "''Z'' was the third feature film from Greek-born Costa-Gavras, but it is the movie that captured him to the world's attention, winning a Best Foreign Language Film Oscar. It introduced the director's signature approach of combining overt political messages with edge-of-the-seat tension."<ref>{{cite web |title=Z |last=Berardinelli |first=James |url=http://preview.reelviews.net/movies/z/z.html |year=2006 |work=reelviews.com }}</ref> [[Jonathan Richards (author)|Jonathan Richards]] wrote in 2009: "It's hard to overstate the impact that this Oscar-winning [[Procedural drama|procedural thriller]] had in 1969, on a world roiling in political activism, repression, and discord. In the U.S., the [[Vietnam War]] was on the front burner, the populace was passionately engaged, and the police riots outside the [[1968 Democratic National Convention|'68 Chicago Democratic Convention]] and the murder of Black Panther [[Fred Hampton]] were raw wounds. With this stylish, intense indictment of the assassination of a leftist political leader by a right-wing government cabal in his native Greece, director Costa-Gavras struck a nerve that resonated here and around the globe."<ref>{{cite web |last=Richards |first=Jonathan |title=In the Dark |url=http://jonrichardsplace.com/Z.html |year=2009 |access-date=6 May 2014 |archive-date=3 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303215627/http://jonrichardsplace.com/Z.html |url-status=dead }}<!--Rotten Tomatoes indicates that this quote came from film.com, but this hasn't been confirmed.--></ref>

In 2009, [[Armond White]] praised the film and wrote: "Ending with a provocative, unorthodox tally of fascist clampdowns on freedom of expression and the arts, Costa-Gavras angles his exposé with a frightening coda that encapsulates the on-going political struggle. He avoids hippie optimism and foresees contemporary cynicism with a basic thriller device: a warning. ''Z'' carries the reverberations of that cultural shift from enlightenment to paranoia in each of its shrewdly devised tropes from common genres. Costa-Gavras expresses the tension and terror of political conspiracy that haunted the democratic and anti-war movements of the sixties—and still does."<ref>{{cite web |author1=Armond White |title=Z: Sounding the Alarm |url=https://www.criterion.com/current/posts/1275-z-sounding-the-alarm |website=The Criterion Channel |access-date=20 July 2024 |date=October 25, 2009}}</ref>

On [[Rotten Tomatoes]], the film has a 94% "fresh" score based on 51 reviews. The site's consensus states: "Powerfully effective, this [[anti-fascist]] political thriller stands out as both high-conscience [[melodrama]] and high-tempo [[action movie]]."<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/z/ | title=Z (1969) | work=[[Rotten Tomatoes]] | date=8 December 1969 | publisher=[[Flixster]] | access-date=7 January 2021}}</ref> [[Metacritic]], which uses a [[Weighted arithmetic mean|weighted average]], assigned the {{#switch:  | episode = episode | series = series | season = season | film }} a score of 86 out of 100, based on 19 critics, indicating "universal acclaim".<ref name="Metacritic">{{cite web |title=''Z'' |url=https://www.metacritic.com/movie/z-1969 |website=[[Metacritic]] |publisher=[[Fandom (website)#Fandom, Inc.|Fandom, Inc.]] |access-date=31 January 2026 |archive-url= |archive-date= |url-status=}}</ref>

The film was voted in ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'''s list of "The 15 Best Political Films of All Time."<ref>{{cite magazine |author1=Cosgrove|title=The 15 Best Political Films of All Time: The Votes Are In|url=https://entertainment.time.com/2012/09/05/the-15-best-political-films-of-all-time-the-votes-are-in/slide/z/|magazine=TIME|publisher=TIME USA, LLC.|access-date=29 June 2021|date=August 22, 2012|first=Ben}}</ref>

The film was selected to be screened in the Cannes Classics section of the [[2015 Cannes Film Festival]].<ref name="Classics">{{cite web |url=http://www.festival-cannes.com/en/article/61328.html|title=Cannes Classics 2015|access-date=30 April 2015|date=29 April 2015|work=Cannes Film Festival|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518095033/http://www.festival-cannes.com/en/article/61328.html|archive-date=18 May 2015}}</ref>

===Box office===
The film had a total of 3,952,913 admissions in France and was the 4th highest-grossing film of the year.<ref name="JPBox Office">{{cite web|url=http://www.jpbox-office.com/fichfilm.php?id=9023&affich=france|title=Z (1969)- JPBox-Office|publisher=jpbox-office.com}}</ref> It was also very popular in the United States grossing $17.3 million,<ref name=gross/> being one of the top five highest-grossing non-English language films.<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=January 7, 1991|title=Top 60 foreign-language films in the U.S.|page=19|last=Cohn|first=Lawrence}}</ref>

== Awards and nominations ==
''Z'' was the second foreign-language film in [[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences|Academy]] history to receive a nomination for [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]], after ''[[La Grande Illusion|Grand Illusion]]''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://emanuellevy.com/oscar/oscar-history-foreign-language-films-as-best-picture-nominees-1/ |title=Oscar: Foreign Language Films as Best Picture Nominees |last=Levy |first=Emanuel |publisher=Emanuellevy.com |date=25 July 2006 |access-date=13 November 2017 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171113235036/http://emanuellevy.com/oscar/oscar-history-foreign-language-films-as-best-picture-nominees-1/ |archive-date=13 November 2017 |df=dmy-all |author-link=Emanuel Levy}}</ref> At the [[27th Golden Globe Awards]], its producers refused the award to protest the film's exclusion from the [[Best Motion Picture – Drama]] category.<ref name="GlobeRefusal">{{cite web |title=Trivia |url=https://www.goldenglobes.com/trivia-0 |access-date=2 November 2017 |work=Golden Globes website|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151107034345/https://www.goldenglobes.com/trivia-0|archive-date=7 November 2015}}</ref>

== Legacy ==
Filmmakers [[Paul Greengrass]] and [[Aki Kaurismäki]] listed the film in their top 10 films of all time for the 2012 ''[[Sight and Sound]]'' poll<ref>{{cite web |title=Votes for Z (1968) |url=https://www2.bfi.org.uk/films-tv-people/4ce2b6bb7e02a/sightandsoundpoll2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170727110519/http://www.bfi.org.uk/films-tv-people/4ce2b6bb7e02a/sightandsoundpoll2012 |url-status=dead |archive-date=27 July 2017 |access-date=29 June 2021 |website=BFI |publisher=British Film Institute}}</ref> and other films directors such as [[Michael Haneke]], [[Paul Schrader]] and [[John Woo]] have listed it as one of their favorite films.<ref>{{cite web |author1=LaCinetek |title=Z by Costa-Gavras |url=https://www.lacinetek.com/fr-en/film/z-costa-gavras-vod |website=LaCinetek |date=1968 |access-date=20 July 2024}}</ref>

The French filmmaker [[Mathieu Kassovitz]] listed the film as influential to his work.<ref>{{cite book |author1=Higbee|title=Mathieu Kassovitz|date=2006|publisher=Manchester University Press|isbn=9780719071461|page=11|quote=One final and important influence from 1970s French Cinema is Costa-Gavras. A regular visitor to the apartment block where Kassovitz grew up – his son lived in the same building – Costa-Gavras was another of the filmmakers Kassovitz discovered through his parents: ‘Môme, mon père m’a montrè ses films et ce que j’ai fait a ètè influencè par des films comme Z ou L’Aveu. Des films forts, profonds, oû l’on touch à des sujets importants, primordiaux’ (Kassovitz 1998).|first=Will}}</ref> The French filmmaker [[Rachid Bouchareb]] listed ''Z'' as an influence on his film [[Outside the Law (2010 film)|''Outside the Law'']].<ref>{{cite book |author1=Gott|author2=Kealhofer-Kemp|title=ReFocus: The Films of Rachid Bouchareb|date=September 21, 2020|publisher=Edinburgh University Press|isbn=9781474466530|page=107|quote=When Bouchareb was asked specifically about the titles that influenced his controversial film Outside the Law (2010), he said: “It was a mix. A lot of political movies like Z by Costa-Gavras and Gillo Pontecorvo’s The Battle of Algiers.”|first=Michael|first2=Leslie}}</ref>

It is regarded as one of American filmmaker [[Oliver Stone]]'s favorite films that inspired his filmmaking.<ref>{{cite web |author1=Ritman|date=February 17, 2020|title=Oliver Stone to Head Jury of Inaugural Red Sea Film Festival in Saudi Arabia|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-news/oliver-stone-head-jury-red-sea-film-festival-saudi-arabia-1279627/|access-date=29 June 2021|website=Hollywood Reporter|publisher=The Hollywood Reporter, LLC.|quote=Stone will also present a classic film that inspired him, Costa Gavras’ Z.|first=Alex}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author1=Matt Zoller Seitz |title=The Oliver Stone Experience |author2=Ramin Bahrani |author3=Kiese Laymon |date=September 13, 2016 |publisher=ABRAMS |isbn=9781613128145 |page=78}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author1=Lavington|title=Virgin Film: Oliver Stone|date=November 30, 2011|publisher=Ebury Publishing|isbn=9780753547663|quote=One film often referred to by Stone in interviews was Z (Constantin Costa Gavras, 1968) and its influence is immediately apparent.|first=Stephen}}</ref> [[John Milius]] also cited the film as an influence.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Thompson |first=Richard |date=July–August 1976 |title=STOKED |journal=[[Film Comment]] |pages=10–21}}</ref>

The American filmmaker [[Steven Soderbergh]] listed ''Z'' as an inspiration on his film ''[[Traffic (2000 film)|Traffic]]'' and stated that he "wanted to make it like [Costa-Gavras]'s Z".<ref>{{cite book |author1=Soderbergh|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=t2y9xsq0gUMC&dq=Steven+Soderbergh+Costa-Gavras+Z&pg=PA107|title=Steven Soderbergh - Interviews|date=2002|publisher=University Press of Mississippi|isbn=9781578064298|editor1-last=Kaufman|editor1-first=Anthony|page=107|chapter=Ed Kelleher/1998|access-date=12 July 2021|first=Steven}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ho3dBwAAQBAJ&dq=Steven+Soderbergh+Costa-Gavras+Z&pg=PT128 |title=Steven Soderbergh - Interviews, Revised and Updated |date=2015 |publisher=University Press of Mississippi |isbn=9781626745407 |editor1-last=Kaufman |editor1-first=Anthony |access-date=12 July 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8z6ikCJ4wAgC&dq=Steven+Soderbergh+Costa-Gavras+Z&pg=PT190 |title=The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh |date=January 28, 2011 |publisher=University Press of Kentucky |isbn=9780813139890 |editor1-last=Palmer |editor1-first=R. Barton |quote=Soderbergh called Traffic his “$47 million Dogme film” and used hand-held camera, available light, and (ostensibly) improvistational performance in an attempt to present a realistic story about illegal drugs. He prepared by analyzing two political films made in a realist style: Battle of Algiers (Gillo Pontecorvo, 1966) and Z (Constantin Costa-Gavras, 1969), both of which he described as having “that great feeling of things that are caught, instead of staged, which is what we were after.” |access-date=12 July 2021 |editor2-last=Sanders |editor2-first=Steven M.}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author1=Gallagher|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ucfjPQRtZDQC&dq=Steven+Soderbergh+Costa-Gavras+Z&pg=PA55|title=Another Steven Soderbergh Experience - Authorship and Contemporary Hollywood|date=April 4, 2013|publisher=University of Texas Press|isbn=9780292748811|page=55|chapter=Hollywood Authorship and Transhistorical Taste Cultures|access-date=12 July 2021|first=Mark}}</ref>

The American filmmaker [[William Friedkin]] listed ''Z'' as one of his favorite films and mentioned the film's influence on him when directing his film ''[[The French Connection (film)|The French Connection]]'': "After I saw ''Z'', I realized how I could shoot ''The French Connection''. Because he [Costa-Gavras] shot ''Z'' like a [[documentary]]. It was a fiction film but it was made like it was actually happening. Like the camera didn't know what was gonna happen next. And that is an induced technique. It looks like he happened upon the scene and captured what was going on as you do in a documentary. My first films were documentaries too. So I understood what he was doing but I never thought you could do that in a feature at that time until I saw ''Z''."<ref>Archived at [https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211211/p-APzEjrklc Ghostarchive]{{cbignore}} and the [https://web.archive.org/web/20130612082549/http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p-APzEjrklc&gl=US&hl=en Wayback Machine]{{cbignore}}: {{cite web |title=William Friedkin's Favorite Films of all Time |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p-APzEjrklc |access-date=29 June 2021 |website=YouTube | date=12 June 2013 |publisher=Fade In Magazine}}{{cbignore}}</ref> As an homage, Friedkin cast actor [[Marcel Bozzuffi]] in a similar role.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Archives |first=L. A. Times |date=1988-02-04 |title=M. Bozzuffi; Tough Guy in French Films |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-02-04-mn-40280-story.html |access-date=2023-03-04 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}}</ref>

The American actor and filmmaker [[Ben Affleck]] listed the film as an influence for his film [[Argo (2012 film)|''Argo'']].<ref>{{cite web |author1=Vineyard|title=Ben Affleck on Why He Got to Look Hot in Argo|url=https://www.vulture.com/2012/10/ben-affleck-argo-interview.html|website=Vulture|publisher=Vox Media, LLC.|access-date=11 April 2023|date=October 10, 2012|quote=Affleck: "I haven’t done a movie that I haven’t ripped off from another one! [Laughs.] This movie, we ripped off All the President’s Men, for the CIA stuff, a John Cassavetes movie called The Killing of a Chinese Bookie, which we really used as a reference for the California stuff, and then there was kind of a Battle of Algiers, Z/Missing/Costa-Gavras soup of movies, that we used for the rest of it."|first=Jennifer}}</ref>

The movie provided the inspiration for the name of Z Magazine, now [[ZNetwork]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=About Z |url=https://znetwork.org/about-z/ |website=ZNetwork |language=en-US}}</ref>
